In addition to biopsy samples, the urologist can completely remove very small cancer growths during the cystoscopy. However, if a tumor is found, you’ll need to have it removed in an operating room at a clinic or hospital. This procedure is further explained in Chapter Cystoscopy A cystoscopy is an exam to look inside the urethra and bladder for any signs of cancer. If anything looks suspicious, the urologist can use a small tool on the cystoscope to remove tiny tissue samples for testing (biopsy). A flexible cystoscope (upper left) is used for viewing and biopsy. A rigid cystoscope (bottom right) is more invasive, but it can also remove small tumors. In a very similar exam, called a ureteroscopy, the cystoscope goes a little farther to examine the upper parts of the urinary tract—the ureters and inner kidneys. A ureteroscopy is done only if something seems abnormal with the ureters or kidneys. After a cystoscopy After the procedure, you may have one or more of these side effects: Bleeding from your urethra, which can appear bright pink in your urine or on toilet paper A burning sensation during urination Urinating more often for the next day or two If a tissue sample was taken for a biopsy, it will be sent to a lab and tested for cancer. Imaging Imaging means taking detailed pictures (images) of the insides of the body. The images can show the size, location, and other features of cancer. Imaging can reveal where the cancer started and whether the cancer has spread (metastasized). After your scan, your images will be studied by a radiologist. A radiologist is a doctor who’s an expert in interpreting imaging tests. The radiologist will send the results to your doctor or care team. This information helps to plan the next steps of your care. Your doctor or other health care provider will discuss the results with you. Be sure to ask any questions you have. Is blue light cystoscopy better? Cystoscopy commonly uses a white light to see inside the bladder. Some newer cystoscopes now use a blue light. When combined with a special dye injected into the bladder, blue light cystoscopy can identify tumors a little more distinctly than white light. Another technology called narrow-band imaging also helps detect tumors more clearly during cystoscopy but doesn’t require a dye. While both blue light cystoscopy and narrow-band imaging may potentially detect tumors better than standard white light, they’re relatively new and still in the “testing phase.” More research will show whether they can replace or be used with white light as the standard detection method. Types of imaging include x-rays, computed tomography (CT), positron emission tomography (PET), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and ultrasound. CT scan A CT scan takes many x-rays of the same body part from different angles. A computer combines all the x-ray pictures to make a series of cross-sectional images. To look for cancer that has spread beyond the bladder, you may have a CT scan of your abdomen and pelvis. The pelvis is the area of the lower abdomen located between the hip bones; it contains reproductive organs as well as the bladder and rectum. A CT scanner is a large machine that has a tunnel in the middle. During the test, you’ll lie on a table that moves slowly through the tunnel. Pillows or straps may be used to help keep you still during the test. PET/CT scan A PET scan uses a radioactive drug injected into a vein to see where cancer cells are in the body. Cancer cells show up as bright spots on PET scans. When a PET scan is combined with CT, it’s called a PET/CT scan. PET/CT creates detailed images that are useful in certain clinical situations for finding cancer that has spread outside the bladder. A PET/CT scan can be done with one or two machines, depending on the cancer center. MRI MRI uses radio waves and powerful magnets to take pictures of the inside of the body. An MRI is used to get a more detailed view of cancer within the bladder or urinary tract. It’s also used to see if cancer has spread to the liver, nearby lymph nodes, or the bones in your pelvis. Like a CT scanner, an MRI is a large machine with a tunnel in the middle. Unlike CT, MRI doesn’t use radiation (x-rays). An MRI also makes much more noise and takes longer than a CT scan. Tell your team if you get nervous in small spaces. You may be given a sedative (medicine) to help you relax. You’ll need to remain as motionless as possible during each scan. You may be positioned with pillows or bolsters to help you keep still. Imaging To look for cancer that has spread beyond the bladder, you may have an imaging scan of your abdomen and pelvis. Because an MRI uses magnets, you can’t bring any metal objects (such as a cell phone, wristwatch, belt with a metal buckle, or jewelry) into the imaging room. Other types of imaging CT and MRI are commonly used to see how far bladder cancer has spread. Other types of imaging are sometimes used to look for cancer in other parts of the urinary tract or other parts of the body: Urogram uses a contrast solution and either CT or MRI to see how well your entire urinary tract is working. The contrast makes the lining of your kidneys, ureters, and bladder easier to see. You may have a urogram if you’re feeling symptoms such as pain in your side or back, or if you have blood in your urine. Renal ultrasound shows your kidneys, ureters, and bladder in real time. It’s the same technology used to look at a baby in the womb. A renal ultrasound is a painless, non-surgical test that produces black and white images of your kidneys and other organs.

pathologist. The pathologist will compare the cancer cells to normal cells. The more different they look, the higher the grade. And the higher the grade, the faster the cancer is expected to spread. LG means that the cancer cells are low grade (slow growing). HG means that the cancer cells are high grade (fast growing). The inner lining of the bladder is made of urothelial cells. Most cases of bladder cancer start in the urothelial cells. So this type of cancer is called urothelial cancer. But in rare cases, urothelial cell cancer has features that look like other types of cells. These are referred to as subtypes. Some of them include: Glandular subtype Squamous cell subtype Micropapillary subtype Plasmacytoid subtype Sarcomatoid subtype Nested subtype Lymphoepithelioma-like subtype Microcystic and tubular subtype It’s important to investigate whether you have one of these or another subtype. In general, treatment for these uncommon subtypes is similar in the early stages to treatment for typical urothelial cancer. However, some subtypes might grow or advance faster than typical urothelial cell cancer. And faster growth might mean it needs more aggressive treatment. Key points An important thing about bladder cancer is whether it has or it hasn’t grown into the muscle layer. Cancer that has invaded the muscle needs more aggressive treatment. The stage of cancer describes how deep it has grown into the bladder wall and how far it has spread. Cancer stage is used to determine which tests and treatments will help you receive the best outcome. Bladder cancer at stage 0 and stage 1 haven’t invaded the muscle layer. Stage 0 means that abnormal cells have grown on the inside lining of the bladder. Stage 1 means that a tumor has formed and has invaded the layer of connective tissue in the bladder wall. Stages 2, 3, and 4 bladder cancers are muscle-invasive. The tumor has invaded the muscle layer of the bladder wall. In stage 3 bladder cancer, the tumor has grown into the fat layer around the bladder. There may also be cancer in nearby lymph nodes. Stage 4 is metastatic bladder cancer. This is cancer that has spread outside the bladder and to distant sites in the body. Cancer grade is an estimate of how fast the cancer is expected to grow. Low grade bladder cancer is slow growing. High grade cancer grows more quickly. We want your feedback! Our goal is to provide helpful and easy-to-understand information on cancer. Take our survey to let us know what we got right and what we could do better. This chapter explains the different treatment options for bladder cancer. Many people with bladder cancer receive more than one type of treatment. Together, you and your care team will choose a treatment plan that’s right for you. Treatment for bladder cancer is based on many things. This includes the extent, severity, and type of cancer. It also includes your age, your ability to perform daily tasks, your other health issues, and the availability and affordability of drugs. Importantly, treatment is also based on your wishes and preferences. There are several ways to treat bladder cancer. It’s likely that you’ll need a few different types of treatment over months or years. Treatments include: Surgery – The goal of surgery is to take out the tumor and sometimes the surrounding tissue. Surgery procedures range from snipping a single tumor from the bladder lining to removing the entire bladder and other organs. Intravesical therapy – Intravesical therapy involves filling the bladder with a liquid medication that helps destroy cancer cells. Systemic therapy – Systemic therapy is typically an intravenous (IV) treatment that treats cancer anywhere in the whole body. Types of systemic therapy include chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and targeted therapy. Radiation therapy – Radiation therapy is a local therapy, which means it affects a specific area of the body. Sometimes chemotherapy or another therapy is added to radiation therapy to enhance treatment. Clinical trial – Clinical trials are done to test experimental treatments. You may be able to join a clinical trial at any time. Surgery Types of surgery for bladder cancer include tumor removal and bladder removal. Tumor removal For bladder cancer, a surgical procedure called a resection removes the tumor but leaves the rest of the bladder in place. The full name of the procedure is called a transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT, sometimes pronounced tur-bit). Even though it has a complicated name, the concept of TURBT is simple. It’s a procedure that removes tumors through the urethra without having to cut into the abdomen. The tumor can then be tested to provide a more detailed diagnosis. TURBT is done in an operating room in a clinic or hospital. You’ll be given anesthesia to put you to sleep. The urologist then guides an instrument with a small cutting device through the urethra and into the bladder. The instrument is used to examine and remove the tumor from the bladder lining. The goals of TURBT are to: Confirm the initial bladder cancer diagnosis. Take a sample of the bladder wall to see if the tumor has invaded the muscle layer. Remove all the visible tumor. After the procedure, most people can go home the same day. But you’ll need a few days to rest and recover. You may feel pain or burning when you urinate and have blood in your urine for the following 2 weeks or so. Another TURBT procedure may be needed about 2 to 6 weeks after the first one. The second TURBT is done to make sure all the tumor is removed. Or it may be done to get a deeper biopsy sample for the pathologist to examine. A treatment called intravesical therapy is often done in combination with TURBT.

entities.description: A tumor is an abnormal mass of tissue that forms when cells grow and divide uncontrollably, and it may be benign or malignant. Tumors can arise in virtually any part of the body, including the colon, bladder, brain, central nervous system, oral mucosa, prostate, kidney, cervix, lung, pancreas, skin, rectum, and anal area. They are central to cancer diagnosis and treatment planning, and their size (often measured in centimeters or millimeters), depth of invasion, and extent of spread are key components in staging various cancers, such as nasopharyngeal carcinoma, head and neck cancers, cervical cancer, prostate cancer, and anal cancer (using the TNM system). Tumors can be primary (the original site of cancer) or metastatic (spread from another location), and they may invade nearby tissues, block organs (e.g., the bowel), or spread to lymph nodes and other parts of the body. They are detected and characterized through imaging tests (e.g., x-rays, mammograms, PET scans), endoscopy, cystoscopy, and biopsy procedures, and samples may be analyzed for biomarkers (e.g., dMMR). Treatment approaches include surgery (such as TURBT for bladder tumors), radiation therapy, and chemotherapy, which aim to shrink, kill, or remove the tumor. In specific contexts, tumors may present as one or multiple masses (e.g., in primary CNS lymphoma) or as lesions (e.g., squamous cell skin cancer), and their behavior and management depend on the cancer type and stage.

Cervical cancer is a type of cancer that occurs in the cervix, the lower part of the female reproductive system, and is characterized by the uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells in cervical tissues. It is primarily caused by long-term (persistent) infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV), and it is a common cancer of the female reproductive system. The disease can manifest in several histological types, including squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, adenosquamous carcinoma, and small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of the cervix (NECC). Cervical cancer is often detected through screening methods such as Pap smears, and diagnosis is typically confirmed by cervical biopsy. The cancer is staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system, and staging is crucial as it determines treatment options and prognosis. Treatment approaches vary and may include surgery, radiation therapy, systemic therapy (such as chemotherapy), and chemoradiation, with the choice of treatment based on the cancer stage and risk factors such as lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI). Cervical cancer can spread to lymph nodes and, if untreated or not diagnosed early, may recur locally or regionally or spread to distant organs; therefore, surveillance and follow-up care are critical for managing recurrence and metastasis. The disease is closely linked to HPV, and a history of cervical cancer increases the risk of anal cancer, as both share the same viral cause. Consequently, screening for cervical cancer is recommended for patients with anal cancer, and female survivors of anal cancer may also be screened for cervical cancer. Additionally, p16, a biomarker, can be found in cervical cancer tissues.

The bladder is a hollow, muscular organ located in the pelvis that stores urine before it is released from the body. In adults, it has a capacity of up to 2 cups. It is part of the urinary tract and is lined with urothelial cells. The bladder is situated near the prostate in males (which surrounds the urethra just beneath the bladder) and near the cervix in females. It is also adjacent to the seminal vesicles.

The bladder is the primary site where bladder cancer originates. It is examined for signs of cancer or cancer spread using procedures such as cystoscopy and various imaging tests. In the context of cancer treatment, the bladder may be targeted by intravesical chemotherapy (delivered directly into its interior) or radiation therapy aimed at the tumor area. In advanced cases, the bladder may be partially or fully removed via cystectomy, or entirely removed during pelvic exenteration, which then requires urinary diversion.

The bladder can be affected by other cancers: it may be invaded by anal cancer in stage IIIB or IIIC, affected by ovarian cancer spread in Stage 2B, or involved when cervical cancer spreads to nearby organs in stage 4A. Additionally, an enlarged prostate or prostate cancer can impact the bladder. In radiation therapy for cervical cancer, techniques like IMRT aim to reduce radiation exposure to the bladder.

On PET scans, the bladder normally appears bright due to the excretion and accumulation of radiotracer or contrast material; this is a normal finding and not necessarily indicative of cancer. The bladder is also involved in excreting contrast material during imaging studies.

The liver is a large, vital organ located on the right side of the body under the rib cage, playing a central role in the digestive system. It performs numerous critical functions, including filtering blood, detoxifying chemicals and toxins, processing nutrients, producing bile, breaking down fats, helping regulate blood sugar, and synthesizing coagulation factors and other essential proteins. The liver also produces lymph and is the site where primary liver cancers, such as hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and intrahepatic bile duct cancer, can develop.

Given its extensive metabolic and filtration roles, the liver is a common and clinically significant site for distant metastasis from many types of cancer. It is frequently affected by metastatic spread from colon, rectal, anal, breast, bladder, cervical, ovarian, pancreatic, stomach, esophageal, prostate, kidney, thyroid, throat (including nasopharyngeal), and lung cancers, as well as from leukemias (such as CLL and AML) and lymphomas (such as DLBCL). In many of these cancers, liver involvement indicates advanced or stage 4 disease (e.g., stage 4B for cervical and bladder cancers, stage IV for anal cancer) and significantly influences treatment decisions, often requiring systemic therapy or local interventions like stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) or ablative techniques.

The liver's health and function are routinely assessed through blood tests, including liver function tests (LFTs), comprehensive metabolic panels (CMP), and chemistry profiles, which measure enzymes, proteins, and other markers (e.g., ALP). These tests are essential for monitoring potential damage from chemotherapy drugs (such as high-dose methotrexate) and for evaluating the impact of cancers like CLL, which can cause the liver to swell due to cancer cell buildup. Imaging modalities such as CT, MRI, and ultrasound are used to detect metastatic lesions in the liver and to assess its size and condition during physical examinations. Overall, the liver is a crucial organ whose health is integral to overall bodily function and whose involvement in cancer spread is a key factor in staging, prognosis, and therapeutic planning.

Performance status Your care team will want to know how well you can do ordinary day-to-day activities—like taking a walk, climbing stairs, cooking dinner, carrying laundry, or taking a bath or shower. This evaluation is called performance status. The more activities you can do, the better your performance status. Your care team uses this evaluation to get a sense of the level of treatment you may be able to handle and whether you may be eligible for a clinical trial. Imaging Imaging tests take pictures (images) of the insides of your body. The images show areas in the body that might have cancer. The images can reveal a lymphoma’s location, size, and other features. MRI Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the most useful imaging technique for identifying primary CNS lymphoma. An MRI scan is good at showing the spine and soft tissues, including the brain, as well as other details that are helpful for planning surgery. MRI uses radio waves and powerful magnets to take pictures of the inside of the body. During an MRI, you’ll lie on a table that slides into the scanning machine. (An open MRI scanner may be an option at some health care centers.) It’s important to lie still during the test to get the best pictures. The machine makes loud noises but you can wear earplugs. An MRI of the brain or spinal cord usually requires a contrast agent (also called contrast dye or just contrast). Contrast highlights areas in organs, blood vessels, or other tissues to make them easier to see. The contrast is injected into the bloodstream through an intravenous (IV) line before or during the imaging test and later flushed out in urine. The contrast agent used for primary CNS lymphoma is called gadolinium. You’ll have multiple MRI tests throughout diagnosis and treatment. An MRI should be done early on if your symptoms suggest a brain tumor. It’s also used right after treatment to see how well the treatment worked. You’ll have more MRIs during follow-up to watch for any recurrence or new growth. CT If MRI is unavailable or not recommended for you, you might have a computed tomography (CT or CAT) scan instead. A CT scan uses x-rays to take many images of your body from different angles. A computer then combines the pictures to make a 3D image. After imaging After the MRI or CT scan, your images will be studied by a radiologist, an expert in analyzing images of the nervous system. The radiologist will convey the imaging results to your care team. This information helps your team plan what the next steps of your care should be. If your imaging results suggest a primary CNS lymphoma, the next step is a biopsy. MRI of the brain Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the most useful imaging technique for identifying primary CNS lymphoma. It’s important to lie still during the test to get the best images. Straps or other devices may help you avoid moving. Biopsy If imaging scans show something that may be a primary CNS lymphoma, your care providers will want to take a sample and test it. A procedure that removes a small piece of tissue for testing is called a biopsy. Getting a biopsy is the only way to be certain that you have cancer. A biopsy also gives your care team clues on how to treat it. The standard method for diagnosing primary CNS lymphoma is a stereotactic biopsy. It’s the recommended procedure when a brain tumor is in a hard-to-reach or vital area. It aims to remove only enough of the tumor to make a diagnosis. A stereotactic biopsy is done by a neurosurgeon in an operating room. First, you’ll be fitted with a frame or several tiny markers around your head to aid the surgery. Next, you’ll be given anesthesia to go to sleep. A small area of your hair will be shaved down to the scalp. The neurosurgeon will then make a little opening in your skull and insert a thin, hollow needle into the brain to remove a sliver of the tumor. A computerized navigation system, connected to MRI or CT imaging, will allow the surgeon to target and remove the sample with a high degree of precision. After removal, the opening in your scalp will be closed with sutures and you’ll be able to go home. What an MRI shows An MRI scan highlights primary CNS lymphoma in the brain. People with primary CNS lymphoma may have one or multiple tumors appear on their scan. Image: Stephanie E. Weiss, MD, FASTRO The tissue sample will be sent to a laboratory for analysis. A specialist called a pathologist will examine the tissue under a microscope. If the tissue is cancerous, the pathologist will identify the type and grade of the cancer. The testing process will take about a week to complete. If stereotactic biopsy is unavailable at your hospital or medical center, ask to be referred to a

main treatments for a glioma are surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy. These are often combined with one another for more complete treatment. Another option to consider is participating in a clinical trial for a potential new treatment. Treatment may be able to stop the glioma from growing and keep it stabilized for a time. This may last for months or years. However, even with the best treatment, gliomas usually grow back eventually. So periodic follow-up visits and additional rounds of treatment are recommended. It’s true that gliomas are eventually fatal for most patients. Many people diagnosed with a glioma have a difficult road ahead. Still, there’s hope. New therapies designed to treat specific types of gliomas are currently being studied in clinical trials. The number of these trials has increased in recent years, offering more hope to people living with this disease. Also, be aware that survival statistics come from research done several (or many) years ago. Those statistics may not reflect the improvements offered by today’s diagnostic tests and treatments. What’s next? This chapter provided a brief introduction on gliomas. The next chapter explains the tests needed to diagnose and monitor this disease. A message to caregivers and loved ones This book is for you, too. This book will help you understand this disease and the challenges it presents. People with tumors in the central nervous system (the brain and spinal cord) commonly develop problems with brain function. This can show itself in multiple ways, such as slower thinking, memory loss, difficulty moving or walking, trouble speaking, inability to do everyday activities, changes in behavior, losing one’s sense of self, and other problems. Helping a person with a brain tumor can be challenging and time-consuming. You may be providing physical, mental, emotional, and hands-on support. You may be taking the patient to appointments, helping to lessen side effects, and even assisting with treatment decisions. Gather as much help as you can. Start with the online resources listed in the back of this book. Key points h Gliomas develop from brain cells called glial cells. Glial cells support the function of nerve cells in the brain and the spinal cord. Gliomas can disrupt the brain’s ability to function properly. Gliomas can be difficult to treat because they frequently invade and blend into the normal parts of the brain. What causes gliomas is unknown. What is known is that gliomas often start with an abnormality (mutation) that makes glial cells grow out of control. The 3 most common types of glioma tumors are astrocytomas, oligodendrogliomas, and glioblastomas. h Several different tests and procedures are usually needed to diagnose a glioma. Gliomas can be treated but usually return at some point. 66 Don’t Google your diagnosis and assume that statistics define your life! Every person’s brain tumor story and situation is different.” 2 Glioma testing Health and symptom Imaging Biopsy Lab testing Your tumor type What’s next? Key points Different tests are needed to find out whether you have a glioma and what type it is. Testing also suggests what kind of therapy is most appropriate for you. You’ll need a variety of tests to diagnose a brain tumor and to make a treatment plan. (If you’ve already had testing and received a glioma diagnosis, you can turn to Chapter 3 to read about your treatment options.) Testing begins with an examination of your general health and an evaluation of your symptoms. Bring someone with you to listen, ask questions, and write down the answers. Health and symptoms Your care team needs to have all of your health information. They’ll ask you about any health problems and treatments you’ve had. Be prepared to talk about any illness or injury you’ve had and when it happened. Tell your care team about any symptoms you have. Symptoms Each part of the brain has its own job to do. Different parts of the brain manage different parts of the body. Symptoms occur when an area of the brain doesn’t work properly. Symptoms are often related to the location of the tumor in the brain as well as the size of the tumor. Symptoms develop as the glioma grows against, or weaves itself into, a part of the brain. This growth can cause swelling (edema) in the brain tissue around the tumor. Sometimes a tumor blocks the flow of fluid (cerebrospinal fluid) in and around the brain. Some people with low-grade gliomas never have symptoms. Low-grade gliomas generally grow slowly and can develop for years before they’re diagnosed. High-grade gliomas can cause a range of symptoms. These gliomas can grow quickly, developing in months or weeks. However, symptoms can also be caused by medical problems other than tumors. So for the most accurate diagnosis, be sure to tell your provider and care team about any and all symptoms you’re having, even if the symptoms seem unrelated. Common symptoms include: Headaches – Headaches are very common and often the first symptom in people with a glioma. Headaches can be worse in the morning, wake you up in the middle of the night, and occur with nausea and vomiting. Seizures – Seizures are also frequent in people with brain tumors. Seizures are often an early sign of a glioma, especially in low-grade gliomas. Fatigue – Fatigue is another common symptom of a glioma. Fatigue can be debilitating, frequent, emotionally overwhelming, and not related to how much sleep you get or how much activity you do. However, physical activity or exercise can sometimes help. Nausea and vomiting – Nausea and vomiting can be caused by the tumor putting increased pressure on the brain. Problems with thinking and speech – Examples include confusion, memory loss, and speech difficulties. Weakness or problems moving – People with a brain tumor may have muscle weakness on one side of the body, or difficulty with walking or balance. Changes in personality or mood – Changes in behavior

A care team is a multidisciplinary group of healthcare professionals who collaborate to provide comprehensive medical care, diagnosis, treatment, and support for patients, particularly those with cancer or other complex conditions. The team typically includes board-certified medical experts from various fields, such as doctors (e.g., pulmonologists, thoracic radiologists, thoracic surgeons, oncologists, hematologists, hematopathologists, breast specialists, gynecologists, radiologists, dietitians, and therapists), nurses, specialists, technologists, pharmacists, and support staff. They work together to plan and implement treatment, interpret test results (including imaging, CBC measurements, and other diagnostics), discuss treatment options and potential side effects (including effects on fertility), and guide patients through diagnostic and therapeutic processes. The care team is central to patient communication and support, encouraging patients to share information, ask questions, discuss preferences, and make shared decisions about their care. They also provide guidance on preparation for procedures (such as imaging tests and surgery), manage symptoms and side effects, and offer resources for issues like smoking cessation, claustrophobia, and emotional support. The team may specialize in specific conditions, including lung, breast, bladder, pancreatic, thyroid, prostate, glioma, CNS lymphoma, AML, ALL, CLL, NPC, and other cancers, and is responsible for coordinating all aspects of a patient's medical journey, from diagnosis through treatment and recovery.

Chemotherapy is a systemic cancer treatment that uses drugs to kill or slow the growth of cancer cells, particularly fast-dividing cells, throughout the body. It is administered by medical oncologists or oncology nurses, typically intravenously, orally, or topically, and is given in cycles (e.g., 14, 21, or 28 days). Chemotherapy can be used alone or combined with other therapies, including radiation (chemoradiation), surgery, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and immune checkpoint inhibitors (especially when PD-L1 or PD-1/PD-L1 is expressed). It is a standard treatment for many cancers, including AML, ALL, primary CNS lymphoma, gliomas, anal cancer, colon cancer, ovarian cancer, cervical cancer, bladder cancer, prostate cancer, breast cancer, and squamous cell skin cancer, among others. Specific regimens vary by cancer type and may include platinum-based drugs (e.g., cisplatin, carboplatin), taxanes (e.g., paclitaxel), antimetabolites (e.g., 5-FU, capecitabine), mitomycin, oxaliplatin, irinotecan, and anthracyclines. Chemotherapy can be delivered systemically (through the bloodstream), intravenously, orally, intraperitoneally, intravesically, intrathecally, or intraocularly, depending on the cancer and treatment goal. It may be used before surgery (neoadjuvant), after surgery (adjuvant), as primary treatment for metastatic disease, or in high doses during stem cell rescue. Side effects are common and include nausea, vomiting, fatigue, diarrhea, constipation, hair loss, mouth sores, loss of appetite, fever, infection, and low blood cell counts. Chemotherapy can also affect fertility and other bodily functions, so preventive measures and birth control may be recommended during treatment. Smoking during chemotherapy can increase lung problems. Long-term side effects may include other cancers, heart disease, and infertility. Chemotherapy is often a key component of treatment plans and may be recommended based on cancer stage, molecular markers (e.g., PD-L1 expression), and response to other treatments.

A clinical trial is a type of medical research study conducted with human participants to evaluate new treatments, therapies, procedures, or preventive measures—such as drugs, devices, chemopreventive agents, or tests like ctDNA—for diseases, particularly cancer. These studies aim to determine the safety, effectiveness, and potential benefits of investigational approaches, with the goal of advancing medical care and bringing new treatments to individuals. Clinical trials are conducted in phases: Phase 1 assesses safety and side effects, Phase 2 evaluates effectiveness against specific cancers, Phase 3 compares the new treatment to standard therapies, and Phase 4 monitors long-term safety after approval. If a drug, device, or treatment approach is found safe and effective, it may be approved by the U.S. FDA.

Trials are governed by specific protocols and eligibility criteria, which may include factors such as a patient's performance status, as determined by their care team. They are managed by a dedicated research team, and participation requires informed consent. Placebos are rarely used alone in cancer trials. There is no enrollment fee, and the sponsor covers research-related costs; however, standard care costs may be billed to insurance.

Clinical trials are recommended or strongly encouraged for patients with various cancers, including anal cancer (especially metastatic), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL)—where they are the preferred treatment for certain subtypes like BCR::ABL1-negative and BCR::ABL1-like B-ALL—primary CNS lymphoma (recommended for all patients by NCCN experts), metastatic cervical cancer, thyroid cancer (particularly for recurrence or metastatic disease), gliomas, cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), bladder cancer, breast cancer, ovarian cancer (persistent or recurrent), and lung cancer. They offer patients access to experimental therapies, including chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and systemic therapy, and may be an option when standard therapies are not available or appropriate. Participation allows patients to receive investigational treatments while contributing to medical knowledge, though outcomes may vary. Patients are encouraged to ask their care team about clinical trials and may join at any time.

A physical exam is a clinical assessment performed by a healthcare provider to evaluate a patient's overall health, detect signs of disease, and guide medical decisions. It is a routine medical check-up that includes measuring vital signs (such as blood pressure, heart rate, and temperature), checking body measurements (like height and weight), and listening to the lungs and heart. The exam also involves examining the eyes, ears, nose, and throat, as well as palpating (feeling) the abdomen, pelvis, and lymph nodes to assess organ size and detect abnormalities such as enlarged lymph nodes, lumps, or swelling in the spleen or liver.

This examination is used across a wide range of medical contexts, including general health assessments, pre-anesthesia evaluations, and cancer screening or monitoring. It helps identify signs of various conditions, including breast abnormalities, basal cell skin cancer, and cancers such as ALL, AML, CLL, liver cancer, NPC, bladder cancer, and colon cancer. Physical exams are also performed periodically during chemotherapy (every 1 to 3 cycles) to monitor treatment effectiveness and side effects, and are part of short-term follow-up after procedures like total thyroidectomy, alongside blood tests. Additionally, they are included in surveillance schedules for stages 2 and 3 colon cancer to check for recurrence or spread.

The physical exam provides critical information to the care team about a patient's treatment readiness, overall health, and functional abilities, and is used to detect signs of cancer recurrence or other health issues. It is a general health test that may also include assessing the throat and airway, skin, and other body systems to ensure a comprehensive evaluation.

NCCN GUIDELINES FOR PATIENTS are a comprehensive, patient-friendly publication series developed by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN). These guidelines serve as plain-language, evidence-based resources that translate the expert recommendations of the NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology into accessible information for people with cancer, their caregivers, and providers. The guidelines are designed to help patients understand their diagnosis, treatment options, side effects, and supportive care, thereby improving communication with their care teams and enabling shared decision-making.

The resources cover a wide range of cancer types, including anal cancer, rectal cancer, melanoma, squamous cell skin cancer, thyroid cancer, throat cancer, colon cancer, pancreatic cancer, acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), and adolescent and young adult cancers, as well as HPV-related topics. They also address specific care concerns such as fertility preservation, anemia, neutropenia, nausea and vomiting, and immunotherapy side effects. The guidelines are trusted by both patients and providers for clearly explaining current care recommendations made by respected experts, based on the latest research and practices at leading cancer centers.

These guidelines are widely accessible through multiple platforms, including the official website at NCCN.org/patientguidelines and the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app. The content is regularly updated to reflect the most current evidence and practices, and the NCCN encourages user feedback through surveys to continuously improve the guidelines. Overall, NCCN GUIDELINES FOR PATIENTS empower individuals to better understand their cancer care, prepare for discussions with their medical teams, and make informed decisions about their treatment journey.

entities.description:
Prostate cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ. This condition can manifest in two primary forms: early-stage (localized), where the cancer remains confined within the prostate, and advanced-stage (metastatic), where it spreads to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

Chemotherapy is a systemic cancer treatment that uses drugs to kill or slow the growth of cancer cells, particularly fast-dividing cells, throughout the body. It is administered by medical oncologists or oncology nurses, typically intravenously, orally, or topically, and is given in cycles (e.g., 14, 21, or 28 days). Chemotherapy can be used alone or combined with other therapies, including radiation (chemoradiation), surgery, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and immune checkpoint inhibitors (especially when PD-L1 or PD-1/PD-L1 is expressed). It is a standard treatment for many cancers, including AML, ALL, primary CNS lymphoma, gliomas, anal cancer, colon cancer, ovarian cancer, cervical cancer, bladder cancer, prostate cancer, breast cancer, and squamous cell skin cancer, among others. Specific regimens vary by cancer type and may include platinum-based drugs (e.g., cisplatin, carboplatin), taxanes (e.g., paclitaxel), antimetabolites (e.g., 5-FU, capecitabine), mitomycin, oxaliplatin, irinotecan, and anthracyclines. Chemotherapy can be delivered systemically (through the bloodstream), intravenously, orally, intraperitoneally, intravesically, intrathecally, or intraocularly, depending on the cancer and treatment goal. It may be used before surgery (neoadjuvant), after surgery (adjuvant), as primary treatment for metastatic disease, or in high doses during stem cell rescue. Side effects are common and include nausea, vomiting, fatigue, diarrhea, constipation, hair loss, mouth sores, loss of appetite, fever, infection, and low blood cell counts. Chemotherapy can also affect fertility and other bodily functions, so preventive measures and birth control may be recommended during treatment. Smoking during chemotherapy can increase lung problems. Long-term side effects may include other cancers, heart disease, and infertility. Chemotherapy is often a key component of treatment plans and may be recommended based on cancer stage, molecular markers (e.g., PD-L1 expression), and response to other treatments.

Targeted therapy is a form of cancer treatment that uses drugs or other substances to precisely identify and attack specific molecules, genetic mutations, or abnormal proteins involved in the growth, progression, and spread of cancer cells. It is a type of systemic therapy, meaning it travels throughout the body, and is designed to focus on unique or specific features of cancer cells, thereby minimizing damage to normal, healthy cells compared to traditional chemotherapy.

This approach is used across a wide range of cancers, including acute myeloid leukemia (AML), cervical cancer, prostate cancer, bladder cancer, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, squamous cell skin cancer, and breast cancer (such as HER2-positive cases). It is often guided by biomarker testing or specific genetic profiling, such as identifying mutations like PIK3CA, the BCR::ABL protein, or markers like PSMA. Examples of targeted therapy drugs include PARP inhibitors, Gemtuzumab ozogamicin, Gilteritinib, quizartinib, midostaurin, sorafenib, ivosidenib, bevacizumab, mirvetuximab soravtansine-gynx, tisotumab vedotin, and EGFR inhibitors.

Targeted therapy may be used in various scenarios, including for cancers that have returned, metastasized, or are resistant to other treatments, such as radioactive iodine (RAI) therapy for thyroid cancer. It can be administered alone or in combination with other treatments like chemotherapy. While it can be highly effective, it may also have side effects, which can include allergic reactions, fatigue, low platelet counts, body aches, rash, high blood pressure, and abnormal bleeding. Some serious side effects may affect the heart, skin, or digestive system. Additionally, targeted therapy can affect fertility, so it is important for patients to discuss this potential impact with their healthcare provider before starting treatment.

Prostate cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ. This condition can manifest in two primary forms: early-stage (localized), where the cancer remains confined within the prostate, and advanced-stage (metastatic), where it spreads to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

Genetic testing is a medical procedure that analyzes DNA from samples such as blood, saliva, urine, or tumor tissue to identify genetic mutations and abnormalities. It serves two primary purposes: detecting inherited (germline) mutations that increase cancer risk and guiding personalized treatment, prognosis, and preventive measures. In the context of cancer, genetic testing is distinct from tumor mutation testing, which only examines mutations within the tumor itself. For inherited risk assessment, it is often recommended for individuals with a family history of cancer, such as breast, ovarian, prostate, or other hereditary cancer syndromes, and can identify mutations in genes like BRCA1, BRCA2, and BCR::ABL1. In hematologic malignancies like acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), genetic testing looks for changes in leukemia cells—including mutations, deletions, insertions, inversions, amplifications, and translocations—to determine disease aggressiveness and guide treatment decisions. For ovarian cancer, genetic testing is recommended for all patients to assess hereditary risk and inform therapy. In some cases, genetic testing of biopsy samples may help diagnose specific cancers, such as follicular or oncocytic thyroid cancer, by identifying genetic markers. Overall, genetic testing is a versatile tool used across various cancers to identify inherited or somatic mutations, support family history assessment, and tailor prevention and treatment strategies.

Genetic testing is a medical procedure that analyzes DNA from samples such as blood, saliva, urine, or tumor tissue to identify genetic mutations and abnormalities. It serves two primary purposes: detecting inherited (germline) mutations that increase cancer risk and guiding personalized treatment, prognosis, and preventive measures. In the context of cancer, genetic testing is distinct from tumor mutation testing, which only examines mutations within the tumor itself. For inherited risk assessment, it is often recommended for individuals with a family history of cancer, such as breast, ovarian, prostate, or other hereditary cancer syndromes, and can identify mutations in genes like BRCA1, BRCA2, and BCR::ABL1. In hematologic malignancies like acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), genetic testing looks for changes in leukemia cells—including mutations, deletions, insertions, inversions, amplifications, and translocations—to determine disease aggressiveness and guide treatment decisions. For ovarian cancer, genetic testing is recommended for all patients to assess hereditary risk and inform therapy. In some cases, genetic testing of biopsy samples may help diagnose specific cancers, such as follicular or oncocytic thyroid cancer, by identifying genetic markers. Overall, genetic testing is a versatile tool used across various cancers to identify inherited or somatic mutations, support family history assessment, and tailor prevention and treatment strategies.

Targeted therapy is a form of cancer treatment that uses drugs or other substances to precisely identify and attack specific molecules, genetic mutations, or abnormal proteins involved in the growth, progression, and spread of cancer cells. It is a type of systemic therapy, meaning it travels throughout the body, and is designed to focus on unique or specific features of cancer cells, thereby minimizing damage to normal, healthy cells compared to traditional chemotherapy.

This approach is used across a wide range of cancers, including acute myeloid leukemia (AML), cervical cancer, prostate cancer, bladder cancer, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, squamous cell skin cancer, and breast cancer (such as HER2-positive cases). It is often guided by biomarker testing or specific genetic profiling, such as identifying mutations like PIK3CA, the BCR::ABL protein, or markers like PSMA. Examples of targeted therapy drugs include PARP inhibitors, Gemtuzumab ozogamicin, Gilteritinib, quizartinib, midostaurin, sorafenib, ivosidenib, bevacizumab, mirvetuximab soravtansine-gynx, tisotumab vedotin, and EGFR inhibitors.

Targeted therapy may be used in various scenarios, including for cancers that have returned, metastasized, or are resistant to other treatments, such as radioactive iodine (RAI) therapy for thyroid cancer. It can be administered alone or in combination with other treatments like chemotherapy. While it can be highly effective, it may also have side effects, which can include allergic reactions, fatigue, low platelet counts, body aches, rash, high blood pressure, and abnormal bleeding. Some serious side effects may affect the heart, skin, or digestive system. Additionally, targeted therapy can affect fertility, so it is important for patients to discuss this potential impact with their healthcare provider before starting treatment.

Cancer cells are abnormal cells that develop genetic mutations, allowing them to grow and divide uncontrollably, avoid normal cell death, and invade surrounding tissues. They can spread to other parts of the body through the blood or lymphatic system, forming new tumors and indicating metastasis. These cells differ from normal cells in behavior and can crowd out healthy cells, leading to damage and symptoms.

Cancer cells can be detected through various diagnostic methods, including biopsy samples, blood tests (such as ctDNA testing), urine cytology, and imaging techniques like PET scans, where they appear as bright spots due to their high uptake of radioactive sugar-based tracers. In specific contexts, such as prostate cancer, they may be targeted by tracers in PET and PSMA/PET imaging, and in cases of HPV presence, they show increased p16 expression, aiding in diagnosis.

These abnormal cells are central to many cancer types, including bladder, prostate, breast, ovarian, anal, and primary CNS lymphoma, where they can be found in the cerebrospinal fluid, brain, or eyes. They may block lymph vessels in the breast, leading to inflammatory breast cancer symptoms, or be filtered out by lymph nodes, as seen in Hodgkin lymphoma. Cancer cells can express proteins like PD-1/PD-L1 or have mutations that guide treatment decisions.

Treatment approaches targeting cancer cells include chemotherapy, high-dose chemotherapy, intravesical therapy, systemic therapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, and radiation therapy, all aimed at killing or inhibiting these harmful cells. In biopsy samples, patterns of cancer cells, such as Gleason patterns in prostate cancer, are analyzed to determine aggressiveness and risk of spread to lymph nodes or other body parts.

Treatment options Treatment options are often described in the following ways: Preferred therapies have the most evidence they work better and may be safer than other therapies. Other recommended therapies may not work quite as well as preferred therapies, but they can still help treat cancer. Therapies used in certain cases work best for people with specific cancer features or health circumstances. Chemotherapy Chemotherapy is the standard of care for treating AML. Chemotherapy kills fast-dividing cells throughout the body, including cancer cells and normal cells. Standard of care is the best-known way to treat a particular disease based on past clinical trials. There may be more than one treatment regimen that is considered standard of care. Ask your care team what treatment options are available and if a clinical trial might be right for you. Chemotherapy is most often a liquid that is slowly injected into a vein with a needle. The final dose differs between people because it is based on body weight. In most cases, chemotherapy is given in cycles of treatment days followed by days of rest. This allows the body to recover before the next cycle. Cycles vary in length depending on which chemotherapy is used. You might spend time in the hospital during treatment. Types of chemotherapy There are many types of chemotherapy used to treat AML. Often chemotherapies are combined. This is called multi-agent chemotherapy or a multi-agent regimen. Each chemotherapy works in a different way and causes different side effects. Talk to your care team about the types of chemotherapy you will be given, when you will get them, and what side effects to expect. Antimetabolites Antimetabolites prevent the building blocks of DNA from being used. Examples include: Cladribine (Mavenclad) Clofarabine (Clolar) Cytarabine (Ara-C) Fludarabine Methotrexate Anthracyclines Anthracyclines damage and disrupt the making of DNA causing cell death of both cancerous and non-cancerous cells. Some anthracyclines can cause heart issues. They may not be an option for you. There is a limit to how much you can receive in your lifetime. Anthracycline examples include daunorubicin, idarubicin (Idamycin PFS), and mitoxantrone (Novantrone). Dual-drug liposome of cytarabine and daunorubicin (CPX-351 or Vyxeos) includes an antimetabolite and an anthracycline. Cytarabine Cytarabine is an anthracycline. Cytarabine (also called Ara-C) is used in many treatment regimens. It might be used alone or in combination with other drugs. It might be given as a single dose to reduce a very high white blood cell count. There are different doses for cytarabine (Ara-C): Standard High (HiDAC) Intermediate Low (LDAC) The dose you will receive is based on many factors. Ask your care team for the details of your treatment. What is the dose? How often is treatment received? How many treatment cycles are needed? Will I need to spend time in the hospital? If so, for how long? Cytarabine or methotrexate may be used to treat AML in the fluid that surrounds the spine or brain. In this case, it is injected into the spinal fluid. This is called intrathecal chemotherapy. Hypomethylating agents Methyl groups are molecules found in DNA. Leukemia cells often have too many methyl groups. These extra groups can block genes from being turned on and off. Hypomethylating agents (HMAs) block methyl groups from binding to DNA. They turn silenced genes back on, which allows leukemic blasts to mature into normal cells. Azacitidine (Vidaza) and decitabine (Dacogen) are HMAs. Targeted therapies seek out how cancer cells grow, divide, and move in the body. These drugs stop the action of molecules that help cancer cells grow and/or survive. It attaches to a cell surface protein called CD33, then enters the cell. Once inside, chemotherapy is released. Many leukemic blasts have CD33 proteins. Mismatch repair testing Mismatch repair (MMR) or microsatellite instability (MSI) testing is recommended for everyone diagnosed with colon cancer. This feature of some colon cancers is a type of biomarker. Biomarkers are targetable changes of a cancer that help guide your treatment. Testing involves analyzing a piece of the colon tumor in a lab. Depending on the method used, an abnormal result is called either microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) or mismatch repair deficient (dMMR). Tumors that do not have these changes are referred to as microsatellite stable (MSS) or mismatch repair proficient (pMMR). Those with a first-degree relative with colorectal cancer are more likely to have this cancer compared to the average person. Most colon cancers occur for unknown reasons. Two such conditions include Lynch syndrome and familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP). People born with Lynch syndrome are at high risk of developing colon, endometrial, and ovarian cancers. entities.description: A care team is a multidisciplinary group of healthcare professionals who collaborate to provide comprehensive medical care, diagnosis, treatment, and support for patients, particularly those with cancer or other complex conditions. The team typically includes board-certified medical experts from various fields, such as doctors (e.g., pulmonologists, thoracic radiologists, thoracic surgeons, oncologists, hematologists, hematopathologists, breast specialists, gynecologists, radiologists, dietitians, and therapists), nurses, specialists, technologists, pharmacists, and support staff. They work together to plan and implement treatment, interpret test results (including imaging, CBC measurements, and other diagnostics), discuss treatment options and potential side effects (including effects on fertility), and guide patients through diagnostic and therapeutic processes. The care team is central to patient communication and support, encouraging patients to share information, ask questions, discuss preferences, and make shared decisions about their care. They also provide guidance on preparation for procedures (such as imaging tests and surgery), manage symptoms and side effects, and offer resources for issues like smoking cessation, claustrophobia, and emotional support. The team may specialize in specific conditions, including lung, breast, bladder, pancreatic, thyroid, prostate, glioma, CNS lymphoma, AML, ALL, CLL, NPC, and other cancers, and is responsible for coordinating all aspects of a patient's medical journey, from diagnosis through treatment and recovery.

It is primarily caused by long-term (persistent) infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV), and it is a common cancer of the female reproductive system. The disease can manifest in several histological types, including squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, adenosquamous carcinoma, and small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of the cervix (NECC). Cervical cancer is often detected through screening methods such as Pap smears, and diagnosis is typically confirmed by cervical biopsy. The cancer is staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system, and staging is crucial as it determines treatment options and prognosis. Treatment approaches vary and may include surgery, radiation therapy, systemic therapy (such as chemotherapy), and chemoradiation, with the choice of treatment based on the cancer stage and risk factors such as lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI). Cervical cancer can spread to lymph nodes and, if untreated or not diagnosed early, may recur locally or regionally or spread to distant organs; therefore, surveillance and follow-up care are critical for managing recurrence and metastasis. The disease is closely linked to HPV, and a history of cervical cancer increases the risk of anal cancer, as both share the same viral cause. Consequently, screening for cervical cancer is recommended for patients with anal cancer, and female survivors of anal cancer may also be screened for cervical cancer. Additionally, p16, a biomarker, can be found in cervical cancer tissues.

Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is a type of cancer that arises from squamous cells, which are thin, flat cells lining the surface of the skin, mucous membranes, and various internal organs. This cancer can develop in multiple locations throughout the body, and its characteristics, prevalence, and treatment approaches vary depending on the site of origin.

In the context of cervical cancer, squamous cell carcinoma is the most common type, originating from the squamous cells lining the ectocervix (the outer part of the cervix). Treatment decisions for cervical SCC are based on the cancer stage and tumor grade, among other factors. Ovarian transposition (surgically moving the ovaries out of the radiation field) may be considered as an option for some patients with this type of cervical cancer.

Squamous cell carcinoma is also the most common type of anal cancer, starting in the squamous cells found in the skin and other tissues of the anal region. Diagnosis is typically made via biopsy, and the disease can range from early stages (such as squamous intraepithelial lesions, including SISCCA) to more advanced stages. Additionally, SCC is the most common type of throat cancer and head and neck cancer, often caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, and it forms in the thin, flat cells of mucous membranes. It is also the specific type of nasopharyngeal cancer for which TNM staging information is provided.

In the lungs, squamous cell carcinoma is a subtype of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) that starts in the flat cells lining the bronchi (airways). It accounts for approximately 3 out of 10 lung cancers. In the bladder, SCC is a non-urothelial type of bladder cancer, which is less common than urothelial carcinoma and is considered rare.

Overall, squamous cell carcinoma is a versatile cancer type that can affect various organs, with its management and prognosis depending on the specific location, stage, and individual patient factors.

Symptoms are physical or mental signs of illness or injury that patients may experience and should report to their care team or doctor. They are feelings, problems, or functional changes that can indicate the presence of a disease or condition, and they play a key role in guiding diagnosis, treatment decisions, and monitoring. Symptoms may be specific to certain cancers or conditions—for example, breast issues may present as a lump, pain, nipple thickening or discharge, or changes in breast shape or size; bladder cancer may involve blood in urine; prostate cancer can cause urinary issues, bone pain, or blood in urine, especially in advanced stages; and primary CNS lymphoma or gliomas may cause headaches, nausea, vomiting, seizures, changes in eyesight, or muscle weakness due to pressure on the brain. Side effects are unwanted or adverse physical and emotional conditions that can result from cancer treatment, including treatments for acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), primary CNS lymphoma, and bladder cancer. These effects can be short-term or long-term, and may range from mild discomfort to severe or life-altering conditions. Common side effects include pain, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, hair loss, mouth sores, loss of appetite, skin irritation or rash, problems swallowing, dry mouth, thick saliva, changes in taste, soreness, urinary issues, infections, vision problems, bleeding, bruising, nerve damage, and low blood cell counts. Side effects from radiation therapy to the neck may include skin rash, swallowing difficulties, dry mouth, thick saliva, taste changes, and tiredness. Systemic therapies can cause tiredness, nausea, organ damage, and long-term risks such as other cancers or heart disease. Some side effects may appear years after treatment.

These adverse effects are typically managed by the patient’s care team, which may include oncology nurses, pharmacists, and other specialists, through a shared effort between the patient and healthcare providers. Patients are encouraged to discuss side effects with their care team to prevent or manage them effectively. In some cases, side effects may be severe enough to require stopping maintenance therapy if they become too harsh or unsafe. Certain behaviors, such as smoking or vaping, can worsen side effects during and after treatment, including after surgery. Supportive care is often used to manage symptoms like nausea, fatigue, and hair loss. Overall, side effects are a significant aspect of cancer treatment that require careful monitoring, communication, and coordinated management to ensure patient well-being.

Recurrence, also known as relapse, refers to the return of cancer after a period of treatment or remission. This phenomenon is common across various cancer types, including bladder, breast, cervical, ovarian, prostate, basal cell skin, primary CNS lymphoma, and head and neck cancers. Recurrence can manifest locally (at the original site), regionally (in nearby lymph nodes), or at distant sites in the body, depending on the cancer type.

For bladder cancer, recurrence is a frequent occurrence that necessitates ongoing monitoring and regular follow-up testing. In breast cancer, recurrence may be local or distant. Cervical cancer recurrence can occur locally, regionally, or at distant sites, and often requires imaging, exploratory surgery, and biomarker testing to guide further treatment. Ovarian cancer recurrence also demands further management and monitoring. Prostate cancer recurrence can be detected through imaging tests such as MRI or PSMA-PET scans, and is a key factor in risk assessment. Basal cell skin cancer recurrence involves the cancer returning to the original area or spreading to lymph nodes or distant parts of the body, indicating a need for continued surveillance.

Monitoring for recurrence typically involves imaging tests like MRI, PSMA-PET, and other surveillance methods, including regular physical exams and blood tests. In some cases, such as higher-risk thyroid cancer, TSH suppression is used as a monitoring strategy. Symptoms of recurrence can vary but may include pelvic pain, bloating, and fatigue, particularly in gynecologic cancers.

Treatment for recurrence depends on the location and extent of the disease and may involve additional therapies such as surgery, radiation therapy, radioactive iodine (RAI), or adjustments to chemotherapy regimens. Biomarker testing is often employed to guide treatment decisions. Certain cancer subtypes and features can increase the risk of recurrence, and radiation therapy may be used in high-risk patients to prevent it. Overall, recurrence requires vigilant follow-up and individualized management to address the return of disease effectively.

Radiation therapy is a cancer treatment modality that uses high-energy radiation—such as x-rays, gamma rays, electrons, photons, or protons—to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. It is planned and prescribed by a radiation oncologist and delivered by radiation therapists or other specialists. This treatment is often used as a local therapy to target specific areas of the body, and it may be combined with chemotherapy (chemoradiation), surgery, or systemic therapies, depending on the cancer type and stage.

Radiation therapy is applicable to a wide range of cancers, including anal, bladder, brain (e.g., gliomas and primary CNS lymphoma), breast, cervical, prostate, rectal, skin (basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma), thyroid, and perianal cancers, as well as chordoma and metastatic anal cancer. It can be used as a primary treatment, an adjunct after surgery to eliminate remaining cancer cells, or as palliative care to relieve pain. Techniques include external beam radiation therapy (EBRT), intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT), stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT), whole-brain radiation therapy (WBRT), and brachytherapy (internal radioactive material).

Treatment is typically given over several weeks, with common schedules of five sessions per week, each session lasting 30 to 60 minutes. While effective, radiation therapy can cause side effects, which may appear during treatment or years later. These include skin rash, problems swallowing, dry mouth, thick saliva, changes in taste, tiredness, headaches, nausea, vision problems, cataracts, and long-term cognitive issues. Radiation to the head and neck can affect endocrine glands, hearing, and other functions, requiring pre- and post-treatment monitoring. Additionally, radiation therapy can impact fertility—for example, in rectal cancer it may damage ovarian and testicular function—and prior exposure to radiation, especially at a young age (e.g., to the chest), is a risk factor for certain cancers, such as basal cell skin cancer and small cell lung cancer.

For some cancers, radiation therapy is a preferred or standard treatment option. For instance, IMRT is often preferred for anal cancer, and radiation is a main treatment for gliomas and primary CNS lymphoma. In prostate cancer, it may be used in both early and advanced stages, though it may be avoided or delayed for lower-risk patients. On the day you begin taking capecitabine, a single intravenous dose of mitomycin will be given. Another dose of mitomycin is usually given at the start of week Mitomycin and 5-FU is another regimen recommended for use with radiation therapy. 5-FU is given by continuous (constant) infusion over several days. Create a medical binder A medical binder or notebook is a great way to organize all of your records in one place. Make copies of blood tests, imaging results, and reports about your specific type of cancer. It will be helpful when getting a second opinion. Choose a binder that meets your needs. Use online patient portals to view your test results and other records. Download or print the records to add to your binder. Add a section for questions and to take notes. Bring your medical binder to appointments. You never know when you might need it! Imaging tests Imaging tests take pictures of the inside of your body. Imaging tests show the primary tumor, or where the cancer started, and look for cancer in other parts of the body. A radiologist, an expert in interpreting imaging tests, will write a report and send this report to your health care provider (HCP). It is likely that the report will be sent directly to you through your patient portal or patient access system. You should discuss these results with your HCP. You will not have all of the following tests. Contrast material Contrast material is used to improve the pictures of the inside of the body. Contrast materials are not dyes, but substances that help enhance and improve the images of several organs and structures in the body. It is used to make the pictures clearer. The contrast is not permanent and will leave your body in your urine immediately after the test. The types of contrast vary and are different for CT and MRI. Tell your care team if you have had allergic reactions to contrast in the past. This is important. You might be given medicines to avoid the effects of those allergies. Contrast might not be used if you have a serious allergy or if your kidneys aren’t working well. CT scan A computed tomography (CT or CAT) scan uses x-rays and computer technology to take pictures of the inside of the body. It takes many x-rays of the same body part from different angles. All the images are combined to make one detailed picture. A CT scan of your head, neck, and chest, may be one of the tests to look for cancer. In most cases, contrast will be used. MRI scan A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan uses radio waves and powerful magnets to take pictures of the inside of the body. It does not use x-rays. Because of the very strong magnets used in the MRI machine, tell the technologist if you have any metal in your body. During the test, you will likely be asked to hold your breath for 10 to 20 seconds as the technician collects the images. Contrast is often used. A closed MRI has a capsule-like design where the magnet surrounds you. An open MRI has a magnetic top and bottom, which allows for an opening on each end. Closed MRIs are more common than open MRIs, so if you have claustrophobia (a dread or fear of enclosed spaces), be sure to talk to your care team about it. A tracer is a substance injected into a vein to see where cancer cells are in the body and if they are using sugar produced by your body to grow. Cancer cells show up as bright spots on PET scans. However, not all tumors will appear on a PET scan. Also, not all bright spots are cancer. This is similar to the sonogram used for pregnancy. A wand-like probe (transducer) will be held and moved on your neck using gel. Ultrasound is painless and does not use x-rays, so it can be repeated as needed. Ultrasound is good at showing small areas of cancer that are near the skin. Sometimes, an ultrasound or CT is used to guide a biopsy. It is commonly performed by dentists and oral surgeons in everyday practice and may be used to plan treatment for dentures, braces, extractions, and implants. Smoking and vaping can limit how well cancer treatment works and prevent wound healing. They also greatly increase your chances of having side effects

Chemotherapy is a systemic cancer treatment that uses drugs to kill or slow the growth of cancer cells, particularly fast-dividing cells, throughout the body. It is administered by medical oncologists or oncology nurses, typically intravenously, orally, or topically, and is given in cycles (e.g., 14, 21, or 28 days). Chemotherapy can be used alone or combined with other therapies, including radiation (chemoradiation), surgery, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and immune checkpoint inhibitors (especially when PD-L1 or PD-1/PD-L1 is expressed). It is a standard treatment for many cancers, including AML, ALL, primary CNS lymphoma, gliomas, anal cancer, colon cancer, ovarian cancer, cervical cancer, bladder cancer, prostate cancer, breast cancer, and squamous cell skin cancer, among others. Specific regimens vary by cancer type and may include platinum-based drugs (e.g., cisplatin, carboplatin), taxanes (e.g., paclitaxel), antimetabolites (e.g., 5-FU, capecitabine), mitomycin, oxaliplatin, irinotecan, and anthracyclines. Chemotherapy can be delivered systemically (through the bloodstream), intravenously, orally, intraperitoneally, intravesically, intrathecally, or intraocularly, depending on the cancer and treatment goal. It may be used before surgery (neoadjuvant), after surgery (adjuvant), as primary treatment for metastatic disease, or in high doses during stem cell rescue. Side effects are common and include nausea, vomiting, fatigue, diarrhea, constipation, hair loss, mouth sores, loss of appetite, fever, infection, and low blood cell counts. Chemotherapy can also affect fertility and other bodily functions, so preventive measures and birth control may be recommended during treatment. Smoking during chemotherapy can increase lung problems. Long-term side effects may include other cancers, heart disease, and infertility. Chemotherapy is often a key component of treatment plans and may be recommended based on cancer stage, molecular markers (e.g., PD-L1 expression), and response to other treatments.

Radiation therapy is a cancer treatment modality that uses high-energy radiation—such as x-rays, gamma rays, electrons, photons, or protons—to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. It is planned and prescribed by a radiation oncologist and delivered by radiation therapists or other specialists. This treatment is often used as a local therapy to target specific areas of the body, and it may be combined with chemotherapy (chemoradiation), surgery, or systemic therapies, depending on the cancer type and stage.

Radiation therapy is applicable to a wide range of cancers, including anal, bladder, brain (e.g., gliomas and primary CNS lymphoma), breast, cervical, prostate, rectal, skin (basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma), thyroid, and perianal cancers, as well as chordoma and metastatic anal cancer. It can be used as a primary treatment, an adjunct after surgery to eliminate remaining cancer cells, or as palliative care to relieve pain. Techniques include external beam radiation therapy (EBRT), intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT), stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT), whole-brain radiation therapy (WBRT), and brachytherapy (internal radioactive material).

Treatment is typically given over several weeks, with common schedules of five sessions per week, each session lasting 30 to 60 minutes. While effective, radiation therapy can cause side effects, which may appear during treatment or years later. These include skin rash, problems swallowing, dry mouth, thick saliva, changes in taste, tiredness, headaches, nausea, vision problems, cataracts, and long-term cognitive issues. Radiation to the head and neck can affect endocrine glands, hearing, and other functions, requiring pre- and post-treatment monitoring. Additionally, radiation therapy can impact fertility—for example, in rectal cancer it may damage ovarian and testicular function—and prior exposure to radiation, especially at a young age (e.g., to the chest), is a risk factor for certain cancers, such as basal cell skin cancer and small cell lung cancer.

For some cancers, radiation therapy is a preferred or standard treatment option. For instance, IMRT is often preferred for anal cancer, and radiation is a main treatment for gliomas and primary CNS lymphoma. In prostate cancer, it may be used in both early and advanced stages, though it may be avoided or delayed for lower-risk patients. For skin cancers like squamous cell carcinoma, radiation is used when surgery is not possible or as an adjunct to reduce recurrence
