CT scan, also known as Computed Tomography scan, is a diagnostic imaging technique that uses X-rays and computer technology to create detailed, cross-sectional, and often three-dimensional (3D) images of the inside of the body. The procedure involves taking multiple X-ray images from different angles, which are then combined by a computer to produce comprehensive pictures. CT scans are frequently performed with the use of contrast material to enhance image clarity and are typically completed in under 30 minutes.

This imaging modality serves a wide range of medical purposes. It is commonly used as an alternative to MRI when MRI is unavailable or not recommended. In oncology, CT scans are essential for detecting various cancers, including breast, colon, and ovarian cancer, as well as for identifying cancer spread (metastasis) to organs such as the liver, lungs, and lymph nodes. They are also used to detect adrenal tumors, bleeding, leukemia spread, and abnormalities in the neck and chest. Additionally, CT scans are employed to determine the extent of cancer beyond primary sites, such as the bladder or ovaries, and for surveillance in stages 2 and 3 colon cancer to monitor for recurrence.

Beyond diagnosis, CT imaging plays a critical role in treatment and procedural guidance. It is used during radiation therapy simulation to create precise treatment plans by obtaining pictures of the cancer site. CT scans also guide biopsies, particularly lymph node biopsies, ensuring accurate sampling. Furthermore, CT scans can be combined with PET scans (PET/CT) to enhance cancer detection and are recommended for further evaluation when suspicious lymph nodes are found. Overall, CT scanning is a versatile and widely used diagnostic tool for detecting cancer, guiding interventions, and assessing disease extent.

A physical exam is a clinical assessment performed by a healthcare provider to evaluate a patient's overall health, detect signs of disease, and guide medical decisions. It is a routine medical check-up that includes measuring vital signs (such as blood pressure, heart rate, and temperature), checking body measurements (like height and weight), and listening to the lungs and heart. The exam also involves examining the eyes, ears, nose, and throat, as well as palpating (feeling) the abdomen, pelvis, and lymph nodes to assess organ size and detect abnormalities such as enlarged lymph nodes, lumps, or swelling in the spleen or liver.

This examination is used across a wide range of medical contexts, including general health assessments, pre-anesthesia evaluations, and cancer screening or monitoring. It helps identify signs of various conditions, including breast abnormalities, basal cell skin cancer, and cancers such as ALL, AML, CLL, liver cancer, NPC, bladder cancer, and colon cancer. Physical exams are also performed periodically during chemotherapy (every 1 to 3 cycles) to monitor treatment effectiveness and side effects, and are part of short-term follow-up after procedures like total thyroidectomy, alongside blood tests. Additionally, they are included in surveillance schedules for stages 2 and 3 colon cancer to check for recurrence or spread.

The physical exam provides critical information to the care team about a patient's treatment readiness, overall health, and functional abilities, and is used to detect signs of cancer recurrence or other health issues. It is a general health test that may also include assessing the throat and airway, skin, and other body systems to ensure a comprehensive evaluation.

Symptoms are physical or mental signs of illness or injury that patients may experience and should report to their care team or doctor. They are feelings, problems, or functional changes that can indicate the presence of a disease or condition, and they play a key role in guiding diagnosis, treatment decisions, and monitoring. Symptoms may be specific to certain cancers or conditions—for example, breast issues may present as a lump, pain, nipple thickening or discharge, or changes in breast shape or size; bladder cancer may involve blood in urine; prostate cancer can cause urinary issues, bone pain, or blood in urine, especially in advanced stages; and primary CNS lymphoma or gliomas may cause headaches, nausea, vomiting, seizures, changes in eyesight, or muscle weakness due to pressure on the brain. Symptoms of CLL can include swollen lymph nodes and fatigue, while symptoms of SCLC may not appear until later stages, underscoring the importance of early detection. Symptoms of recurrence, such as pelvic pain, bloating, weight loss, and fatigue, should also be reported. Additionally, symptoms may include issues like frequent peeing, difficulty peeing or pooping, and sexual problems, which are assessed to understand their impact on quality of life. Symptoms can also be signs of disease or treatment side effects, such as pain or nausea, which supportive care aims to relieve. It is important to note that screening is intended for individuals without symptoms, and patients are advised to report any symptoms to their care team. Symptoms are physical or mental signs reported by the patient that aid in diagnosis and help care teams assess disease status, and they may influence whether monitoring or treatment is chosen.

Medical history, also referred to as health history, is a comprehensive record of a patient’s past and current health information. This record encompasses all health issues and treatments a person has experienced throughout their life, including past and present illnesses, injuries, medicines, symptoms, surgeries, and current medications. It may also include family history and lifestyle factors, providing a detailed overview of the patient's overall health.

This information is utilized by care teams and healthcare professionals to inform treatment decisions, determine the best treatment approach or plan, and guide diagnosis and evaluation for a wide range of conditions, including chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC), bladder cancer, stomach cancer, liver cancer, and basal cell skin cancer. Additionally, medical history is reviewed during specific clinical processes such as consult meetings and pre-anesthesia assessments, and it is used to inform cancer care and overall patient management.

Cancer is a broad category of diseases characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells, which can potentially spread to other parts of the body. It encompasses numerous specific types, including head and neck cancer, colon cancer, breast cancer and its subtypes, cervical cancer, chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), acute lymphoblastic leukemia, acute myeloid leukemia (AML), bladder cancer, ovarian cancer, skin cancer, blood cancers, primary CNS lymphoma, lymphoma, differentiated high-grade carcinoma of the thyroid, and cancers affecting the ovaries, adrenal glands, and other organs. Cancer can develop from precancerous conditions like adenomas, spread through organ walls, cause bone damage, appear as tumors, and affect various bodily functions, including fertility and pregnancy. The disease may run in families, making family health history an important factor in risk assessment and genetic predisposition. Diagnosis and monitoring involve a range of procedures, including imaging tests such as PET scans, bone scans, mammograms, MRIs, and cystoscopy, as well as biopsies and biomarker, tumor marker, and genetic testing. Cancer appears brighter in PET scans due to increased sugar metabolism. Treatment options include radiation therapy, systemic therapy, targeted therapy, chemotherapy, and participation in clinical trials for new treatments, with considerations for side effects, emotional and physical impacts, fertility and bone health, and the importance of quitting smoking to improve outcomes. The disease can be local or metastatic, and its staging, grading, and treatment are tailored to the specific type and context.

Prostate cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ. This condition can manifest in two primary forms: early-stage (localized), where the cancer remains confined within the prostate, and advanced-stage (metastatic), where it spreads to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped glands distributed throughout the body, including the neck, armpits, groin, pelvis, near the rectum, stomach, thyroid, bladder, and colon. They are part of the lymphatic and immune systems, containing immune cells such as lymphocytes, and function to filter lymph fluid, remove foreign particles, germs, and harmful substances, and help fight infection and disease. There are over 300 lymph nodes in the head and neck alone.

Lymph nodes play a critical role in the body’s immune response and are a primary site where many cancers—such as breast, prostate, lung, colorectal, bladder, cervical, ovarian, pancreatic, kidney, thyroid, anal, stomach, esophageal, skin (including basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma), and head and neck cancers—may spread. Their involvement is a key factor in cancer staging (e.g., the N score in the TNM system) and prognosis, and they are often examined during physical exams for enlargement, which may indicate infection or cancer spread.

Lymph nodes can be assessed through imaging tests such as MRI, CT, FDG-PET/CT, ultrasound, PSMA/PET, and EUS, and may be biopsied (including sentinel or axillary lymph node biopsy) or removed during surgery (e.g., colectomy, neck dissection, or transabdominal surgery) to determine whether cancer has spread. Enlarged lymph nodes may also result from the buildup of cancerous cells, as seen in conditions like chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), follicular lymphoma, B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma, and mediastinal gray zone lymphoma. In some cancers, such as hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), spread to nearby lymph nodes is uncommon.

Lymph nodes are also involved in defining specific cancer stages, such as stage 3C cervical cancer (involvement of pelvic or para-aortic nodes) and stage 3 bladder cancer (nodes near the bladder). In lymphomas, cancer originating in lymph nodes can weaken the immune system, and involvement outside the nodes is termed extranodal disease. Overall, lymph nodes are essential immune organs whose status is crucial in diagnosing, staging, and treating many diseases, particularly cancers.

Metastasis is the process by which cancer cells spread from the primary tumor (the original site of cancer) to other parts of the body, forming secondary tumors. Metastasis is a key indicator of advanced-stage cancer, often defining stage 4 disease (e.g., stage 4B cervical cancer), and is a critical component of cancer staging systems, such as the TNM system, where the "M" category indicates whether metastasis has occurred. In some cancers, such as basal cell skin cancer, metastasis is rare but possible, especially in advanced cases, while in very high-risk cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), it is a recognized risk. To confirm the presence of metastatic cancer, a biopsy of the metastatic site may be required, with the type of biopsy depending on the location of the spread. Imaging techniques are also used to detect metastasis, particularly in cases like prostate cancer. For prostate cancer, germline testing looks for characteristic changes in these genes: BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, CHEK2, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PALB2, PMS2, and others. Some mutations can put you at risk for more than one type of cancer. Germline mutations in genes like BRCA1 or BRCA2 are also related to breast cancer, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, and skin cancer (melanoma). Germline mutations in MSH2, MSH6, MLH1, and PMS2 are related to colorectal and uterine cancers in addition to prostate cancer. If a germline mutation is suspected based on your family’s or your own health history, you should ask about testing. Your doctor can talk to you about testing or refer you to a genetic counselor. A genetic counselor is an expert who has special training in genetic diseases. A genetic counselor can help you decide whether you would like to undergo germline testing and help you interpret the results of these tests. Germline testing is recommended for those with prostate cancer and any of the following: Family members or relatives who have or had prostate cancer, breast cancer, ovarian cancer, intestinal cancer, and certain other cancers Family history of mutations in certain genes including BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, CHEK2, and others High-risk, very-high-risk, regional, or metastatic prostate cancer regardless of family history Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry Having any other type of cancer Talk to your medical providers and/or a genetic counselor about your family history of cancer. Molecular biomarker testing In biomarker testing, a sample from your biopsy is tested to look at its molecular components. This information helps figure out how likely your cancer could spread to other parts of the body. Biomarker testing can be considered for those with localized, regional, or metastatic prostate cancer. Biomarker testing is sometimes called genomic testing, tumor profiling, or molecular tumor testing. The main reason to have a molecular biomarker test is to help assess whether you have lower risk or higher risk prostate cancer. If you have lower risk cancer, you may be able to avoid or delay treatment such as surgery or radiation therapy, which means you’d also avoid or delay any treatment-related complications and side effects. At the same time, a molecular biomarker test can flag those who have higher risk prostate cancer, which may give them a head start on treatment. After you’ve had all these tests to find out if you have prostate cancer, your care team will put together all your test results to figure out whether your prostate cancer is lower risk or higher risk. Once your level of risk has been identified, your team will assess whether you need treatment and, if so, what your treatment plan will be. Key points An unusually high amount of PSA in the bloodstream may be a sign of prostate cancer. h A digital rectal exam is the simplest way to check the size and texture of your prostate. A biopsy is used to confirm (diagnose) prostate cancer. It’s a procedure that removes samples of cells or tissue to find cancer. Imaging tests may be used to see if the cancer has spread beyond the prostate. Imaging may not be needed for earlystage prostate cancer. To find out if you have an inherited risk for cancer, you can talk to your doctor about germline testing or ask to be referred to a genetic counselor. This chapter explains each of these characteristics. After being told you have cancer, your next thought may be, “How soon can I start treatment to get rid of it?” The fact is, a lot of patients with early-stage prostate cancer don’t need treatment right away. Many never need treatment. Figuring out whether someone needs treatment and which treatment to use requires an assessment of their risks. A risk assessment is a process for identifying potential problems and then considering what would happen if those problems occurred. In the case of early-stage prostate cancer, a risk assessment considers how likely the cancer is to remain within the prostate or to spread to outside the prostate. A risk assessment also considers whether the cancer may come back after treatment (recurrence) and, if so, whether it can be controlled with a different type of treatment. To assess risk, your care providers use these tools: risk groups, life expectancy, nomograms, and molecular biomarker tests. Although you may not receive all of them, let’s look at each of these assessment tools in turn: Risk groups Your care team will look at the clinical characteristics of your cancer, such as your prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level, biopsy results, and other test results. From this information, your providers can classify your disease into one of five different risk groups, from very low risk to very high risk. Why do you need to know your risk group? Because your risk group is the basis for your prognosis. A prognosis predicts the likely course and outcome of a disease. Your prognosis guides your treatment options. For example, patients with lower risk generally get minimal treatment or no treatment at all. Patients with higher risk usually get more aggressive treatment. PSA level A simple blood test will tell you how much prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is in your bloodstream. A high PSA level may indicate a risk for prostate cancer. However, high PSA levels can vary by age, race, and other factors: Age – PSA level tends to increase with age. For people in their 40s, a PSA level above 5 ng/mL is very suspicious for disease. For those in their 60s, 5 ng/mL or higher is suspicious. A PSA level of 10 ng/mL or higher is a danger sign at any age. Race – Normal PSA levels tend to be higher in Black males than in white males—about 1 point higher on average among males of the same age. Researchers don’t know the reason for this difference, but they’re investigating it. Enlarged prostate – The larger the prostate, the more PSA it can make. Other health issues besides cancer can also cause an enlarged prostate. h Sex and exercise – PSA may increase after ejaculation or vigorous exercise. Your doctor may recommend avoiding sex and exercise for 2 or 3 days before a PSA test. This short break allows PSA to return to its usual level. Drugs and supplements – Some medicines, herbals, and supplements can also affect PSA level. Biopsy – PSA level rises temporarily after a biopsy of the prostate. 66 Now more than ever, those living with cancer are living better, longer lives thanks to the power of research and advancements in treatment.” PSA level doesn’t tell the whole story, though. There are other ways that PSA can be interpreted, such as PSA density. PSA density If you have a larger prostate, you’re also likely to have a higher PSA level. But that doesn’t mean you have a greater risk for prostate cancer. To adjust for this, care providers calculate PSA density. PSA density is the amount of PSA compared to the size of the prostate. PSA density is calculated by dividing the PSA level by the prostate size. The size of the prostate is measured by transrectal ultrasound or MRI scan. A higher PSA density (above 15 ng/ mL², for example) indicates a greater likelihood of cancer. PSA density also accounts for those with small and very small prostates, who could have prostate cancer even with low PSAs. Grade Group If cancer cells are found in your biopsy samples, further testing can identify your cancer risk. Results from these tests may indicate that the cancer will grow and spread quickly, for example. Or the results may suggest that the cancer will grow very slowly and not spread outside of the prostate at all. This information helps plan the best treatment for your type of cancer. By looking at your biopsy samples, the pathologist will identify certain cancer cell patterns (called Gleason patterns), which are used to calculate your Gleason score, which translates to your Grade Group, which estimates your risk. This can be confusing at first (Gleason patterns? Gleason score? Grade Group?) but it’s not all that complicated in the end. Read on. Gleason patterns After studying your biopsy sample under a microscope, the pathologist will assign a number based on the “pattern” of cancer cells (Gleason pattern) in the sample. A cancer cell pattern that looks more like normal and healthy cells is given a lower number. A cell pattern that looks more abnormal is assigned a higher number. So the lowest (most normal) pattern number is Gleason score If prostate tumors contained only one pattern of cancer cells, estimating risk would be much easier. But prostate biopsies often contain more than one pattern of cells. To account for this, the two most common Gleason patterns found in the biopsy sample are combined into a single Gleason score. The pattern of cancer cells that takes up the largest area in the sample is assigned the first number. The pattern that accounts for the secondlargest area is given the second number. Add these two numbers together and you get a Gleason score. For example: pattern pattern Gleason score of 7 A Gleason score represents how much your biopsy sample looks like normal prostate tissue. It also estimates how aggressive your prostate cancer is—how quickly it might grow and whether it will spread. A higher Gleason score means the cancer is more likely to grow and spread quickly than a cancer with a lower Gleason score. Gleason scores range from 6 to 10, where 6 is the lowest score. A Gleason score of 7 is intermediate-grade, and 8 to 10 is high-grade. This can be confusing because 6 seems like it would be a medium score, not a low score. So to make Gleason scores simpler to use, they can be organized into Grade Groups. Grade Groups A Grade Group is a way to interpret a Gleason score. So cancer with a Gleason score of 6 is assigned as Grade Group 1 to show that it is the lowest score. Likewise, cancer with a Gleason score of 9 or 10 becomes Grade Group 5, the highest score. Imaging tests are medical procedures that create pictures of the inside of the body, used to detect, locate, and evaluate tumors, assess cancer extent, and check for cancer spread. These tests are essential for staging cancer, planning treatment, monitoring tumor response during chemotherapy, and detecting recurrence during surveillance. They are also used to visualize internal structures, guide biopsies, and identify abnormalities such as enlarged lymph nodes, organ involvement, or areas of infection or bleeding.

Imaging tests include a wide range of techniques such as CT scans, MRI, PET scans, FDG-PET/CT, ultrasound, X-rays, mammograms, and bone scans. These modalities are applied across various cancer types, including breast, prostate, colon, rectal, esophageal, liver, kidney, ovarian, thyroid, adrenal, bone, and throat cancers, as well as leukemias like ALL and AML, and lymphomas such as CBCL and NPC. For example, mammograms, ultrasounds, and MRIs are used to visualize breast tissue; CT and MRI are primary methods for colon cancer staging; and ultrasound is used to detect thyroid nodules and cancer.

Imaging tests are interpreted by a radiologist and are used to reveal a tumor’s location, size, and other features, as well as to detect cancer spread to distant sites. In certain cancers, such as early-stage prostate cancer, imaging may not be necessary, but in others, like leukemia, they help detect spread outside the bone marrow to areas such as the brain, lymph nodes, liver, spleen, and skin. Overall, imaging tests are indispensable diagnostic and monitoring tools in oncology, providing detailed visual information that guides clinical decisions across the cancer care continuum.

Prostate cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ. This condition can manifest in two primary forms: early-stage (localized), where the cancer remains confined within the prostate, and advanced-stage (metastatic), where it spreads to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

Blood tests are a broad category of diagnostic procedures and laboratory analyses performed on blood samples to assess overall health, evaluate organ function, and detect, diagnose, and monitor various diseases—particularly cancer. These tests are used across a wide range of cancers, including liver, bladder, AML (acute myeloid leukemia), CML (chronic myeloid leukemia), ALL (acute lymphoblastic leukemia), cervical, bone, pancreatic, esophageal, FL (follicular lymphoma), ovarian, stomach, kidney, prostate, colon, adrenal tumors, primary CNS lymphoma, and NPC (nasopharyngeal carcinoma). They are also used in general health checks and to guide treatment planning, with results often included in medical records and binders for patient reference.

Blood tests measure various blood components, such as blood cell counts, blood chemistry, and organ function markers (e.g., liver and kidney function). Common tests include the complete blood count (CBC), comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP), blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine, liver function tests (LFTs), and chemistry profiles. Specific tests may also detect tumor markers or other indicators, such as carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) for colon cancer, CA-125 for ovarian cancer, PSA for prostate cancer, and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), thyroglobulin (Tg), and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies (Tg ab) for monitoring cancer recurrence. Blood tests can also measure hormone levels to detect abnormalities related to adrenal tumors or assess endocrine function.

These tests are essential for establishing the extent of cancer, guiding treatment decisions, and monitoring for recurrence or response to therapy. They are performed by drawing a blood sample through a needle from a vein in the arm. Blood tests are used to detect markers or abnormalities related to cancer, evaluate blood cell counts, and rule out other conditions. They are often ordered as part of initial testing, during chemotherapy, or if recurrence is suspected, and are critical for patients to understand and keep copies of their results.

A biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically under a microscope, to diagnose cancer and determine its characteristics. It is a key diagnostic tool used to confirm the presence of cancer cells, identify the specific type and histology of a tumor, and guide treatment decisions. Biopsies are performed on various organs and tissues, including the prostate, breast, lung, liver, brain (e.g., primary CNS lymphoma), ovary, thyroid, lymph nodes, bone, skin, bladder, kidney, esophagus, pancreas, adrenal gland, anal canal, and bone marrow, among others.

The procedure is often guided by imaging techniques such as ultrasound, CT, MRI, or EUS, or performed during scoping procedures like cystoscopy. Biopsies may be conducted after abnormal screening results, when a tumor is detected, or when follow-up examinations indicate growth or spread of cancer. In some cases, a biopsy is performed before starting chemotherapy or steroid therapy to avoid altering the appearance of cells, and it is sometimes combined with HPV testing or biomarker analysis to guide targeted therapy.

There are several types of biopsies, including fine-needle aspiration (FNA), fine-needle biopsy (FNB), core needle biopsy (CNB), incisional biopsy, excisional biopsy, stereotactic biopsy, and skin biopsy. The choice of biopsy type depends on the location and nature of the suspected cancer. For example, excisional biopsy is preferred for Hodgkin lymphoma, while stereotactic biopsy is standard for primary CNS lymphoma. Biopsy is an invasive procedure and may carry risks such as infection, bleeding, and pain, particularly in procedures like prostate biopsy, which is typically performed by a urologist.

Once the tissue or fluid sample is removed, it is sent to a pathologist, who examines it for cancer cells and writes a pathology report. The results of a biopsy are crucial for confirming a cancer diagnosis, determining tumor characteristics such as Gleason patterns and scores (in prostate cancer), hormone and HER2 receptor status (in breast cancer), and molecular features, and for staging the cancer. Biopsy results also influence treatment plans, and patients are encouraged to understand and keep copies of their pathology reports. In some cases, a biopsy may be the only way to confirm a cancer diagnosis, and it is essential for guiding appropriate and timely treatment.

Ultrasound is a versatile, non-invasive diagnostic imaging technique that uses high-energy sound waves to create real-time pictures of the inside of the body. It is painless and does not involve exposure to x-rays, making it a safe and widely used tool across many medical fields. Ultrasound is commonly employed to visualize the size, shape, and location of thyroid nodules, helping to detect thyroid cancer and monitor tumor growth during active surveillance. It is also frequently used to examine lymph nodes, where it can detect small areas of cancer near the skin and guide fine-needle biopsies with real-time visualization for accurate sampling. In addition, ultrasound is used to evaluate breast tissue abnormalities found on mammograms, guide prostate biopsies, and serve as the first diagnostic step for suspected ovarian cancer, using both transabdominal and transvaginal approaches. It is also applied in renal ultrasound for non-invasive assessment of organs, in echocardiograms to examine the heart, and may be used to examine the testicles for lymphoma spread, though this is not always necessary. Overall, ultrasound is an effective imaging method for guiding procedures, detecting small superficial cancers, and providing real-time, detailed images of internal structures across a wide range of clinical applications.

A physical exam is a clinical assessment performed by a healthcare provider to evaluate a patient's overall health, detect signs of disease, and guide medical decisions. It is a routine medical check-up that includes measuring vital signs (such as blood pressure, heart rate, and temperature), checking body measurements (like height and weight), and listening to the lungs and heart. The exam also involves examining the eyes, ears, nose, and throat, as well as palpating (feeling) the abdomen, pelvis, and lymph nodes to assess organ size and detect abnormalities such as enlarged lymph nodes, lumps, or swelling in the spleen or liver.

This examination is used across a wide range of medical contexts, including general health assessments, pre-anesthesia evaluations, and cancer screening or monitoring. It helps identify signs of various conditions, including breast abnormalities, basal cell skin cancer, and cancers such as ALL, AML, CLL, liver cancer, NPC, bladder cancer, and colon cancer. Physical exams are also performed periodically during chemotherapy (every 1 to 3 cycles) to monitor treatment effectiveness and side effects, and are part of short-term follow-up after procedures like total thyroidectomy, alongside blood tests. Additionally, they are included in surveillance schedules for stages 2 and 3 colon cancer to check for recurrence or spread.

The physical exam provides critical information to the care team about a patient's treatment readiness, overall health, and functional abilities, and is used to detect signs of cancer recurrence or other health issues. It is a general health test that may also include assessing the throat and airway, skin, and other body systems to ensure a comprehensive evaluation.

These tests are essential for determining the extent and spread of cancer, which is critical for staging the disease and guiding treatment decisions. Imaging is used across various cancer types: for pancreatic cancer, it helps decide if surgery is an option; for cervical cancer, techniques such as FDG-PET/CT, CT with contrast, and MRI detect recurrence or spread, typically ordered based on symptoms or stage; for prostate cancer, imaging is used alongside PSA tests to evaluate presence and spread, visualizing the prostate and surrounding areas; for lymphoma, it identifies the location, size, and features of the disease; for adrenal tumors, it often detects them incidentally; for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), it assesses spread to lymph nodes and beyond; for bladder cancer, it visualizes the bladder and surrounding areas to stage and plan treatment; for brain tumors and gliomas, MRI and CT scans aid in diagnosis; and for anal cancers (stage II and III), imaging is used for surveillance after treatment, with yearly imaging recommended for three years to monitor for recurrence or further spread. Imaging is performed by specialists such as thoracic radiologists and is a key component of treatment planning and post-treatment monitoring across oncology.

A PET scan, or positron emission tomography scan, is a diagnostic imaging test that uses a radioactive tracer (often a radioactive form of sugar or glucose) to detect and evaluate cancer cells in the body. The tracer is injected into the patient, and because cancer cells have higher metabolic activity and consume more glucose than normal cells, they appear as bright spots on the scan. However, not all bright spots are necessarily cancer—they can also indicate inflammation, infection, or normal organ activity.

PET scans are used to determine the extent of cancer, detect metastasis, and monitor how well treatment is working. The test can be combined with other imaging modalities for more precise results, most commonly with computed tomography (CT) in a procedure called PET/CT, or occasionally with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). This combination provides both metabolic and anatomical information, improving accuracy in staging and monitoring.

In summary, a PET scan is a nuclear medicine imaging technique that highlights cancerous cells based on their glucose uptake and metabolic activity, and it is frequently paired with CT or MRI to enhance diagnostic accuracy and guide treatment decisions.

Lymphatic system Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) begins in the lymphatic system. The lymphatic or lymph system is a major part of the body’s immune system. It is a germ- and cancer-fighting network of tissues and organs that includes the bone marrow, spleen, thymus, lymph nodes, and lymphatic vessels. Lymphatic vessels are a network of thin tubes that carry lymphatic fluid (lymph) and white blood cells into all the tissues of the body. White blood cells, such as lymphocytes cells, help fight infection and other diseases. Lymphatic system The lymphatic or lymph system is part of the immune system. It includes lymph vessels, lymph nodes, tonsils, thymus, spleen, and bone marrow. As lymph travels throughout your body, it passes through hundreds of small beanshaped structures called lymph nodes. Lymph nodes make immune cells that help the body fight infection. They also filter the lymph fluid and remove foreign material such as bacteria and cancer cells. Lymphocytes Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) is a cancer of lymphocytes. A lymphocyte is a type of white blood cell that helps fight and prevent infection. Lymphocytes are found in blood and lymph tissue, and every organ in the body. Lymph tissue includes lymph vessels and lymph nodes. Lymphocytes normally grow in response to infection or inflammation. When they grow on their own without proper regulation, they can develop into lymphoma. Germinal centers Follicular lymphoma (FL) starts in the temporary germinal centers (GCs) of lymph nodes. These germinal centers are short-lived structures that form in response to infection or inflammation. When B cells within germinal centers grow out of control, it can form FL. There are 3 main types of lymphocytes: B lymphocytes or B cells make antibodies. An antibody is a protein that specifically targets infections or cancer cells and recruits other parts of the immune system. T lymphocytes or T cells help fight infections, cancer, and control immune responses. Natural killer (NK) cells can kill tumor cells or virus-infected cells. Follicular lymphoma starts in mature B cells. Follicular lymphoma Follicular lymphoma (FL) is a common type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL). It is a slow-dividing, slow-growing B-cell lymphoma that typically forms tumors in lymph nodes. However, FL can form tumors in other parts of the body such as the bone marrow. This is called extranodal (outside of the lymph node) disease. Not everyone with FL needs treatment right away. How does FL develop? In lymph nodes, temporary germinal centers (GCs) form in response to an immune stressor such as infection or inflammation. This is normal. But, when cells within germinal centers grow without proper regulation, it can develop into FL. In FL, excess amounts of abnormal B lymphocytes group together to form clusters (follicles) in the lymph nodes. It might be helpful to know that these short-lived germinal centers are different than those found in some subtypes of Burkitt lymphoma (BL) and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). There are 2 zones in the germinal center: light and dark. B cells in the light zone are called centrocytes. They are smaller, less in number, and divide less than B cells in the dark zone. B cells within the dark zone are called centroblasts. They are larger than the cells in the light zone and reproduce (divide) more. The types of cells found in your FL help determine the grade, which then determines the stage. The stage tells if your cancer should be treated as classic FL, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, transformed FL, or individualized. Grading The types of cells found in your FL help determine the grade. Grades include 1, 2, 3A, and 3B. Grade 3B contains only centroblasts (large cells), while the other grades contain mixtures of centrocytes (small cells) and centroblasts (large cells). The more centroblasts, the higher the grade. The grade helps tell how your lymphoma should be treated. Two different organizations categorize FL based on grade. In the 2022 World Health Organization classification (WHO5), follicular lymphoma grades 1, 2, and 3A are termed classic FL (cFL). International Consensus classification (ICC) groups grades 1 and 2 as cFL. A tumor is an abnormal mass of tissue that forms when cells grow and divide uncontrollably, and it may be benign or malignant. Tumors can arise in virtually any part of the body, including the colon, bladder, brain, central nervous system, oral mucosa, prostate, kidney, cervix, lung, pancreas, skin, rectum, and anal area. They are central to cancer diagnosis and treatment planning, and their size (often measured in centimeters or millimeters), depth of invasion, and extent of spread are key components in staging various cancers, such as nasopharyngeal carcinoma, head and neck cancers, cervical cancer, prostate cancer, and anal cancer (using the TNM system). Tumors can be primary (the original site of cancer) or metastatic (spread from another location), and they may invade nearby tissues, block organs (e.g., the bowel), or spread to lymph nodes and other parts of the body. They are detected and characterized through imaging tests (e.g., x-rays, mammograms, PET scans), endoscopy, cystoscopy, and biopsy procedures, and samples may be analyzed for biomarkers (e.g., dMMR). Treatment approaches include surgery (such as TURBT for bladder tumors), radiation therapy, and chemotherapy, which aim to shrink, kill, or remove the tumor. In specific contexts, tumors may present as one or multiple masses (e.g., in primary CNS lymphoma) or as lesions (e.g., squamous cell skin cancer), and their behavior and management depend on the cancer type and stage.

Breast cancer is a disease that originates in the cells of the breast, most commonly arising from the epithelial cells of the terminal duct lobular units (TDLUs). It can be classified as ductal or lobular, and includes various subtypes such as inflammatory breast cancer. The disease is characterized by the uncontrolled growth of cells, which can spread through invasive growth into surrounding tissues and metastasize to distant parts of the body, including the bone, lungs, liver, brain, or distant lymph nodes. When breast cancer spreads to another organ, such as the lungs, it is still referred to as breast cancer, not as a new type of cancer.

Breast cancer can affect anyone, regardless of gender assigned at birth. It is associated with inherited germline mutations in genes such as BRCA1 and BRCA2, and a family history of the disease can increase the risk of other cancers, including pancreatic, prostate, and thyroid cancers. The disease is staged based on tumor size, lymph node involvement, metastasis, and biomarkers, and staging is often performed both before and after surgery. Unlike some cancers such as AML, breast cancer has distinct stages.

Breast cancer influences medical guidance, including birth control recommendations, and is a focus of preventive health measures. It may be screened for during regular checkups, including in populations such as anal cancer survivors. Biomarker testing, tumor markers, and genetic testing are commonly used in its diagnosis and management. The pathologist determines how far the cancer has grown within the colon wall. They also test the removed lymph nodes for cancer. These results are used to assign the cancer a stage. In a colostomy, the remaining upper part of the colon is attached to an opening on the surface of the abdomen. This opening is called a stoma. Stool exits the body through the stoma and enters a bag attached to the skin. This is typically only needed for a short time. For colon cancer surgery, the colostomy can often be reversed with another operation. Colostomy is also known as diversion because it diverts (redirects) the flow of stool. Colostomy If the two healthy ends of the remaining colon cannot be safely reconnected after the cancer is removed, a colostomy may be performed. A colostomy connects a part of the colon to the outside of the abdomen. This creates an opening in your abdomen that allows stool to pass through. Cancer cells are abnormal cells that develop genetic mutations, allowing them to grow and divide uncontrollably, avoid normal cell death, and invade surrounding tissues. They can spread to other parts of the body through the blood or lymphatic system, forming new tumors and indicating metastasis. These cells differ from normal cells in behavior and can crowd out healthy cells, leading to damage and symptoms.

Cancer cells can be detected through various diagnostic methods, including biopsy samples, blood tests (such as ctDNA testing), urine cytology, and imaging techniques like PET scans, where they appear as bright spots due to their high uptake of radioactive sugar-based tracers. In specific contexts, such as prostate cancer, they may be targeted by tracers in PET and PSMA/PET imaging, and in cases of HPV presence, they show increased p16 expression, aiding in diagnosis.

These abnormal cells are central to many cancer types, including bladder, prostate, breast, ovarian, anal, and primary CNS lymphoma, where they can be found in the cerebrospinal fluid, brain, or eyes. They may block lymph vessels in the breast, leading to inflammatory breast cancer symptoms, or be filtered out by lymph nodes, as seen in Hodgkin lymphoma. Cancer cells can express proteins like PD-1/PD-L1 or have mutations that guide treatment decisions.

Treatment approaches targeting cancer cells include chemotherapy, high-dose chemotherapy, intravesical therapy, systemic therapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, and radiation therapy, all aimed at killing or inhibiting these harmful cells. In biopsy samples, patterns of cancer cells, such as Gleason patterns in prostate cancer, are analyzed to determine aggressiveness and risk of spread to lymph nodes or other body parts.

Prostate cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ. This condition can manifest in two primary forms: early-stage (localized), where the cancer remains confined within the prostate, and advanced-stage (metastatic), where it spreads to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

A care team is a multidisciplinary group of healthcare professionals who collaborate to provide comprehensive medical care, diagnosis, treatment, and support for patients, particularly those with cancer or other complex conditions. The team typically includes board-certified medical experts from various fields, such as doctors (e.g., pulmonologists, thoracic radiologists, thoracic surgeons, oncologists, hematologists, hematopathologists, breast specialists, gynecologists, radiologists, dietitians, and therapists), nurses, specialists, technologists, pharmacists, and support staff. They work together to plan and implement treatment, interpret test results (including imaging, CBC measurements, and other diagnostics), discuss treatment options and potential side effects (including effects on fertility), and guide patients through diagnostic and therapeutic processes. The care team is central to patient communication and support, encouraging patients to share information, ask questions, discuss preferences, and make shared decisions about their care. They also provide guidance on preparation for procedures (such as imaging tests and surgery), manage symptoms and side effects, and offer resources for issues like smoking cessation, claustrophobia, and emotional support. The team may specialize in specific conditions, including lung, breast, bladder, pancreatic, thyroid, prostate, glioma, CNS lymphoma, AML, ALL, CLL, NPC, and other cancers, and is responsible for coordinating all aspects of a patient's medical journey, from diagnosis through treatment and recovery.

Imaging tests are medical procedures that create pictures of the inside of the body, used to detect, locate, and evaluate tumors, assess cancer extent, and check for cancer spread. These tests are essential for staging cancer, planning treatment, monitoring tumor response during chemotherapy, and detecting recurrence during surveillance. They are also used to visualize internal structures, guide biopsies, and identify abnormalities such as enlarged lymph nodes, organ involvement, or areas of infection or bleeding.

Imaging tests include a wide range of techniques such as CT scans, MRI, PET scans, FDG-PET/CT, ultrasound, X-rays, mammograms, and bone scans. These modalities are applied across various cancer types, including breast, prostate, colon, rectal, esophageal, liver, kidney, ovarian, thyroid, adrenal, bone, and throat cancers, as well as leukemias like ALL and AML, and lymphomas such as CBCL and NPC. For example, mammograms, ultrasounds, and MRIs are used to visualize breast tissue; CT and MRI are primary methods for colon cancer staging; and ultrasound is used to detect thyroid nodules and cancer.

Imaging tests are interpreted by a radiologist and are used to reveal a tumor’s location, size, and other features, as well as to detect cancer spread to distant sites. In certain cancers, such as early-stage prostate cancer, imaging may not be necessary, but in others, like leukemia, they help detect spread outside the bone marrow to areas such as the brain, lymph nodes, liver, spleen, and skin. Overall, imaging tests are indispensable diagnostic and monitoring tools in oncology, providing detailed visual information that guides clinical decisions across the cancer care continuum.

Bone marrow is the soft, spongy tissue found in the center of most bones, rich in blood vessels, and composed of red marrow (containing blood stem cells) and yellow marrow (mostly fat). It is a critical part of the body’s hematopoietic (blood-forming) and lymphatic systems, serving as the primary site where all blood cells—including red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets—are produced. Blood (hematopoietic) stem cells within the bone marrow multiply and differentiate into these various cell types, including B cells and lymphocytes, which are essential for immune function.

In the context of blood cancers, bone marrow is the primary site where leukemias such as Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL), Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML), and Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) originate. In ALL, the bone marrow produces an excess of immature lymphocytes called lymphoblasts, and diagnosis is confirmed when 20% or more of these cells are present. In AML, there is a buildup of myeloblasts in the marrow, and examination via aspirate and biopsy is crucial for diagnosis. For CLL, bone marrow tests may be performed to investigate low blood cell counts, and mutations in marrow cells are linked to disease development. Bone marrow is also a site where tumors can form in other lymphomas, such as follicular lymphoma (as extranodal disease), diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), and non-mediastinal gray zone lymphomas, and it may be tested for cancer spread in primary CNS lymphoma.

Bone marrow samples are obtained through biopsy or aspiration and are used for various diagnostic tests, including karyotyping, FISH, and other genetic analyses, because the tissue contains actively growing cells that can reveal leukemia-specific chromosomal changes. Additionally, bone marrow is vulnerable to damage from cancer and its treatments, and stem cell rescue procedures aim to restore its function. Overall, bone marrow is essential for blood cell production, immune response, and is a central focus in the diagnosis and monitoring of hematologic malignancies.

Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped glands distributed throughout the body, including the neck, armpits, groin, pelvis, near the rectum, stomach, thyroid, bladder, and colon. They are part of the lymphatic and immune systems, containing immune cells such as lymphocytes, and function to filter lymph fluid, remove foreign particles, germs, and harmful substances, and help fight infection and disease. There are over 300 lymph nodes in the head and neck alone.

Lymph nodes play a critical role in the body’s immune response and are a primary site where many cancers—such as breast, prostate, lung, colorectal, bladder, cervical, ovarian, pancreatic, kidney, thyroid, anal, stomach, esophageal, skin (including basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma), and head and neck cancers—may spread. Their involvement is a key factor in cancer staging (e.g., the N score in the TNM system) and prognosis, and they are often examined during physical exams for enlargement, which may indicate infection or cancer spread.

Lymph nodes can be assessed through imaging tests such as MRI, CT, FDG-PET/CT, ultrasound, PSMA/PET, and EUS, and may be biopsied (including sentinel or axillary lymph node biopsy) or removed during surgery (e.g., colectomy, neck dissection, or transabdominal surgery) to determine whether cancer has spread. In some cancers, such as hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), spread to nearby lymph nodes is uncommon.

Lymph nodes are also involved in defining specific cancer stages, such as stage 3C cervical cancer (involvement of pelvic or para-aortic nodes) and stage 3 bladder cancer (nodes near the bladder). In lymphomas, cancer originating in lymph nodes can weaken the immune system, and involvement outside the nodes is termed extranodal disease. Overall, lymph nodes are essential immune organs whose status is crucial in diagnosing, staging, and treating many diseases, particularly cancers.

If you're given a diagnosis of primary CNS lymphoma, you’ll have more tests to find out how far the cancer extends within the central nervous system or if it has spread to another area of the body. Tests are also used to help plan your treatment. Tests for diagnosis If you haven’t yet been diagnosed with primary CNS lymphoma, you’ll first have a physical examination and some general assessments of your health. These include a neurological exam and an evaluation of your level of activity. After these, you’ll have imaging scans and one or more biopsies. Neurological exam This exam involves some simple tests to check your alertness, balance, coordination, reflexes, hearing, and other senses. Your doctor may also perform an eye exam to look at the health of the nerves in the back of your eye. Performance status Your care team will want to know how well you can do ordinary day-to-day activities—like taking a walk, climbing stairs, cooking dinner, carrying laundry, or taking a bath or shower. This evaluation is called performance status. The more activities you can do, the better your performance status. Your care team uses this evaluation to get a sense of the level of treatment you may be able to handle and whether you may be eligible for a clinical trial. Imaging Imaging tests take pictures (images) of the insides of your body. The images show areas in the body that might have cancer. The images can reveal a lymphoma’s location, size, and other features. MRI Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the most useful imaging technique for identifying primary CNS lymphoma. An MRI scan is good at showing the spine and soft tissues, including the brain, as well as other details that are helpful for planning surgery. MRI uses radio waves and powerful magnets to take pictures of the inside of the body. During an MRI, you’ll lie on a table that slides into the scanning machine. (An open MRI scanner may be an option at some health care centers.) It’s important to lie still during the test to get the best pictures. The machine makes loud noises but you can wear earplugs. An MRI of the brain or spinal cord usually requires a contrast agent (also called contrast dye or just contrast). Contrast highlights areas in organs, blood vessels, or other tissues to make them easier to see. The contrast is injected into the bloodstream through an intravenous (IV) line before or during the imaging test and later flushed out in urine. A biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically under a microscope, to diagnose cancer and determine its characteristics. It is a key diagnostic tool used to confirm the presence of cancer cells, identify the specific type and histology of a tumor, and guide treatment decisions. Biopsies are performed on various organs and tissues, including the prostate, breast, lung, liver, brain (e.g., primary CNS lymphoma), ovary, thyroid, lymph nodes, bone, skin, bladder, kidney, esophagus, pancreas, adrenal gland, anal canal, and bone marrow, among others.

The procedure is often guided by imaging techniques such as ultrasound, CT, MRI, or EUS, or performed during scoping procedures like cystoscopy. Biopsies may be conducted after abnormal screening results, when a tumor is detected, or when follow-up examinations indicate growth or spread of cancer. In some cases, a biopsy is performed before starting chemotherapy or steroid therapy to avoid altering the appearance of cells, and it is sometimes combined with HPV testing or biomarker analysis to guide targeted therapy.

There are several types of biopsies, including fine-needle aspiration (FNA), fine-needle biopsy (FNB), core needle biopsy (CNB), incisional biopsy, excisional biopsy, stereotactic biopsy, and skin biopsy. The choice of biopsy type depends on the location and nature of the suspected cancer. For example, excisional biopsy is preferred for Hodgkin lymphoma, while stereotactic biopsy is standard for primary CNS lymphoma. Biopsy is an invasive procedure and may carry risks such as infection, bleeding, and pain, particularly in procedures like prostate biopsy, which is typically performed by a urologist.

Once the tissue or fluid sample is removed, it is sent to a pathologist, who examines it for cancer cells and writes a pathology report. The results of a biopsy are crucial for confirming a cancer diagnosis, determining tumor characteristics such as Gleason patterns and scores (in prostate cancer), hormone and HER2 receptor status (in breast cancer), and molecular features, and for staging the cancer. Biopsy results also influence treatment plans, and patients are encouraged to understand and keep copies of their pathology reports. In some cases, a biopsy may be the only way to confirm a cancer diagnosis, and it is essential for guiding appropriate and timely treatment.

A biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically under a microscope, to diagnose cancer and determine its characteristics. It is a key diagnostic tool used to confirm the presence of cancer cells, identify the specific type and histology of a tumor, and guide treatment decisions. Biopsies are performed on various organs and tissues, including the prostate, breast, lung, liver, brain (e.g., primary CNS lymphoma), ovary, thyroid, lymph nodes, bone, skin, bladder, kidney, esophagus, pancreas, adrenal gland, anal canal, and bone marrow, among others.

The procedure is often guided by imaging techniques such as ultrasound, CT, MRI, or EUS, or performed during scoping procedures like cystoscopy. Biopsies may be conducted after abnormal screening results, when a tumor is detected, or when follow-up examinations indicate growth or spread of cancer. In some cases, a biopsy is performed before starting chemotherapy or steroid therapy to avoid altering the appearance of cells, and it is sometimes combined with HPV testing or biomarker analysis to guide targeted therapy.

There are several types of biopsies, including fine-needle aspiration (FNA), fine-needle biopsy (FNB), core needle biopsy (CNB), incisional biopsy, excisional biopsy, stereotactic biopsy, and skin biopsy. The choice of biopsy type depends on the location and nature of the suspected cancer. For example, excisional biopsy is preferred for Hodgkin lymphoma, while stereotactic biopsy is standard for primary CNS lymphoma. Biopsy is an invasive procedure and may carry risks such as infection, bleeding, and pain, particularly in procedures like prostate biopsy, which is typically performed by a urologist.

Once the tissue or fluid sample is removed, it is sent to a pathologist, who examines it for cancer cells and writes a pathology report. The results of a biopsy are crucial for confirming a cancer diagnosis, determining tumor characteristics such as Gleason patterns and scores (in prostate cancer), hormone and HER2 receptor status (in breast cancer), and molecular features, and for staging the cancer. Biopsy results also influence treatment plans, and patients are encouraged to understand and keep copies of their pathology reports. In some cases, a biopsy may be the only way to confirm a cancer diagnosis, and it is essential for guiding appropriate and timely treatment.

Adenocarcinoma is a type of cancer that originates in glandular cells, which are responsible for producing and secreting mucus and other fluids. This cancer can arise in various organs, and its characteristics and prevalence vary depending on the location.

In the lungs, adenocarcinoma is a common subtype of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). It forms from mucus-making cells lining the alveoli (air sacs) and airways. It is the most common subtype of lung cancer, accounting for approximately 4 out of 10 cases.

In the colon and rectum, adenocarcinoma is the most common type of cancer. It typically starts in an adenoma, a type of polyp, and is considered a malignant tumor. It represents the most common form of colon cancer and the most common type of rectal cancer.

In the stomach, adenocarcinoma is the most common type of cancer, starting in the mucus-secreting cells lining the stomach wall and accounting for almost all stomach cancers.

In the cervix, adenocarcinoma arises from glandular cells, particularly those in the endocervix, and accounts for about 2 out of 10 cervical cancer cases. It is one of the main types of cervical cancer addressed in treatment guidelines, with treatment based on the cancer stage. Low-grade forms may be considered for less aggressive surgery.

In the bladder, adenocarcinoma is a rare, non-urothelial type of cancer that originates from glandular cells.

The prostate is located deep inside the lower body. It makes semen and is important for sexual reproduction. Prostate: A gland in the male reproductive system. A gland is an organ that makes fluids or chemicals the body needs. The prostate gland makes a protein (prostate-specific antigen, or PSA) that nourishes and helps transmit semen. The prostate also contains muscles that help propel semen through the urethra during ejaculation. Semen: A fluid made up of liquids from the prostate and the seminal vesicles as well as sperm from the testicles. During ejaculation, semen is released from the body through the urethra and out through the penis. Urethra: A tube that carries urine from the bladder and out of the body. The prostate wraps around the urethra just beneath the bladder. Seminal vesicles: Two glands that make another part of the fluid that becomes semen. The seminal vesicles are located above the prostate and behind the bladder. Bladder: An organ that holds urine. What causes prostate cancer? Many people who develop prostate cancer wonder where it came from and how they got it. Cancer researchers don’t know exactly what causes prostate cells to grow out of control (become cancerous). The fact is, everyone with a prostate has a risk of getting prostate cancer. But several factors are linked to a higher risk of prostate cancer. These are called risk factors. A risk factor is anything that increases your chance of getting cancer. Risk factors don’t necessarily cause prostate cancer, but people with prostate cancer usually have one or more of these risk factors: Age The biggest risk factor for prostate cancer is age. Prostate cancer is diagnosed most often in those aged 65 years and above. Your chances of getting prostate cancer increase as you become older. Family history Your family health history is information about the diseases and health conditions in your family. A family history reflects a pattern of certain diseases among family members. Having a close family member with prostate cancer (a sibling or parent) increases the chance of getting it yourself. Those with a family history of certain other cancers (breast, ovarian, colon, pancreatic, and other cancers) may also be at a higher risk for prostate cancer. Genetic factors When cancer “runs in the family,” genetic testing can be done to find specific genetic changes (mutations) known to be linked with prostate cancer or other cancers. For instance, having an inherited genetic change in the BRCA2 gene increases the risk of getting prostate cancer. But genetic abnormalities that aren’t inherited can occur, too. Race In the United States, Black males are more likely than white males to develop prostate cancer. Prostate cancer in Black males is also more likely to occur at an earlier age and be more aggressive and more advanced when diagnosed. Black males are also twice as likely to die from prostate cancer compared with white males. Prostate cancer is diagnosed less often in Hispanic and Asian males than in white and Black males. Several things may contribute to these differences, such as barriers to accessing health care (including early detection screening), biological and genetic factors, and other causes. Specialists are researching each of these areas. In light of these issues, Black males may want to talk with their health care providers about getting screening tests earlier than what’s recommended for other males. What does aggressive mean? When health care professionals describe cancer as aggressive, they mean the cancer is likely to grow or spread more rapidly than average. Aggressive is also used to describe therapy that’s stronger or more intense than other treatment options. Diet and lifestyle No one particular diet has been found to prevent prostate cancer or to cause prostate cancer. However, eating food that’s high in fat, such as meat and dairy products, has been linked with an increased risk of prostate cancer. Eating more fruits and vegetables may reduce this risk. Exercise and losing weight may also decrease the aggressiveness of prostate cancer and the likelihood of dying from it. On the other hand, smoking and obesity increase the risks of developing and dying from prostate cancer. What is early-stage prostate cancer? Prostate cancer can be grouped into earlystage cancer or advanced-stage cancer. Early stage Early-stage prostate cancer has not spread beyond the prostate. The cancer usually grows slowly and stays in the prostate. Cancer that is contained entirely within the prostate is called localized prostate cancer. This book is all about early-stage (localized) prostate cancer. Advanced stage Advanced stage means that cancer cells have spread outside the prostate to other areas in the body. This spreading is called metastasis or metastatic cancer. Metastatic prostate cancer has spread to the lymph nodes, bones, liver, lungs, and other organs. Advanced-stage prostate cancer can be separated into two types: Cancer that grows from the prostate gland to nearby lymph nodes, but no farther, is called regional prostate cancer. (It’s also called locally advanced prostate cancer. This book will call it regional prostate cancer to avoid confusion between localized and locally advanced.) Cancer that spreads outside the prostate to other parts of the body is called metastatic prostate cancer. Early vs. advanced prostate cancer Early-stage prostate cancer has not visibly spread beyond the prostate gland. It usually grows slowly and stays within the prostate. This is also called metastatic prostate cancer. Can prostate cancer be cured? Early-stage prostate cancer is highly treatable and often curable. Prostate cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ. This condition can manifest in two primary forms: early-stage (localized), where the cancer remains confined within the prostate, and advanced-stage (metastatic), where it spreads to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

Breast cancer is a disease that originates in the cells of the breast, most commonly arising from the epithelial cells of the terminal duct lobular units (TDLUs). It can be classified as ductal or lobular, and includes various subtypes such as inflammatory breast cancer. The disease is characterized by the uncontrolled growth of cells, which can spread through invasive growth into surrounding tissues and metastasize to distant parts of the body, including the bone, lungs, liver, brain, or distant lymph nodes. When breast cancer spreads to another organ, such as the lungs, it is still referred to as breast cancer, not as a new type of cancer.

Breast cancer can affect anyone, regardless of gender assigned at birth. It is associated with inherited germline mutations in genes such as BRCA1 and BRCA2, and a family history of the disease can increase the risk of other cancers, including pancreatic, prostate, and thyroid cancers. The disease is staged based on tumor size, lymph node involvement, metastasis, and biomarkers, and staging is often performed both before and after surgery. Unlike some cancers such as AML, breast cancer has distinct stages.

Breast cancer influences medical guidance, including birth control recommendations, and is a focus of preventive health measures. It may be screened for during regular checkups, including in populations such as anal cancer survivors. Biomarker testing, tumor markers, and genetic testing are commonly used in its diagnosis and management. A personal or family history of breast cancer is also relevant to assessing risks for other cancers, such as thyroid cancer.

Family history is a comprehensive record of the health conditions and diseases—such as cancer, heart disease, and diabetes—that have occurred in a patient's blood relatives. It is a critical tool used by healthcare providers to assess an individual's inherited or genetic risk for a wide range of illnesses, including various types of cancer and other chronic conditions. The information gathered typically includes the specific diseases present in relatives, the nature of the biological relationship, and the age at which these conditions were diagnosed.

This assessment is particularly important in oncology, where a family history of certain cancers can significantly elevate an individual's risk. For example, having a close relative with prostate cancer increases the chance of developing the disease, and a family history of related cancers (such as breast, ovarian, colon, or pancreatic) also raises this risk. Similarly, a family history of thyroid cancer or related syndromes increases the likelihood of developing thyroid cancer. In the context of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), relatives of affected individuals are 7 to 8 times more likely to develop the disease, and a family history of leukemia can influence treatment decisions and prompt testing for leukemia predisposition syndromes. Family history is also a recognized risk factor for bladder cancer, and it is used to assess hereditary risk for ovarian and stomach cancers. In cases of acute myeloid leukemia (AML), understanding family history is vital for identifying potential hereditary factors.

Beyond risk assessment, family history plays a crucial role in guiding clinical care. It informs genetic testing recommendations, such as germline testing when cancer occurrences in relatives indicate an inherited risk, and helps in diagnosing conditions like basal cell skin cancer. While some cancers, such as head and neck cancers, are not typically inherited, family history is still collected to rule out any rare genetic predispositions. Ultimately, this information is used to create personalized screening plans, guide treatment decisions, and determine whether further genetic evaluation is necessary for the patient and their family members.

Genetic testing is a medical procedure that analyzes DNA from samples such as blood, saliva, urine, or tumor tissue to identify genetic mutations and abnormalities. It serves two primary purposes: detecting inherited (germline) mutations that increase cancer risk and guiding personalized treatment, prognosis, and preventive measures. In the context of cancer, genetic testing is distinct from tumor mutation testing, which only examines mutations within the tumor itself. For inherited risk assessment, it is often recommended for individuals with a family history of cancer, such as breast, ovarian, prostate, or other hereditary cancer syndromes, and can identify mutations in genes like BRCA1, BRCA2, and BCR::ABL1. In hematologic malignancies like acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), genetic testing looks for changes in leukemia cells—including mutations, deletions, insertions, inversions, amplifications, and translocations—to determine disease aggressiveness and guide treatment decisions. For ovarian cancer, genetic testing is recommended for all patients to assess hereditary risk and inform therapy. In some cases, genetic testing of biopsy samples may help diagnose specific cancers, such as follicular or oncocytic thyroid cancer, by identifying genetic markers. Overall, genetic testing is a versatile tool used across various cancers to identify inherited or somatic mutations, support family history assessment, and tailor prevention and treatment strategies.

Cancer is a broad category of diseases characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells, which can potentially spread to other parts of the body. It encompasses numerous specific types, including head and neck cancer, colon cancer, breast cancer and its subtypes, cervical cancer, chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), acute lymphoblastic leukemia, acute myeloid leukemia (AML), bladder cancer, ovarian cancer, skin cancer, blood cancers, primary CNS lymphoma, lymphoma, differentiated high-grade carcinoma of the thyroid, and cancers affecting the ovaries, adrenal glands, and other organs. Cancer can develop from precancerous conditions like adenomas, spread through organ walls, cause bone damage, appear as tumors, and affect various bodily functions, including fertility and pregnancy. The disease may run in families, making family health history an important factor in risk assessment and genetic predisposition. Diagnosis and monitoring involve a range of procedures, including imaging tests such as PET scans, bone scans, mammograms, MRIs, and cystoscopy, as well as biopsies and biomarker, tumor marker, and genetic testing. Cancer appears brighter in PET scans due to increased sugar metabolism. Treatment options include radiation therapy, systemic therapy, targeted therapy, chemotherapy, and participation in clinical trials for new treatments, with considerations for side effects, emotional and physical impacts, fertility and bone health, and the importance of quitting smoking to improve outcomes. The disease can be local or metastatic, and its staging, grading, and treatment are tailored to the specific type and context.

The prostate is located deep inside the lower body. It makes semen and is important for sexual reproduction. Prostate: A gland in the male reproductive system. A gland is an organ that makes fluids or chemicals the body needs. The prostate gland makes a protein (prostate-specific antigen, or PSA) that nourishes and helps transmit semen. The prostate also contains muscles that help propel semen through the urethra during ejaculation.
