The seminal vesicles are located above the prostate and behind the bladder. Bladder: An organ that holds urine. What causes prostate cancer? Many people who develop prostate cancer wonder where it came from and how they got it. Cancer researchers don’t know exactly what causes prostate cells to grow out of control (become cancerous). The fact is, everyone with a prostate has a risk of getting prostate cancer. But several factors are linked to a higher risk of prostate cancer. These are called risk factors. A risk factor is anything that increases your chance of getting cancer. Risk factors don’t necessarily cause prostate cancer, but people with prostate cancer usually have one or more of these risk factors: Age The biggest risk factor for prostate cancer is age. Prostate cancer is diagnosed most often in those aged 65 years and above. Your chances of getting prostate cancer increase as you become older. Family history Your family health history is information about the diseases and health conditions in your family. A family history reflects a pattern of certain diseases among family members. Prostate cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ. This condition can manifest in two primary forms: early-stage (localized), where the cancer remains confined within the prostate, and advanced-stage (metastatic), where it spreads to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

The liver is a large, vital organ located on the right side of the body under the rib cage, playing a central role in the digestive system. It performs numerous critical functions, including filtering blood, detoxifying chemicals and toxins, processing nutrients, producing bile, breaking down fats, helping regulate blood sugar, and synthesizing coagulation factors and other essential proteins. The liver also produces lymph and is the site where primary liver cancers, such as hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and intrahepatic bile duct cancer, can develop.

Given its extensive metabolic and filtration roles, the liver is a common and clinically significant site for distant metastasis from many types of cancer. It is frequently affected by metastatic spread from colon, rectal, anal, breast, bladder, cervical, ovarian, pancreatic, stomach, esophageal, prostate, kidney, thyroid, throat (including nasopharyngeal), and lung cancers, as well as from leukemias (such as CLL and AML) and lymphomas (such as DLBCL). In many of these cancers, liver involvement indicates advanced or stage 4 disease (e.g., stage 4B for cervical and bladder cancers, stage IV for anal cancer) and significantly influences treatment decisions, often requiring systemic therapy or local interventions like stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) or ablative techniques.

The liver's health and function are routinely assessed through blood tests, including liver function tests (LFTs), comprehensive metabolic panels (CMP), and chemistry profiles, which measure enzymes, proteins, and other markers (e.g., ALP). These tests are essential for monitoring potential damage from chemotherapy drugs (such as high-dose methotrexate) and for evaluating the impact of cancers like CLL, which can cause the liver to swell due to cancer cell buildup. Imaging modalities such as CT, MRI, and ultrasound are used to detect metastatic lesions in the liver and to assess its size and condition during physical examinations. Overall, the liver is a crucial organ whose health is integral to overall bodily function and whose involvement in cancer spread is a key factor in staging, prognosis, and therapeutic planning.

It starts in squamous cells, which are found in the tissues that form the surface of the skin and in other areas of the body. The risk factor most strongly linked with anal cancer is long-term infection with HPV. HPV is an extremely common sexually transmitted virus. Other risk factors for anal cancer include HIV infection, immunosuppressant use, a history of certain cancers or pre-cancers, certain autoimmune disorders, smoking, and a history of anal sex or sexually transmitted infection. h Recommended testing after diagnosis includes DRE, anoscopy, HIV testing, an screening for cervical cancer. Treatment with chemotherapy and radiation (chemoradiation) is recommended for most non-metastatic anal cancers. Surgery to remove the anus may be needed for cancer that does not respond to treatment or that returns after treatment. Metastatic anal cancer is treated with systemic therapy (chemotherapy or immunotherapy). Anal canal cancer (stages I – III) This section provides treatment recommendations for stages I, II, and III anal canal cancer. These stages are nonmetastatic, meaning the cancer has not spread beyond the pelvis. See page 26 for information on metastatic anal cancer. Chemoradiation Chemoradiation is the recommended primary (main) treatment for non-metastatic anal canal cancer. Chemoradiation involves treatment with both chemotherapy and radiation therapy during the same time period. More information on this combined treatment approach is provided next. Radiation therapy Radiation therapy most often uses highenergy x-rays to kill cancer cells. An advanced radiation technique called intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) is the preferred method for treating anal cancer. It is a type of external beam radiation therapy (EBRT). In EBRT, radiation is delivered from outside (external to) the body using a large machine Anal canal cancer (stages I – III) called a linear accelerator. The radiation passes through skin and other tissue to reach the tumor. All types of EBRT are conformal, which means that the radiation beams are shaped to the tumor. What makes IMRT unique compared to other forms of EBRT is that it uses many small beams of different intensities (strengths). This allows a high dose of radiation to be targeted at the tumor while limiting the amount of radiation to the surrounding normal tissue. With IMRT it is possible to reduce radiation to important nearby organs and structures, such as external genitalia and hip joints. This can help reduce treatment-related side effects. Radiation therapy is given in small doses, called fractions. As part of chemoradiation for anal cancer, radiation is typically given Monday through Friday for 5 to 6 weeks (25 to 30 treatment sessions). A planning session, called simulation, is needed before treatment begins. If IMRT is planned, you will most likely lie on your back with your knees out to the side (“frog-legged”) for simulation and for treatment. Pictures of the cancer sites will be obtained with a CT scan. Using the pictures and sophisticated computer software, the radiation team will plan the best radiation dose and number of treatments. During treatment, you will lie on a table as you did for simulation. Devices may be used to keep you from moving. This helps to target the tumor. Ink marks on your skin will help position your body accurately for daily treatments. Your radiation oncologist will devise a treatment plan to aim radiation beams at the anal tumor and lymph nodes in the pelvis and groin. You will be alone in the treatment room. A technician will operate the machine from a nearby room. The technician will be able to see, hear, and speak with you at all times. As treatment is given, you may hear noises. You will not see, hear, or feel the radiation. One session can take less than 10 minutes. Common side effects at the treatment site during the 5 to 6 weeks of radiation treatment include skin irritation, tenderness, redness, and sores or skin breakdown. Discuss the use of over-the-counter ointments with your radiation oncologist. Over-the-counter ointments like Aquaphor or Silvadene can soothe the skin and help with healing. Other short-term side effects of radiation therapy include diarrhea, fatigue, frequent urination or pain while urinating, and nausea. Most of these decrease over time when treatment is over. Radiation therapy side effects may not be felt immediately. They can appear and worsen later in the cycle or even after it is complete. Radiation therapy for anal cancer can also have long-term and potentially serious side effects on fertility, sexual health, and bowel and bladder function. See “Fertility and family planning” on page 14 and Part 3: Survivorship for information on ways to help prevent, limit, or manage these effects. Chemotherapy Chemotherapy is the use of anti-cancer medicines. It is a type of systemic therapy. Most commonly, chemotherapy is given intravenously. This means the medicine(s) are slowly infused into the body through a vein. The medicine(s) travel in the bloodstream to reach cells throughout the body. Chemotherapy can also be given orally. or genomic testing. Biomarker testing includes tests of genes or their products (proteins). It identifies the presence or absence of mutations and certain proteins that might suggest treatment. Proteins are written like this: BRCA. Genes are written with italics like this: BRCA. HER2 and hormone receptor status are part of biomarker testing. Your treatment team will recommend the best types of biomarker testing that are important for you. Tumor markers Your blood or biopsy tissue may be tested for proteins. Examples of some tumor markers in breast cancer include carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), CA 15-3, and CA An increase in the level of certain tumor markers could mean that the cancer has grown or spread (progressed). However, not everyone has elevated levels of these markers and tumor markers alone are not a reliable method of detecting breast cancer. Tumor mutational burden When there are 10 or more mutations per million base pairs of tumor DNA, it is called tumor mutational burden-high (TMB-H). TMB-H can be used to help predict response to cancer treatment using immune checkpoint inhibitors that target the proteins called programmed death protein 1 (PD-1) and programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1). Tumor mutation testing A sample of your tumor or blood may be used to see if the cancer cells have any specific DNA mutations. This is a different type of DNA testing than the genetic testing for mutations you may have inherited from your parents. In tumor mutation testing, only the tumor is tested and not the rest of your body. Certain mutations such as PIK3CA can be targeted with specific therapies. MSI-H/dMMR mutation Microsatellites are short, repeated strings of DNA. When errors or defects occur, they are fixed by mismatch repair (MMR) proteins. Some cancers have DNA mutations for changes that prevent these errors from being fixed. This is called microsatellite instability (MSI) or deficient mismatch repair (dMMR). When cancer cells have more than a normal number of microsatellites, it is called MSI-H (microsatellite instability-high). This is often due to dMMR genes. PD-1 and PD-L1 testing Programmed death protein 1 (PD-1) and programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) are immune proteins. If either protein is expressed on the surface of cancer cells, it can cause your immune cells to ignore the cancer and suppress the anti-tumor immune response. If your cancer expresses either protein, you might have treatment that combines chemotherapy and a checkpoint inhibitor therapy. This is designed to activate your immune system to better fight off the cancer cells. FISH Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) is a testing method that involves special dyes called probes that attach to pieces of DNA, the genetic material in a person’s cells. Immunohistochemistry Immunohistochemistry (IHC) is a special staining process that involves adding a chemical marker to cancer or immune cells. The cells are then studied using a microscope. Next-generation sequencing Next-generation sequencing (NGS) is a highthroughput method used to determine the DNA sequence or gene changes of cancer cells in your tumor. This method would only be used if enough tumor tissue remains after other biomarker testing has been completed. PCR A polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is a lab process that can make millions or billions of copies of your DNA (genetic information). PCR is very sensitive. It can find 1 abnormal cell among more than 100,000 normal cells. These copies called PCR product might be used for NGS. Genetic risk testing About 1 out of 10 breast cancers are hereditary. Depending on your family history or other features of your cancer, your health care provider might refer you for hereditary genetic testing to learn more about your cancer. A genetic counselor or trained provider will speak to you about the results. Tests results may be used to guide treatment planning. Genetic testing is done using blood or saliva (spitting into a cup or a cheek swab). The goal is to look for gene mutations inherited from your biological parents called germline mutations. Some mutations can put you at risk for more than one type of cancer. You can pass these genes on to your children. Also, other family members might carry these mutations. Tell your care team if there is a family history of cancer. BRCA tests Everyone has BRCA genes. Normal BRCA genes help to prevent tumor growth. They help fix damaged cells and help cells grow normally. BRCA mutations put you at risk for more than one type of cancer. Mutations in BRCA1 or BRCA2 increase the risk of breast, ovarian, prostate, colorectal, pancreatic, and melanoma skin cancers. Mutated BRCA genes can also affect how well some treatments work. These tests might be repeated. What is your family cancer health history? Some cancers and other diseases run in families—those who are related to you through genes passed down from biological parent to child. This information is called a family health history. Ask blood relatives about their health issues like heart disease, cancer, and diabetes, and at what age they were diagnosed. For relatives who were diagnosed with cancer, ask them (or other relatives if they are no longer living) what type of cancer they had, if they died from the cancer, and at what age the cancer was diagnosed. Start by asking your parents, siblings, and children. Next, talk to half-siblings, aunts and uncles, nieces and nephews, grandparents, and grandchildren. Write down what you learn about your family history and share this information with your health care provider. Some of the questions to ask include: How old were you when each of these diseases and health conditions was diagnosed? What is our family's ancestry - from what countries did our ancestors originate? Distress screening It is normal to have strong feelings about being diagnosed with cancer

Cancer is a broad category of diseases characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells, which can potentially spread to other parts of the body. It encompasses numerous specific types, including head and neck cancer, colon cancer, breast cancer and its subtypes, cervical cancer, chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), acute lymphoblastic leukemia, acute myeloid leukemia (AML), bladder cancer, ovarian cancer, skin cancer, blood cancers, primary CNS lymphoma, lymphoma, differentiated high-grade carcinoma of the thyroid, and cancers affecting the ovaries, adrenal glands, and other organs. Cancer can develop from precancerous conditions like adenomas, spread through organ walls, cause bone damage, appear as tumors, and affect various bodily functions, including fertility and pregnancy. The disease may run in families, making family health history an important factor in risk assessment and genetic predisposition. Diagnosis and monitoring involve a range of procedures, including imaging tests such as PET scans, bone scans, mammograms, MRIs, and cystoscopy, as well as biopsies and biomarker, tumor marker, and genetic testing. Cancer appears brighter in PET scans due to increased sugar metabolism. Treatment options include radiation therapy, systemic therapy, targeted therapy, chemotherapy, and participation in clinical trials for new treatments, with considerations for side effects, emotional and physical impacts, fertility and bone health, and the importance of quitting smoking to improve outcomes. The disease can be local or metastatic, and its staging, grading, and treatment are tailored to the specific type and context.

Treatment encompasses a broad range of medical interventions—such as surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, hormone therapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and other systemic therapies—used to manage, cure, or slow the progression of various cancers, including head and neck cancer, prostate cancer, acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), primary CNS lymphoma, chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), breast cancer, bone cancer, basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, MGZL, and thyroid cancer. The specific approach is personalized based on diagnostic test results, cancer staging, biomarkers (e.g., BCR::ABL1 protein activity), and patient preferences, with options ranging from minimal or no treatment for low-risk cases to aggressive therapies for high-risk or advanced disease. Treatment aims to slow tumor growth, reduce symptoms, prolong life, and prevent the disease from causing problems, though it may have side effects on hearing, fertility, and other bodily functions. For certain cancers, such as CLL, monitoring may be an option, while for metastatic cancer, targeted therapy or immunotherapy may be employed. Clinical trials are also considered in some cases, and treatment plans are often guided by a multidisciplinary care team, with patient preferences playing a key role in decision-making.

Prostate cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ. This condition can manifest in two primary forms: early-stage (localized), where the cancer remains confined within the prostate, and advanced-stage (metastatic), where it spreads to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

A tumor is an abnormal mass of tissue that forms when cells grow and divide uncontrollably, and it may be benign or malignant. Tumors can arise in virtually any part of the body, including the colon, bladder, brain, central nervous system, oral mucosa, prostate, kidney, cervix, lung, pancreas, skin, rectum, and anal area. They are central to cancer diagnosis and treatment planning, and their size (often measured in centimeters or millimeters), depth of invasion, and extent of spread are key components in staging various cancers, such as nasopharyngeal carcinoma, head and neck cancers, cervical cancer, prostate cancer, and anal cancer (using the TNM system). Tumors can be primary (the original site of cancer) or metastatic (spread from another location), and they may invade nearby tissues, block organs (e.g., the bowel), or spread to lymph nodes and other parts of the body. They are detected and characterized through imaging tests (e.g., x-rays, mammograms, PET scans), endoscopy, cystoscopy, and biopsy procedures, and samples may be analyzed for biomarkers (e.g., dMMR). Treatment approaches include surgery (such as TURBT for bladder tumors), radiation therapy, and chemotherapy, which aim to shrink, kill, or remove the tumor. In specific contexts, tumors may present as one or multiple masses (e.g., in primary CNS lymphoma) or as lesions (e.g., squamous cell skin cancer), and their behavior and management depend on the cancer type and stage.

Metastasis is the process by which cancer cells spread from the primary tumor (the original site of cancer) to other parts of the body, forming secondary tumors. This spread can occur through the blood or lymphatic system, allowing cancer cells to travel to nearby lymph nodes (local metastasis) or to distant organs and tissues (distant metastasis), such as the bones, liver, lungs, or other internal organs. The specific sites of metastasis can vary depending on the type of primary cancer; for example, prostate cancer commonly spreads to lymph nodes and bones, while colon cancer may spread to the liver or lungs, and kidney cancer can lead to metastatic tumors outside the kidney. Metastasis is a key indicator of advanced-stage cancer, often defining stage 4 disease (e.g., stage 4B cervical cancer), and is a critical component of cancer staging systems, such as the TNM system, where the "M" category indicates whether metastasis has occurred. In some cancers, such as basal cell skin cancer, metastasis is rare but possible, especially in advanced cases, while in very high-risk cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), it is a recognized risk. To confirm the presence of metastatic cancer, a biopsy of the metastatic site may be required, with the type of biopsy depending on the location of the spread. Imaging techniques are also used to detect metastasis, particularly in cases like prostate cancer. Overall, metastasis signifies the spread of cancer from its original location to other body areas, such as lymph nodes or distant organs, and is a fundamental factor in determining prognosis and guiding treatment decisions.

Cancer cells are abnormal cells that develop genetic mutations, allowing them to grow and divide uncontrollably, avoid normal cell death, and invade surrounding tissues. They can spread to other parts of the body through the blood or lymphatic system, forming new tumors and indicating metastasis. These cells differ from normal cells in behavior and can crowd out healthy cells, leading to damage and symptoms.

Cancer cells can be detected through various diagnostic methods, including biopsy samples, blood tests (such as ctDNA testing), urine cytology, and imaging techniques like PET scans, where they appear as bright spots due to their high uptake of radioactive sugar-based tracers. In specific contexts, such as prostate cancer, they may be targeted by tracers in PET and PSMA/PET imaging, and in cases of HPV presence, they show increased p16 expression, aiding in diagnosis.

These abnormal cells are central to many cancer types, including bladder, prostate, breast, ovarian, anal, and primary CNS lymphoma, where they can be found in the cerebrospinal fluid, brain, or eyes. They may block lymph vessels in the breast, leading to inflammatory breast cancer symptoms, or be filtered out by lymph nodes, as seen in Hodgkin lymphoma. Cancer cells can express proteins like PD-1/PD-L1 or have mutations that guide treatment decisions.

Treatment approaches targeting cancer cells include chemotherapy, high-dose chemotherapy, intravesical therapy, systemic therapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, and radiation therapy, all aimed at killing or inhibiting these harmful cells. In biopsy samples, patterns of cancer cells, such as Gleason patterns in prostate cancer, are analyzed to determine aggressiveness and risk of spread to lymph nodes or other body parts.

Breast cancer is a disease that originates in the cells of the breast, most commonly arising from the epithelial cells of the terminal duct lobular units (TDLUs). It can be classified as ductal or lobular, and includes various subtypes such as inflammatory breast cancer. The disease is characterized by the uncontrolled growth of cells, which can spread through invasive growth into surrounding tissues and metastasize to distant parts of the body, including the bone, lungs, liver, brain, or distant lymph nodes. When breast cancer spreads to another organ, such as the lungs, it is still referred to as breast cancer, not as a new type of cancer.

Breast cancer can affect anyone, regardless of gender assigned at birth. It is associated with inherited germline mutations in genes such as BRCA1 and BRCA2, and a family history of the disease can increase the risk of other cancers, including pancreatic, prostate, and thyroid cancers. The disease is staged based on tumor size, lymph node involvement, metastasis, and biomarkers, and staging is often performed both before and after surgery. Unlike some cancers such as AML, breast cancer has distinct stages.

Breast cancer influences medical guidance, including birth control recommendations, and is a focus of preventive health measures. It may be screened for during regular checkups, including in populations such as anal cancer survivors. Biomarker testing, tumor markers, and genetic testing are commonly used in its diagnosis and management. A personal or family history of breast cancer is also relevant to assessing risks for other cancers, such as thyroid cancer.

surgery is recommended for most thyroid cancers. The thyroid The thyroid is a butterfly-shaped gland in the front of the neck. It has 2 lobes, a right and a left. A thin piece of tissue called the isthmus connects the lobes. The thyroid makes hormones. These substances are essential for the body to function properly. They circulate in the blood and help regulate body temperature, blood pressure, heart rate, weight, and metabolism (how fast food becomes fuel for your body). The two main hormones made by the thyroid are thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3). Together, these are often referred to simply as “thyroid hormone.” The thyroid uses a mineral from your diet called iodine to produce these hormones. Certain foods and iodized salt contain iodine. There are four pea-sized glands on the back of the thyroid gland. These parathyroid glands control the amount of calcium in your bloodstream. Thyroid gland The thyroid is a butterflyshaped gland in the lower front part of the neck. It makes hormones that control blood pressure, metabolism, and other body functions. Thyroid nodules Thyroid nodules are small, often round areas of abnormal growth within the thyroid gland. Most are not cancerous. Very small nodules usually can't be seen or felt. Your provider may be able to see or feel a large nodule while examining your lower neck. Most thyroid nodules don't cause symptoms. They are often found by imaging tests done for a different reason. Symptoms of a larger nodule could include: A visible lump in the neck Neck pain Voice changes Trouble breathing Problems swallowing Who is at risk? Those assigned female at birth are 3 times more likely to be diagnosed with a thyroid cancer compared to those assigned male at birth. Compared to other cancers, thyroid cancer is often diagnosed earlier in adulthood. It is the most common cancer in adults aged 18 to 33 years. For more information on cancer in this group, see NCCN Guidelines for Patients: Adolescent and Young Adult Cancer at NCCN. org/patientguidelines and on the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app. Anything that increases the chances of developing a disease is called a risk factor. The most well-known risk factors for thyroid cancer are described next. Most people with thyroid cancer have no known risk factors. Radiation exposure Anyone who has had radiation treatment to the head or neck in the past (to treat a childhood cancer, for example) is at increased risk of thyroid cancer. Contact with large amounts of radiation in the environment as a result of a catastrophic event also increases the risk of developing a thyroid cancer. Family history Most thyroid cancers are sporadic, meaning there is no clear cause or risk factor. Only a small number are hereditary, or the result of inherited gene mutations (changes). A personal or family history of thyroid cancer or a related syndrome may increase the risk of thyroid cancer. Syndromes related to thyroid cancer include familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), Carney complex, Cowden syndrome, and multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN). Cowden syndrome is also known as PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome (PHTS). This inherited syndrome can cause follicular thyroid cancer, and other cancers and health problems. Tell your provider if you have a personal or family history of breast, endometrial, or colorectal cancer. Key points The thyroid is a butterfly-shaped gland in the neck. It makes hormones that help regulate metabolism and other body functions. Thyroid cancers start as small, often round areas of abnormal growth called nodules. Most don’t cause symptoms and are benign. Thyroid cancer is the most common cancer in adults aged 18 to 33 years. The most well-known risk factors are radiation exposure and a family history of thyroid cancer. 2 Testing 9 TSH test 9 Ultrasound 10 Biopsy 11 Key points If a thyroid nodule is found or suspected, a thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) blood test and an ultrasound of the thyroid and neck are needed. Your doctor uses the results to decide whether a biopsy is needed. TSH test Thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) is a hormone made by the pituitary gland, located near the base of the brain. TSH controls the hormones made by the thyroid. A TSH blood test can't diagnose thyroid cancer. The level is checked to learn if the nodule is producing thyroid hormone. Nodules that make thyroid hormone are rarely cancerous. A high TSH level usually means that the thyroid hormone levels are low. A low TSH level usually means that the thyroid hormone levels are high. This is called hyperthyroidism or overactive thyroid. Your provider may order a radioactive iodine (RAI) uptake test. entities.description: Chemotherapy is a systemic cancer treatment that uses drugs to kill or slow the growth of cancer cells, particularly fast-dividing cells, throughout the body. It is administered by medical oncologists or oncology nurses, typically intravenously, orally, or topically, and is given in cycles (e.g., 14, 21, or 28 days). Chemotherapy can be used alone or combined with other therapies, including radiation (chemoradiation), surgery, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and immune checkpoint inhibitors (especially when PD-L1 or PD-1/PD-L1 is expressed). It is a standard treatment for many cancers, including AML, ALL, primary CNS lymphoma, gliomas, anal cancer, colon cancer, ovarian cancer, cervical cancer, bladder cancer, prostate cancer, breast cancer, and squamous cell skin cancer, among others. Specific regimens vary by cancer type and may include platinum-based drugs (e.g., cisplatin, carboplatin), taxanes (e.g., paclitaxel), antimetabolites (e.g., 5-FU, capecitabine), mitomycin, oxaliplatin, irinotecan, and anthracyclines. Chemotherapy can be delivered systemically (through the bloodstream), intravenously, orally, intraperitoneally, intravesically, intrathecally, or intraocularly, depending on the cancer and treatment goal. It may be used before surgery (neoadjuvant), after surgery (adjuvant), as primary treatment for metastatic disease, or in high doses during stem cell rescue. Side effects are common and include nausea, vomiting, fatigue, diarrhea, constipation, hair loss, mouth sores, loss of appetite, fever, infection, and low blood cell counts. Chemotherapy can also affect fertility and other bodily functions, so preventive measures and birth control may be recommended during treatment. Smoking during chemotherapy can increase lung problems. Long-term side effects may include other cancers, heart disease, and infertility. Chemotherapy is often a key component of treatment plans and may be recommended based on cancer stage, molecular markers (e.g., PD-L1 expression), and response to other treatments.

Radiation therapy is a cancer treatment modality that uses high-energy radiation—such as x-rays, gamma rays, electrons, photons, or protons—to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. It is planned and prescribed by a radiation oncologist and delivered by radiation therapists or other specialists. This treatment is often used as a local therapy to target specific areas of the body, and it may be combined with chemotherapy (chemoradiation), surgery, or systemic therapies, depending on the cancer type and stage.

Radiation therapy is applicable to a wide range of cancers, including anal, bladder, brain (e.g., gliomas and primary CNS lymphoma), breast, cervical, prostate, rectal, skin (basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma), thyroid, and perianal cancers, as well as chordoma and metastatic anal cancer. It can be used as a primary treatment, an adjunct after surgery to eliminate remaining cancer cells, or as palliative care to relieve pain. Techniques include external beam radiation therapy (EBRT), intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT), stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT), whole-brain radiation therapy (WBRT), and brachytherapy (internal radioactive material).

Treatment is typically given over several weeks, with common schedules of five sessions per week, each session lasting 30 to 60 minutes. While effective, radiation therapy can cause side effects, which may appear during treatment or years later. These include skin rash, problems swallowing, dry mouth, thick saliva, changes in taste, tiredness, headaches, nausea, vision problems, cataracts, and long-term cognitive issues. Radiation to the head and neck can affect endocrine glands, hearing, and other functions, requiring pre- and post-treatment monitoring. Additionally, radiation therapy can impact fertility—for example, in rectal cancer it may damage ovarian and testicular function—and prior exposure to radiation, especially at a young age (e.g., to the chest), is a risk factor for certain cancers, such as basal cell skin cancer and small cell lung cancer.

For some cancers, radiation therapy is a preferred or standard treatment option. For instance, IMRT is often preferred for anal cancer, and radiation is a main treatment for gliomas and primary CNS lymphoma. In prostate cancer, it may be used in both early and advanced stages, though it may be avoided or delayed for lower-risk patients. For skin cancers like squamous cell carcinoma, radiation is used when surgery is not possible or as an adjunct to reduce recurrence

Treatment encompasses a broad range of medical interventions—such as surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, hormone therapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and other systemic therapies—used to manage, cure, or slow the progression of various cancers, including head and neck cancer, prostate cancer, acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), primary CNS lymphoma, chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), breast cancer, bone cancer, basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, MGZL, and thyroid cancer. The specific approach is personalized based on diagnostic test results, cancer staging, biomarkers (e.g., BCR::ABL1 protein activity), and patient preferences, with options ranging from minimal or no treatment for low-risk cases to aggressive therapies for high-risk or advanced disease. Treatment aims to slow tumor growth, reduce symptoms, prolong life, and prevent the disease from causing problems, though it may have side effects on hearing, fertility, and other bodily functions. For certain cancers, such as CLL, monitoring may be an option, while for metastatic cancer, targeted therapy or immunotherapy may be employed. Clinical trials are also considered in some cases, and treatment plans are often guided by a multidisciplinary care team, with patient preferences playing a key role in decision-making.

Targeted therapy is a form of cancer treatment that uses drugs or other substances to precisely identify and attack specific molecules, genetic mutations, or abnormal proteins involved in the growth, progression, and spread of cancer cells. It is a type of systemic therapy, meaning it travels throughout the body, and is designed to focus on unique or specific features of cancer cells, thereby minimizing damage to normal, healthy cells compared to traditional chemotherapy.

This approach is used across a wide range of cancers, including acute myeloid leukemia (AML), cervical cancer, prostate cancer, bladder cancer, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, squamous cell skin cancer, and breast cancer (such as HER2-positive cases). It is often guided by biomarker testing or specific genetic profiling, such as identifying mutations like PIK3CA, the BCR::ABL protein, or markers like PSMA. Examples of targeted therapy drugs include PARP inhibitors, Gemtuzumab ozogamicin, Gilteritinib, quizartinib, midostaurin, sorafenib, ivosidenib, bevacizumab, mirvetuximab soravtansine-gynx, tisotumab vedotin, and EGFR inhibitors.

Targeted therapy may be used in various scenarios, including for cancers that have returned, metastasized, or are resistant to other treatments, such as radioactive iodine (RAI) therapy for thyroid cancer. It can be administered alone or in combination with other treatments like chemotherapy. While it can be highly effective, it may also have side effects, which can include allergic reactions, fatigue, low platelet counts, body aches, rash, high blood pressure, and abnormal bleeding. Some serious side effects may affect the heart, skin, or digestive system. Additionally, targeted therapy can affect fertility, so it is important for patients to discuss this potential impact with their healthcare provider before starting treatment.

Immunotherapy is a type of systemic cancer treatment that leverages and boosts the body’s own immune system to find, reactivate, and destroy cancer cells. It is commonly administered by a medical oncologist and is considered a newer, non-hormone therapeutic approach that works alongside other systemic therapies like chemotherapy and targeted therapy. Immunotherapy is used across a wide range of cancers, including anal, cervical, bladder, ovarian, breast, prostate, colon, skin (squamous cell carcinoma), and primary CNS lymphoma, as well as for acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and metastatic disease.

The treatment often involves immune checkpoint inhibitors—such as pembrolizumab, nivolumab, and ipilimumab—which help reactivate the immune system against tumor cells. For certain cancers, including those with specific biomarkers like dMMR, MSI-H, or PD-1 expression, immunotherapy is a preferred option. It may be used to avoid surgery in anal cancer, to treat recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer with specific biomarkers, or as a recommended approach when cancer progresses during or after chemotherapy. In primary CNS lymphoma, the main immunotherapy drug is rituximab, a monoclonal antibody that targets CD20 proteins on cancer cells.

Eligibility for immunotherapy is often determined through biomarker testing, and it may be delivered systemically or directly into the bladder for certain bladder cancers. While generally effective, immunotherapy can cause side effects, including autoimmune reactions, fatigue, fever, nausea, diarrhea, drowsiness, and low blood cell counts. These side effects are addressed in clinical guidelines. Overall, immunotherapy aims to help patients live longer, manage symptoms, and improve outcomes across various cancer types, particularly in advanced or metastatic stages.

A biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically under a microscope, to diagnose cancer and determine its characteristics. It is a key diagnostic tool used to confirm the presence of cancer cells, identify the specific type and histology of a tumor, and guide treatment decisions. Biopsies are performed on various organs and tissues, including the prostate, breast, lung, liver, brain (e.g., primary CNS lymphoma), ovary, thyroid, lymph nodes, bone, skin, bladder, kidney, esophagus, pancreas, adrenal gland, anal canal, and bone marrow, among others.

The procedure is often guided by imaging techniques such as ultrasound, CT, MRI, or EUS, or performed during scoping procedures like cystoscopy. Biopsies may be conducted after abnormal screening results, when a tumor is detected, or when follow-up examinations indicate growth or spread of cancer. In some cases, a biopsy is performed before starting chemotherapy or steroid therapy to avoid altering the appearance of cells, and it is sometimes combined with HPV testing or biomarker analysis to guide targeted therapy.

There are several types of biopsies, including fine-needle aspiration (FNA), fine-needle biopsy (FNB), core needle biopsy (CNB), incisional biopsy, excisional biopsy, stereotactic biopsy, and skin biopsy. The choice of biopsy type depends on the location and nature of the suspected cancer. For example, excisional biopsy is preferred for Hodgkin lymphoma, while stereotactic biopsy is standard for primary CNS lymphoma. Biopsy is an invasive procedure and may carry risks such as infection, bleeding, and pain, particularly in procedures like prostate biopsy, which is typically performed by a urologist.

Once the tissue or fluid sample is removed, it is sent to a pathologist, who examines it for cancer cells and writes a pathology report. The results of a biopsy are crucial for confirming a cancer diagnosis, determining tumor characteristics such as Gleason patterns and scores (in prostate cancer), hormone and HER2 receptor status (in breast cancer), and molecular features, and for staging the cancer. Biopsy results also influence treatment plans, and patients are encouraged to understand and keep copies of their pathology reports. In some cases, a biopsy may be the only way to confirm a cancer diagnosis, and it is essential for guiding appropriate and timely treatment.

Blood is a vital bodily fluid and tissue that circulates through the body, composed of plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Its primary functions include transporting oxygen and nutrients throughout the body, carrying away waste products, supporting the immune system, and preventing bleeding through clotting. Blood also serves as a medium through which cancer cells can travel to form tumors in distant organs, contributing to metastasis.

As a biological sample, blood is extensively used in medical diagnostics and testing. It can be sampled for liquid biopsy to detect tumor DNA, and it may contain circulating tumor DNA or other biomarkers such as EBV DNA to guide cancer treatment. Blood is utilized for a wide range of tests, including complete blood count (CBC), comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) analysis, and genetic testing to identify germline mutations. It is also a sample source for karyotype testing, as it contains growing cells, and for tumor marker analysis.

In the context of hematologic malignancies, blood is the primary sample type for diagnosing and monitoring conditions such as acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), and chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). In ALL, the presence of too many lymphoblasts in the blood impairs its normal function; in AML, blast accumulation similarly affects blood's ability to work properly. Blood is also used for genetic testing and mutation analysis in leukemia diagnosis and monitoring. Additionally, stem cells can be harvested from blood for cell rescue therapies.

Blood is sometimes described as part of bone tissue, and it flows through the kidneys, carrying waste and nutrients. Overall, blood is a crucial fluid that supports bodily functions, enables disease detection, and plays a central role in cancer diagnosis, monitoring, and spread.

Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped glands distributed throughout the body, including the neck, armpits, groin, pelvis, near the rectum, stomach, thyroid, bladder, and colon. They are part of the lymphatic and immune systems, containing immune cells such as lymphocytes, and function to filter lymph fluid, remove foreign particles, germs, and harmful substances, and help fight infection and disease. There are over 300 lymph nodes in the head and neck alone.

Lymph nodes play a critical role in the body’s immune response and are a primary site where many cancers—such as breast, prostate, lung, colorectal, bladder, cervical, ovarian, pancreatic, kidney, thyroid, anal, stomach, esophageal, skin (including basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma), and head and neck cancers—may spread. Their involvement is a key factor in cancer staging (e.g., the N score in the TNM system) and prognosis, and they are often examined during physical exams for enlargement, which may indicate infection or cancer spread.

Lymph nodes can be assessed through imaging tests such as MRI, CT, FDG-PET/CT, ultrasound, PSMA/PET, and EUS, and may be biopsied (including sentinel or axillary lymph node biopsy) or removed during surgery (e.g., colectomy, neck dissection, or transabdominal surgery) to determine whether cancer has spread. Enlarged lymph nodes may also result from the buildup of cancerous cells, as seen in conditions like chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), follicular lymphoma, B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma, and mediastinal gray zone lymphoma. In some cancers, such as hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), spread to nearby lymph nodes is uncommon.

Lymph nodes are also involved in defining specific cancer stages, such as stage 3C cervical cancer (involvement of pelvic or para-aortic nodes) and stage 3 bladder cancer (nodes near the bladder). In lymphomas, cancer originating in lymph nodes can weaken the immune system, and involvement outside the nodes is termed extranodal disease. Overall, lymph nodes are essential immune organs whose status is crucial in diagnosing, staging, and treating many diseases, particularly cancers.

Prostate cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ. This condition can manifest in two primary forms: early-stage (localized), where the cancer remains confined within the prostate, and advanced-stage (metastatic), where it spreads to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

The lungs are a pair of organs located in the chest, forming a critical part of the respiratory system. They are composed of lobes, bronchi, bronchioles, and alveoli, and their primary function is to facilitate gas exchange—delivering oxygen to the blood and removing carbon dioxide. Lung cancer originates in the cells lining the airways, and the lungs themselves can be the site where various cancers originate and subsequently spread to other parts of the body, such as bone.

In the context of cancer, the lungs are a common and significant site for distant metastasis across multiple cancer types. They are frequently affected by metastatic breast cancer, where cancer cells can form secondary tumors, and are also a common site for spread in bladder cancer, where chest imaging is used to assess whether the disease has advanced. Metastatic thyroid cancer often spreads to the lungs, requiring ongoing monitoring and treatment. The lungs are also a distant organ to which throat cancer (including nasopharyngeal cancer) may metastasize, though this is a less frequent occurrence. In anal cancer, the lungs are a common site for metastatic spread, particularly in stage IV, and CT scans of the chest are used to detect such involvement. Similarly, rectal cancer can spread to the lungs, as detected by CT imaging, and this affects treatment and prognosis. For cervical cancer, the lungs are a potential site of distant metastasis, especially in stage 4B, and local therapies such as stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) or ablative techniques may be used to target tumors in this location. Kidney cancer frequently metastasizes to the lungs, and stomach cancer can also spread there, though less commonly than to the liver or peritoneum. Prostate cancer may spread to the lungs when it metastasizes beyond the prostate, and pancreatic cancer often involves the lungs when it reaches distant sites in stage 4. Colon cancer can spread to the lungs, and in metastatic cases, local therapies may be employed; this spread is a key factor in stage 4 classification and treatment decisions. In locally advanced cervical cancer, the lungs are noted as potential sites of distant metastasis, but in such cases, the cancer has not yet spread to these organs.

Beyond cancer, the lungs are assessed during physical examinations by listening to them to evaluate respiratory health, which is part of overall patient evaluation, including in conditions like acute myeloid leukemia (AML). The liver is a large, vital organ located on the right side of the body under the rib cage, playing a central role in the digestive system. It performs numerous critical functions, including filtering blood, detoxifying chemicals and toxins, processing nutrients, producing bile, breaking down fats, helping regulate blood sugar, and synthesizing coagulation factors and other essential proteins. The liver also produces lymph and is the site where primary liver cancers, such as hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and intrahepatic bile duct cancer, can develop.

Given its extensive metabolic and filtration roles, the liver is a common and clinically significant site for distant metastasis from many types of cancer. It is frequently affected by metastatic spread from colon, rectal, anal, breast, bladder, cervical, ovarian, pancreatic, stomach, esophageal, prostate, kidney, thyroid, throat (including nasopharyngeal), and lung cancers, as well as from leukemias (such as CLL and AML) and lymphomas (such as DLBCL). In many of these cancers, liver involvement indicates advanced or stage 4 disease (e.g., stage 4B for cervical and bladder cancers, stage IV for anal cancer) and significantly influences treatment decisions, often requiring systemic therapy or local interventions like stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) or ablative techniques.

The liver's health and function are routinely assessed through blood tests, including liver function tests (LFTs), comprehensive metabolic panels (CMP), and chemistry profiles, which measure enzymes, proteins, and other markers (e.g., ALP). These tests are essential for monitoring potential damage from chemotherapy drugs (such as high-dose methotrexate) and for evaluating the impact of cancers like CLL, which can cause the liver to swell due to cancer cell buildup. Imaging modalities such as CT, MRI, and ultrasound are used to detect metastatic lesions in the liver and to assess its size and condition during physical examinations. Overall, the liver is a crucial organ whose health is integral to overall bodily function and whose involvement in cancer spread is a key factor in staging, prognosis, and therapeutic planning.

Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped glands distributed throughout the body, including the neck, armpits, groin, pelvis, near the rectum, stomach, thyroid, bladder, and colon. They are part of the lymphatic and immune systems, containing immune cells such as lymphocytes, and function to filter lymph fluid, remove foreign particles, germs, and harmful substances, and help fight infection and disease. There are over 300 lymph nodes in the head and neck alone.

Lymph nodes play a critical role in the body’s immune response and are a primary site where many cancers—such as breast, prostate, lung, colorectal, bladder, cervical, ovarian, pancreatic, kidney, thyroid, anal, stomach, esophageal, skin (including basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma), and head and neck cancers—may spread. Their involvement is a key factor in cancer staging (e.g., the N score in the TNM system) and prognosis, and they are often examined during physical exams for enlargement, which may indicate infection or cancer spread.

Lymph nodes can be assessed through imaging tests such as MRI, CT, FDG-PET/CT, ultrasound, PSMA/PET, and EUS, and may be biopsied (including sentinel or axillary lymph node biopsy) or removed during surgery (e.g., colectomy, neck dissection, or transabdominal surgery) to determine whether cancer has spread. Enlarged lymph nodes may also result from the buildup of cancerous cells, as seen in conditions like chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), follicular lymphoma, B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma, and mediastinal gray zone lymphoma. In some cancers, such as hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), spread to nearby lymph nodes is uncommon.

Lymph nodes are also involved in defining specific cancer stages, such as stage 3C cervical cancer (involvement of pelvic or para-aortic nodes) and stage 3 bladder cancer (nodes near the bladder). In lymphomas, cancer originating in lymph nodes can weaken the immune system, and involvement outside the nodes is termed extranodal disease. Overall, lymph nodes are essential immune organs whose status is crucial in diagnosing, staging, and treating many diseases, particularly cancers.

The abdomen is a major body region that plays a central role in the diagnosis, staging, treatment, and surveillance of various cancers, as well as in certain surgical and imaging procedures. Anatomically, it is the belly area containing the digestive organs (such as the liver, stomach, and colon), the omentum, reproductive organs (in females), and the para-aortic lymph nodes. In cancer care, the abdomen is frequently examined through physical exams and imaging modalities such as CT, MRI, and ultrasound. Cancer is a broad category of diseases characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells, which can potentially spread to other parts of the body. It encompasses numerous specific types, including head and neck cancer, colon cancer, breast cancer and its subtypes, cervical cancer, chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), acute lymphoblastic leukemia, acute myeloid leukemia (AML), bladder cancer, ovarian cancer, skin cancer, blood cancers, primary CNS lymphoma, lymphoma, differentiated high-grade carcinoma of the thyroid, and cancers affecting the ovaries, adrenal glands, and other organs. Cancer can develop from precancerous conditions like adenomas, spread through organ walls, cause bone damage, appear as tumors, and affect various bodily functions, including fertility and pregnancy. The disease may run in families, making family health history an important factor in risk assessment and genetic predisposition. Diagnosis and monitoring involve a range of procedures, including imaging tests such as PET scans, bone scans, mammograms, MRIs, and cystoscopy, as well as biopsies and biomarker, tumor marker, and genetic testing. Cancer appears brighter in PET scans due to increased sugar metabolism. Treatment options include radiation therapy, systemic therapy, targeted therapy, chemotherapy, and participation in clinical trials for new treatments, with considerations for side effects, emotional and physical impacts, fertility and bone health, and the importance of quitting smoking to improve outcomes. The disease can be local or metastatic, and its staging, grading, and treatment are tailored to the specific type and context.

The rectum is the final section of the large intestine and the last part of the large bowel, connecting to the anal canal and storing waste (stool) before it exits the body through the anus. It is part of the gastrointestinal and digestive systems, located in the pelvis, and is adjacent to the anal canal. As an anatomical site, the rectum is where rectal cancer and colorectal cancer can originate, and where polyps may form in conditions like familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP). It is also a site where cancers from nearby organs—such as the cervix (stage 4A) or ovaries (stage 2B)—can spread, and it may be examined for such spread via imaging (MRI, ultrasound, proctoscopy, colonoscopy) or during a rectovaginal exam. The rectum is involved in various medical procedures: it is examined during colonoscopy, used as a route for prostate biopsy (where an ultrasound probe or biopsy needle is inserted through it to visualize the prostate), and may be a site of bleeding as a complication of prostate biopsy. In surgical contexts, the rectum may be removed during pelvic exenteration (requiring fecal diversion) or during abdominoperineal resection (APR) for anal cancer that recurs in the anal area. It is also the focus of treatment procedures for rectal cancer.

Metastasis is the process by which cancer cells spread from the primary tumor (the original site of cancer) to other parts of the body, forming secondary tumors. This spread can occur through the blood or lymphatic system, allowing cancer cells to travel to nearby lymph nodes (local metastasis) or to distant organs and tissues (distant metastasis), such as the bones, liver, lungs, or other internal organs. The specific sites of metastasis can vary depending on the type of primary cancer; for example, prostate cancer commonly spreads to lymph nodes and bones, while colon cancer may spread to the liver or lungs, and kidney cancer can lead to metastatic tumors outside the kidney. Metastasis is a key indicator of advanced-stage cancer, often defining stage 4 disease (e.g., stage 4B cervical cancer), and is a critical component of cancer staging systems, such as the TNM system, where the "M" category indicates whether metastasis has occurred. In some cancers, such as basal cell skin cancer, metastasis is rare but possible, especially in advanced cases, while in very high-risk cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), it is a recognized risk. To confirm the presence of metastatic cancer, a biopsy of the metastatic site may be required, with the type of biopsy depending on the location of the spread. Imaging techniques are also used to detect metastasis, particularly in cases like prostate cancer. Overall, metastasis signifies the spread of cancer from its original location to other body areas, such as lymph nodes or distant organs, and is a fundamental factor in determining prognosis and guiding treatment decisions.

These phases are further divided into stages, which are explained in Chapter Bladder cancer treatment What’s the best treatment for bladder cancer? There’s no single treatment that’s best for everyone. The best treatment for bladder cancer is the treatment that’s best for you. You’ll work with your treatment team to choose which option makes the most sense for you. This choice is based on your cancer stage as well as your overall health and personal preferences. Very often, the best option includes more than one type of therapy. Common treatments for bladder cancer include: Surgery Chemotherapy Immunotherapy Radiation therapy Targeted therapy Surgery, by itself or with other treatments, can be used in many stages of bladder cancer. For less advanced cancer, a minor surgical procedure can be used to remove just the tumor. For more advanced cancer, the entire bladder can be surgically removed. In addition, you may receive chemotherapy or immunotherapy directly into the bladder. For people with metastatic bladder cancer, chemotherapy or immunotherapy is used to treat cancer anywhere in the body. Another treatment option is to join a clinical trial. You’ll also receive treatment for any side effects caused by cancer therapy. Can bladder cancer be cured? Bladder cancer in an early (non-invasive) stage can usually be cured. Treatment for more advanced stage (muscle-invasive) bladder cancer can be complicated but it may still get rid of the cancer. Metastatic bladder cancer is not typically curable, but it is still treatable. And treatments are improving all the time. For most people with bladder cancer, treatment provides a longer and more comfortable life with fewer symptoms. It’s important to know that bladder cancer commonly comes back even after treatment. In fact, bladder cancer is more likely to come back than almost any other kind of cancer. From now on, you and your health care providers will have to keep watching for any sign that the cancer returns. Even so, there’s hope. If the cancer does come back, it can be treated. Many people live with bladder cancer and still have a good quality of life. Plus, new and improved ways to detect and treat bladder cancer are helping people live longer and with fewer side effects than ever before. Experts predict that treatment will improve rapidly over the next few years, with better results for all stages of bladder cancer. As a result of clinical trials, many new treatments for bladder cancer have been approved or are on the horizon. As always, you can try to join a clinical trial at almost any point during cancer care. Key points Bladder cancer happens when abnormal cells in the inner layer of the bladder grow out of control. The most common symptom of bladder cancer is blood in the urine. Bladder cancer comes from abnormal changes (mutations) in the genes of cells. Smoking is the greatest risk factor for bladder cancer. Many bladder cancers can be cured. All bladder cancers can be treated. For most people with bladder cancer, treatment requires more than one type of therapy. Bladder cancer very often comes back even after treatment. You and your care team will need to watch for its return for potentially the rest of your life. 66 Don’t Google your diagnosis and assume that statistics define your life! Intravesical chemotherapy only affects the inside of the bladder. Chemotherapy Chemotherapy is treatment with drugs to kill cancer cells. Most chemotherapy drugs are liquids that are slowly injected into a vein (infusion). The drugs travel in your bloodstream to treat cancer throughout your body. Chemotherapy may also harm some healthy cells, which is why it can cause harsh side effects. Talk to your care team about any potential side effects from your chemotherapy treatment. Chemotherapy may be given before surgery or sometimes after surgery depending on your type or stage of bladder cancer. Chemotherapy alone (without surgery) is sometimes the main treatment for people who have metastatic bladder cancer. What is dose-dense chemotherapy? The term dose-dense refers to a method of speeding up chemotherapy by shortening the amount of time in between treatments (doses). The most common systemic chemotherapy used to treat bladder cancer is a combination of medicines known as dose-dense methotrexate, vinblastine, doxorubicin, and cisplatin (or ddMVAC). A commonly used chemotherapy for bladder cancer is cisplatin, which contains the metal platinum. Platinum-based chemotherapy medicines can be effective against bladder cancer but can also damage the kidneys. People with kidney conditions or other health issues may not be able to have chemotherapy or, if possible, may receive non-platinum chemotherapy medicine. Chemotherapy is given in a sequence of treatments called a cycle. A cycle includes a period of treatments (such as once-a-day for a few days) followed by a time of rest (several days or weeks). This treatment cycle is then repeated a few times. For example, you might have 3 to 6 cycles of chemotherapy over 2 to 3 months. Checkpoint inhibitors are one type of immunotherapy used to treat bladder cancer and other cancers. Checkpoint inhibitors block the natural braking mechanisms in the body to allow your immune system to better identify and fight the cancer. The checkpoint inhibitors for bladder cancer include: Keytruda (pembrolizumab) Opdivo (nivolumab) Bavencio (avelumab) Tecentriq (atezolizumab) Targeted therapy Targeted therapy is a systemic treatment that can pick out and attack certain types of cancer cells. Targeted therapy is more often used for people with specific gene mutations. If you don’t have the mutation that the medicine “targets,” this treatment is unlikely to help. Trodelvy (sacituzumab govitecan-hziy) seeks and latches onto the protein Trop-2, found in large numbers on cancer cells. After being developed and tested in a laboratory, potential new ways of fighting cancer need to be studied in people. If a new drug, device, or treatment approach is found to be safe and effective in a clinical trial, it may be approved by the FDA. Everyone with cancer should carefully consider all of their treatment options, including standard treatments and clinical trials. Talk with your care team about whether a clinical trial may make sense for you. Phases Most cancer clinical trials focus on treatment. Treatment trials are done in phases. Phase 2 trials study how well the drug or approach works against a specific type of cancer. Phase 3 trials test the drug or approach against a standard treatment. If the results are good, it may be approved by the FDA. Phase 4 trials study the long-term safety and benefit of an FDA-approved treatment. Who can enroll? A biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically under a microscope, to diagnose cancer and determine its characteristics. It is a key diagnostic tool used to confirm the presence of cancer cells, identify the specific type and histology of a tumor, and guide treatment decisions. Biopsies are performed on various organs and tissues, including the prostate, breast, lung, liver, brain (e.g., primary CNS lymphoma), ovary, thyroid, lymph nodes, bone, skin, bladder, kidney, esophagus, pancreas, adrenal gland, anal canal, and bone marrow, among others.

The procedure is often guided by imaging techniques such as ultrasound, CT, MRI, or EUS, or performed during scoping procedures like cystoscopy. Biopsies may be conducted after abnormal screening results, when a tumor is detected, or when follow-up examinations indicate growth or spread of cancer. In some cases, a biopsy is performed before starting chemotherapy or steroid therapy to avoid altering the appearance of cells, and it is sometimes combined with HPV testing or biomarker analysis to guide targeted therapy.

There are several types of biopsies, including fine-needle aspiration (FNA), fine-needle biopsy (FNB), core needle biopsy (CNB), incisional biopsy, excisional biopsy, stereotactic biopsy, and skin biopsy. The choice of biopsy type depends on the location and nature of the suspected cancer. For example, excisional biopsy is preferred for Hodgkin lymphoma, while stereotactic biopsy is standard for primary CNS lymphoma. Biopsy is an invasive procedure and may carry risks such as infection, bleeding, and pain, particularly in procedures like prostate biopsy, which is typically performed by a urologist.

Once the tissue or fluid sample is removed, it is sent to a pathologist, who examines it for cancer cells and writes a pathology report. The results of a biopsy are crucial for confirming a cancer diagnosis, determining tumor characteristics such as Gleason patterns and scores (in prostate cancer), hormone and HER2 receptor status (in breast cancer), and molecular features, and for staging the cancer. Biopsy results also influence treatment plans, and patients are encouraged to understand and keep copies of their pathology reports. In some cases, a biopsy may be the only way to confirm a cancer diagnosis, and it is essential for guiding appropriate and timely treatment.

Radiation therapy is a cancer treatment modality that uses high-energy radiation—such as x-rays, gamma rays, electrons, photons, or protons—to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. It is planned and prescribed by a radiation oncologist and delivered by radiation therapists or other specialists. This treatment is often used as a local therapy to target specific areas of the body, and it may be combined with chemotherapy (chemoradiation), surgery, or systemic therapies, depending on the cancer type and stage.

Radiation therapy is applicable to a wide range of cancers, including anal, bladder, brain (e.g., gliomas and primary CNS lymphoma), breast, cervical, prostate, rectal, skin (basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma), thyroid, and perianal cancers, as well as chordoma and metastatic anal cancer. It can be used as a primary treatment, an adjunct after surgery to eliminate remaining cancer cells, or as palliative care to relieve pain. Techniques include external beam radiation therapy (EBRT), intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT), stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT), whole-brain radiation therapy (WBRT), and brachytherapy (internal radioactive material).

Treatment is typically given over several weeks, with common schedules of five sessions per week, each session lasting 30 to 60 minutes. While effective, radiation therapy can cause side effects, which may appear during treatment or years later. These include skin rash, problems swallowing, dry mouth, thick saliva, changes in taste, tiredness, headaches, nausea, vision problems, cataracts, and long-term cognitive issues. Radiation to the head and neck can affect endocrine glands, hearing, and other functions, requiring pre- and post-treatment monitoring. Additionally, radiation therapy can impact fertility—for example, in rectal cancer it may damage ovarian and testicular function—and prior exposure to radiation, especially at a young age (e.g., to the chest), is a risk factor for certain cancers, such as basal cell skin cancer and small cell lung cancer.

For some cancers, radiation therapy is a preferred or standard treatment option. For instance, IMRT is often preferred for anal cancer, and radiation is a main treatment for gliomas and primary CNS lymphoma. In prostate cancer, it may be used in both early and advanced stages, though it may be avoided or delayed for lower-risk patients. For skin cancers like squamous cell carcinoma, radiation is used when surgery is not possible or as an adjunct to reduce recurrence

The bladder is a hollow, muscular organ located in the pelvis that stores urine before it is released from the body. In adults, it has a capacity of up to 2 cups. As always, you can try to join a clinical trial at almost any point during cancer care. Key points Bladder cancer happens when abnormal cells in the inner layer of the bladder grow out of control. The most common symptom of bladder cancer is blood in the urine. Bladder cancer comes from abnormal changes (mutations) in the genes of cells. Smoking is the greatest risk factor for bladder cancer. Many bladder cancers can be cured. All bladder cancers can be treated. For most people with bladder cancer, treatment requires more than one type of therapy. Bladder cancer very often comes back even after treatment. You and your care team will need to watch for its return for potentially the rest of your life. 66 Don’t Google your diagnosis and assume that statistics define your life! Every person’s cancer story and situation is different.” 2 Tests for bladder cancer General health tests Blood and urine tests Cystoscopy and biopsy Imaging Inherited cancer risk Quitting smoking Key points Several tests are needed to diagnose and treat bladder cancer. This chapter explains these tests and what to expect when being tested. Before you can be treated, you’ll need several tests to confirm your diagnosis. These tests measure how much the cancer has grown and how quickly it’s growing. Tests are also used to plan treatment, to find out how well treatment is working, and to check if the cancer comes back after treatment. This chapter describes what tests you may have and what to expect during testing. Bring someone with you to listen, ask questions, and write down the answers. Tests and procedures that you may receive are described next. Not everyone will need all of these tests. Be prepared to list any illness or injury and when it happened. Also, put together a list of your prescription medications and any over-the-counter medicines, herbals, or supplements you take. Tell your doctor about any symptoms you have. Some cancers and other diseases run in families. Your care team will ask about the health history of family members who are blood relatives. This information is called a family history. Ask your family members about their health issues like heart disease, cancers, and diabetes, and at what age they were diagnosed. One sample may be used for several different blood tests: Complete blood count A complete blood count (CBC) measures the levels of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets in your blood. Your doctor will want to know if you have enough red blood cells to carry oxygen throughout your body, white blood cells to fight infection, and platelets to control bleeding. Comprehensive metabolic panel A comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP) measures important chemicals, proteins, and other substances in your blood. Levels that are too high or low could be a sign of a health problem in areas like the kidneys or liver. Who’s on your multidisciplinary care team? Treating bladder cancer takes a team approach. Lowgrade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL) refers to mild dysplasia (CIN 1). High-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL) refers to moderate or severe dysplasia (CIN 2 and 3). HSIL is considered a pre-cancer. Risk factors A risk factor is something that increases the risk of developing a disease. Some people with no known risk factors may develop cervical cancer, while others with risk factors may not. HPV infection Almost all cervical cancers are caused by long-term infection with human papillomavirus (HPV). HPV is an extremely common sexually transmitted infection (STI). Most sexually active people have or had HPV at one point. Most are unaware that they are or were infected. In most people, the immune system gets rid of (“clears”) HPV from the body. In other people, the virus causes long-term cell changes that develop into cancer. The progression to cancer often occurs decades after the initial infection. Experts are still learning why one person gets cervical cancer and another does not. Other types of cancer caused by HPV include anal, head and neck, penile, vaginal, and vulvar cancers. There are more than 100 types (strains) of HPV. Infection with some strains is more likely to lead to cancer. High-risk forms include HPV16 and HPV-Other HPV types can cause abnormal skin growths, called warts, to form on the anus, genitals, or other areas of the body. A vaccine that protects against 9 different strains of HPV, including the highest-risk strains, is available in the United States. While previously only recommended for routine use in adolescents and young adults, vaccination is now an option for adults aged 45 and under. There are two other HPV vaccines available in other parts of the world. One protects against HPV-16 and HPV-18 only. The other targets these and two additional types. The vaccine works best in younger people (ideally under age 13) because they are less likely to have been exposed to HPV. And, while the vaccine can prevent new HPV infections, it does not treat existing HPV infections or HPVrelated cancer. Other risk factors Other risk factors for cervical cancer are listed below. Some of these lead to a higher risk because they either increase the risk of being exposed to HPV or they weaken the immune system, which can make it harder for the body to clear HPV infection. The endocervix is lined with cells that make mucus. These cells are referred to as glandular, gland-like, secretory, or columnar cells. Cancers that form in glandular cells are called adenocarcinomas. Less commonly, the cancer may contain both squamous and adenocarcinoma cells.
