A biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically under a microscope, to diagnose cancer and determine its characteristics. It is a key diagnostic tool used to confirm the presence of cancer cells, identify the specific type and histology of a tumor, and guide treatment decisions. Biopsies are performed on various organs and tissues, including the prostate, breast, lung, liver, brain (e.g., primary CNS lymphoma), ovary, thyroid, lymph nodes, bone, skin, bladder, kidney, esophagus, pancreas, adrenal gland, anal canal, and bone marrow, among others.

The procedure is often guided by imaging techniques such as ultrasound, CT, MRI, or EUS, or performed during scoping procedures like cystoscopy. Biopsies may be conducted after abnormal screening results, when a tumor is detected, or when follow-up examinations indicate growth or spread of cancer. In some cases, a biopsy is performed before starting chemotherapy or steroid therapy to avoid altering the appearance of cells, and it is sometimes combined with HPV testing or biomarker analysis to guide targeted therapy.

There are several types of biopsies, including fine-needle aspiration (FNA), fine-needle biopsy (FNB), core needle biopsy (CNB), incisional biopsy, excisional biopsy, stereotactic biopsy, and skin biopsy. The choice of biopsy type depends on the location and nature of the suspected cancer. For example, excisional biopsy is preferred for Hodgkin lymphoma, while stereotactic biopsy is standard for primary CNS lymphoma. Biopsy is an invasive procedure and may carry risks such as infection, bleeding, and pain, particularly in procedures like prostate biopsy, which is typically performed by a urologist.

Once the tissue or fluid sample is removed, it is sent to a pathologist, who examines it for cancer cells and writes a pathology report. The results of a biopsy are crucial for confirming a cancer diagnosis, determining tumor characteristics such as Gleason patterns and scores (in prostate cancer), hormone and HER2 receptor status (in breast cancer), and molecular features, and for staging the cancer. Biopsy results also influence treatment plans, and patients are encouraged to understand and keep copies of their pathology reports. In some cases, a biopsy may be the only way to confirm a cancer diagnosis, and it is essential for guiding appropriate and timely treatment.

Imaging refers to a broad range of medical techniques used to create pictures of the inside of the body, including computed tomography (CT) scans, PET/CT scans, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), ultrasound, x-rays, and transvaginal ultrasound. These tests are essential for determining the extent and spread of cancer, which is critical for staging the disease and guiding treatment decisions. Imaging is used across various cancer types: for pancreatic cancer, it helps decide if surgery is an option; for cervical cancer, techniques such as FDG-PET/CT, CT with contrast, and MRI detect recurrence or spread, typically ordered based on symptoms or stage; for prostate cancer, imaging is used alongside PSA tests to evaluate presence and spread, visualizing the prostate and surrounding areas; for lymphoma, it identifies the location, size, and features of the disease; for adrenal tumors, it often detects them incidentally; for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), it assesses spread to lymph nodes and beyond; for bladder cancer, it visualizes the bladder and surrounding areas to stage and plan treatment; for brain tumors and gliomas, MRI and CT scans aid in diagnosis; and for anal cancers (stage II and III), imaging is used for surveillance after treatment, with yearly imaging recommended for three years to monitor for recurrence or further spread. Imaging is performed by specialists such as thoracic radiologists and is a key component of treatment planning and post-treatment monitoring across oncology.

CT scan, also known as Computed Tomography scan, is a diagnostic imaging technique that uses X-rays and computer technology to create detailed, cross-sectional, and often three-dimensional (3D) images of the inside of the body. The procedure involves taking multiple X-ray images from different angles, which are then combined by a computer to produce comprehensive pictures. CT scans are frequently performed with the use of contrast material to enhance image clarity and are typically completed in under 30 minutes.

This imaging modality serves a wide range of medical purposes. It is commonly used as an alternative to MRI when MRI is unavailable or not recommended. In oncology, CT scans are essential for detecting various cancers, including breast, colon, and ovarian cancer, as well as for identifying cancer spread (metastasis) to organs such as the liver, lungs, and lymph nodes. They are also used to detect adrenal tumors, bleeding, leukemia spread, and abnormalities in the neck and chest. Additionally, CT scans are employed to determine the extent of cancer beyond primary sites, such as the bladder or ovaries, and for surveillance in stages 2 and 3 colon cancer to monitor for recurrence.

Beyond diagnosis, CT imaging plays a critical role in treatment and procedural guidance. It is used during radiation therapy simulation to create precise treatment plans by obtaining pictures of the cancer site. CT scans also guide biopsies, particularly lymph node biopsies, ensuring accurate sampling. Furthermore, CT scans can be combined with PET scans (PET/CT) to enhance cancer detection and are recommended for further evaluation when suspicious lymph nodes are found. Overall, CT scanning is a versatile and widely used diagnostic tool for detecting cancer, guiding interventions, and assessing disease extent.

Imaging tests are medical procedures that create pictures of the inside of the body, used to detect, locate, and evaluate tumors, assess cancer extent, and check for cancer spread. These tests are essential for staging cancer, planning treatment, monitoring tumor response during chemotherapy, and detecting recurrence during surveillance. They are also used to visualize internal structures, guide biopsies, and identify abnormalities such as enlarged lymph nodes, organ involvement, or areas of infection or bleeding.

Imaging tests include a wide range of techniques such as CT scans, MRI, PET scans, FDG-PET/CT, ultrasound, X-rays, mammograms, and bone scans. These modalities are applied across various cancer types, including breast, prostate, colon, rectal, esophageal, liver, kidney, ovarian, thyroid, adrenal, bone, and throat cancers, as well as leukemias like ALL and AML, and lymphomas such as CBCL and NPC. For example, mammograms, ultrasounds, and MRIs are used to visualize breast tissue; CT and MRI are primary methods for colon cancer staging; and ultrasound is used to detect thyroid nodules and cancer.

Imaging tests are interpreted by a radiologist and are used to reveal a tumor’s location, size, and other features, as well as to detect cancer spread to distant sites. In certain cancers, such as early-stage prostate cancer, imaging may not be necessary, but in others, like leukemia, they help detect spread outside the bone marrow to areas such as the brain, lymph nodes, liver, spleen, and skin. Overall, imaging tests are indispensable diagnostic and monitoring tools in oncology, providing detailed visual information that guides clinical decisions across the cancer care continuum.

Ultrasound is a versatile, non-invasive diagnostic imaging technique that uses high-energy sound waves to create real-time pictures of the inside of the body. It is painless and does not involve exposure to x-rays, making it a safe and widely used tool across many medical fields. Ultrasound is commonly employed to visualize the size, shape, and location of thyroid nodules, helping to detect thyroid cancer and monitor tumor growth during active surveillance. It is also frequently used to examine lymph nodes, where it can detect small areas of cancer near the skin and guide fine-needle biopsies with real-time visualization for accurate sampling. In addition, ultrasound is used to evaluate breast tissue abnormalities found on mammograms, guide prostate biopsies, and serve as the first diagnostic step for suspected ovarian cancer, using both transabdominal and transvaginal approaches. It is also applied in renal ultrasound for non-invasive assessment of organs, in echocardiograms to examine the heart, and may be used to examine the testicles for lymphoma spread, though this is not always necessary. Overall, ultrasound is an effective imaging method for guiding procedures, detecting small superficial cancers, and providing real-time, detailed images of internal structures across a wide range of clinical applications.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is a non-invasive diagnostic imaging technique that uses a powerful magnetic field, radio waves, and a computer to create highly detailed pictures of the inside of the body. Unlike X-rays or CT scans, MRI does not use ionizing radiation, making it a safe option for many patients. The procedure often involves the use of a contrast dye (or contrast material) to enhance the visibility of specific tissues, blood vessels, or abnormalities. MRI machines are available in both closed and open designs, accommodating different patient needs and comfort levels.

MRI is widely utilized across various medical fields for diagnosis, staging, treatment planning, and monitoring. It is particularly effective for imaging soft tissues, including the brain, spine, breasts, prostate, pelvic structures, and the rectal wall. In oncology, MRI is used to detect and stage cancers such as primary CNS lymphoma, gliomas, cervical cancer, bladder cancer, prostate cancer, breast cancer, and rectal cancer. It can also identify the depth of tumor invasion (DOI), assess the spread of cancer to nearby lymph nodes or other organs (e.g., liver, chest), and detect cancer recurrence or metastasis.

In specific clinical scenarios, MRI is recommended for further evaluation when suspicious lymph nodes are found, when ultrasound results are unclear, or when CT results are inconclusive. It is also used to guide biopsies, often in conjunction with computerized navigation systems, and to assist in the placement of brachytherapy applicators and the design of treatment plans. For certain cancers, such as primary CNS lymphoma, MRI is considered the most useful imaging technique for identifying the disease and guiding treatment decisions. In cases of spinal involvement, MRI findings may indicate the need for intrathecal chemotherapy. Additionally, MRI can be combined with PET (positron emission tomography) for more detailed visualization, and it is sometimes used in urography to assess the extent of bladder cancer.

Overall, MRI is a versatile and essential medical imaging tool that provides detailed soft tissue images, supports accurate diagnosis and staging, and plays a critical role in guiding therapeutic interventions across a wide range of conditions.

A PET scan, or positron emission tomography scan, is a diagnostic imaging test that uses a radioactive tracer (often a radioactive form of sugar or glucose) to detect and evaluate cancer cells in the body. The tracer is injected into the patient, and because cancer cells have higher metabolic activity and consume more glucose than normal cells, they appear as bright spots on the scan. However, not all bright spots are necessarily cancer—they can also indicate inflammation, infection, or normal organ activity.

PET scans are used to determine the extent of cancer, detect metastasis, and monitor how well treatment is working. The test can be combined with other imaging modalities for more precise results, most commonly with computed tomography (CT) in a procedure called PET/CT, or occasionally with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). This combination provides both metabolic and anatomical information, improving accuracy in staging and monitoring.

In summary, a PET scan is a nuclear medicine imaging technique that highlights cancerous cells based on their glucose uptake and metabolic activity, and it is frequently paired with CT or MRI to enhance diagnostic accuracy and guide treatment decisions.

Prostate cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

Cervical cancer is a type of cancer that occurs in the cervix, the lower part of the female reproductive system, and is characterized by the uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells in cervical tissues. It is primarily caused by long-term (persistent) infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV), and it is a common cancer of the female reproductive system. The disease can manifest in several histological types, including squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, adenosquamous carcinoma, and small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of the cervix (NECC). Cervical cancer is often detected through screening methods such as Pap smears, and diagnosis is typically confirmed by cervical biopsy. The cancer is staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system, and staging is crucial as it determines treatment options and prognosis. Treatment approaches vary and may include surgery, radiation therapy, systemic therapy (such as chemotherapy), and chemoradiation, with the choice of treatment based on the cancer stage and risk factors such as lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI). Cervical cancer can spread to lymph nodes and, if untreated or not diagnosed early, may recur locally or regionally or spread to distant organs; therefore, surveillance and follow-up care are critical for managing recurrence and metastasis. The disease is closely linked to HPV, and a history of cervical cancer increases the risk of anal cancer, as both share the same viral cause. Consequently, screening for cervical cancer is recommended for patients with anal cancer, and female survivors of anal cancer may also be screened for cervical cancer. In the bladder, adenocarcinoma is a rare, non-urothelial type of cancer that originates from glandular cells.

Bone is a living tissue made of cells (osteocytes, osteoblasts, and osteoclasts), calcium, phosphate, hydroxyapatite (a bone mineral), and collagen. New bone formation, known as ossification, starts in the womb and ends during adolescence, between 10 and 19 years of age. Ossification is complete when the skeleton is done growing. Once ossification is complete, bone is continuously being replaced by a process called remodeling. Remodeling breaks down and rebuilds bone and helps maintain normal calcium levels in the body. At the same time, bone-forming cells called osteoblasts create bone from calcium in the bloodstream. Some types of bone cancer can interrupt this process. but treatment is improving. What is a glioma? A glioma is a type of tumor that grows in the brain. A tumor is an abnormal growth of cells. Gliomas develop from certain brain cells called glial cells. Glial cells support the function of nerve cells (neurons) in the central nervous system (the brain and the spinal cord). Many types of tumors can occur in the central nervous system. Only those that start as glial cells become gliomas. Gliomas are the most common type of malignant (cancerous) brain tumor in adults. Gliomas can happen at any age but occur more often in adults than in children. Gliomas start in the brain or sometimes the spinal cord. But they rarely spread to another area of the body. What makes gliomas so complicated is that they invade and blend into the normal parts of the brain. So gliomas can be very difficult to treat without harming the healthy parts of the brain. Normal cells vs. cancer cells Normal cells follow the body’s rules. Normal cells increase in number only when they’re needed, and they die when they’re old or damaged. Cancer cells don’t follow the rules. Cancer cells can multiply quickly and avoid dying. Cancer cells can crowd out normal cells and take their place. Eventually this damages the body and often results in symptoms. What causes a glioma? No one knows exactly what causes most brain tumors, including gliomas. What experts do know is that brain tumors often start with an abnormality (mutation) in certain cells. This abnormality causes these cells to grow out of control (become cancerous). This type of mutation happens on its own. It’s not typically passed down in families (hereditary mutation). Gliomas occur in both children and adults. This book discusses gliomas only in adults. Are there types of gliomas? There are several types of glioma tumors. The 3 most common types are astrocytomas, oligodendrogliomas, and glioblastomas. They’re made of different kinds of glial cells. Astrocytomas look like star-shaped glial cells called astrocytes. The main job of astrocytes is to maintain the chemical environment that allows communication between nerve cells. Oligodendrogliomas look like oligodendrocytes, which are glial cells that protect electrical signaling in nerve cells. Glioblastomas come from precursor cells that develop into cells like astrocytes and oligodendrocytes. Glioblastomas are the most destructive and dangerous type of glioma tumor. Besides tumor type, gliomas are also categorized by grade. The grade indicates how fast the tumor is likely to grow. A low-grade glioma usually grows slowly while a high-grade glioma often grows rapidly. Although it helps to put gliomas into categories, it’s important to note that each glioma has its own molecular characteristics and behavior. That also means that each person’s glioma is unique. So your progress and experience will be unique to you. Gliomas often occur in the upper part of the brain where they can disrupt important brain functions. Few gliomas in adults have distinct and welldefined edges like the one in this illustration. Most gliomas blend deeply into normal brain tissue and have vague borders. This makes them very difficult to remove entirely. When the tumor is removed, some tumor cells must be left behind to avoid damaging nearby brain tissue. How are gliomas diagnosed? A glioma is often found when it starts causing symptoms. A symptom is a problem or feeling that may be a sign of disease. Gliomas cause symptoms when they put pressure on the brain or invade brain tissue. Some people have many symptoms while others don’t have any. Common symptoms of gliomas include: Unusual or frequent headaches Seizures Changes in personality or mood Nausea and vomiting Difficulty speaking or swallowing Muscle weakness Difficulty with walking, balance, or coordination Symptoms provide clues that something is wrong. But they don’t provide enough information to identify a specific illness. Different tests, physical exams, and surgical procedures are required to diagnose a glioma. If these tests show that you have a glioma, your care team will discuss your treatment options with you. If possible, seek care at a center with experience in treating brain tumors. Diagnosis vs. prognosis What’s the difference between your diagnosis and your prognosis? These two words sound alike but they’re very different. Diagnosis: The identification of an illness based on tests. The diagnosis names what illness you have. Prognosis: The likely course and outcome of a disease. The prognosis predicts how your disease will turn out. Can gliomas be cured? Most gliomas are not curable, but they are usually treatable. Treatment can slow down the tumor’s growth for a period of time, reduce its symptoms, and prolong life. The main treatments for a glioma are surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy. These are often combined with one another for more complete treatment. Another option to consider is participating in a clinical trial for a potential new treatment. Treatment may be able to stop the glioma from growing and keep it stabilized for a time. This may last for months or years. However, even with the best treatment, gliomas usually grow back eventually. So periodic follow-up visits and additional rounds of treatment are recommended. It’s

A care team is a multidisciplinary group of healthcare professionals who collaborate to provide comprehensive medical care, diagnosis, treatment, and support for patients, particularly those with cancer or other complex conditions. The team typically includes board-certified medical experts from various fields, such as doctors (e.g., pulmonologists, thoracic radiologists, thoracic surgeons, oncologists, hematologists, hematopathologists, breast specialists, gynecologists, radiologists, dietitians, and therapists), nurses, specialists, technologists, pharmacists, and support staff. They also provide guidance on preparation for procedures (such as imaging tests and surgery), manage symptoms and side effects, and offer resources for issues like smoking cessation, claustrophobia, and emotional support. It is tailored to the individual’s specific condition, incorporating factors such as cancer type, subtype, stage, grade, tumor histology, and results from diagnostic tests including blood tests, imaging studies, biopsy, and biomarker testing. The plan also takes into account the patient’s performance status, medical history, and personal preferences, ensuring a patient-centered approach.

The treatment plan outlines the specific medical procedures and therapies the patient will undergo, which may include surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, targeted therapies, or systemic therapies, as well as supportive care measures. This plan is a key focus of the NCCN Guidelines for Patients and is used across various cancer types, including acute myeloid leukemia (AML), prostate cancer, rectal cancer, and anal cancer, among others. Ultimately, the treatment plan serves as a personalized document and roadmap that guides the patient and care team through the entire course of cancer care, from initial diagnosis through ongoing management.

Prostate cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ. This condition can manifest in two primary forms: early-stage (localized), where the cancer remains confined within the prostate, and advanced-stage (metastatic), where it spreads to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

Radiation therapy is a cancer treatment modality that uses high-energy radiation—such as x-rays, gamma rays, electrons, photons, or protons—to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. It is planned and prescribed by a radiation oncologist and delivered by radiation therapists or other specialists. This treatment is often used as a local therapy to target specific areas of the body, and it may be combined with chemotherapy (chemoradiation), surgery, or systemic therapies, depending on the cancer type and stage.

Radiation therapy is applicable to a wide range of cancers, including anal, bladder, brain (e.g., gliomas and primary CNS lymphoma), breast, cervical, prostate, rectal, skin (basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma), thyroid, and perianal cancers, as well as chordoma and metastatic anal cancer. It can be used as a primary treatment, an adjunct after surgery to eliminate remaining cancer cells, or as palliative care to relieve pain. Techniques include external beam radiation therapy (EBRT), intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT), stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT), whole-brain radiation therapy (WBRT), and brachytherapy (internal radioactive material).

Treatment is typically given over several weeks, with common schedules of five sessions per week, each session lasting 30 to 60 minutes. While effective, radiation therapy can cause side effects, which may appear during treatment or years later. These include skin rash, problems swallowing, dry mouth, thick saliva, changes in taste, tiredness, headaches, nausea, vision problems, cataracts, and long-term cognitive issues. Radiation to the head and neck can affect endocrine glands, hearing, and other functions, requiring pre- and post-treatment monitoring. Additionally, radiation therapy can impact fertility—for example, in rectal cancer it may damage ovarian and testicular function—and prior exposure to radiation, especially at a young age (e.g., to the chest), is a risk factor for certain cancers, such as basal cell skin cancer and small cell lung cancer.

For some cancers, radiation therapy is a preferred or standard treatment option. For instance, IMRT is often preferred for anal cancer, and radiation is a main treatment for gliomas and primary CNS lymphoma. In prostate cancer, it may be used in both early and advanced stages, though it may be avoided or delayed for lower-risk patients. For skin cancers like squamous cell carcinoma, radiation is used when surgery is not possible or as an adjunct to reduce recurrence

Cervical cancer is a type of cancer that occurs in the cervix, the lower part of the female reproductive system, and is characterized by the uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells in cervical tissues. It is primarily caused by long-term (persistent) infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV), and it is a common cancer of the female reproductive system. The disease can manifest in several histological types, including squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, adenosquamous carcinoma, and small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of the cervix (NECC). Cervical cancer is often detected through screening methods such as Pap smears, and diagnosis is typically confirmed by cervical biopsy. The cancer is staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system, and staging is crucial as it determines treatment options and prognosis. Treatment approaches vary and may include surgery, radiation therapy, systemic therapy (such as chemotherapy), and chemoradiation, with the choice of treatment based on the cancer stage and risk factors such as lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI). Cervical cancer can spread to lymph nodes and, if untreated or not diagnosed early, may recur locally or regionally or spread to distant organs; therefore, surveillance and follow-up care are critical for managing recurrence and metastasis. The disease is closely linked to HPV, and a history of cervical cancer increases the risk of anal cancer, as both share the same viral cause. Consequently, screening for cervical cancer is recommended for patients with anal cancer, and female survivors of anal cancer may also be screened for cervical cancer. Additionally, p16, a biomarker, can be found in cervical cancer tissues.

Surgery is a broad medical procedure involving the physical removal of tumors, cancerous tissue, or other affected areas, and is a primary or common treatment option for many types of cancer. It is used across a wide range of cancers, including early-stage cervical cancer (with types like cone biopsy, trachelectomy, and hysterectomy), bladder cancer (ranging from minor tumor removal to radical cystectomy, which is full bladder removal), and local squamous cell skin cancer (including curettage and electrodesiccation, PDEMA/Mohs surgery, and standard surgical excision). For gliomas, surgery is a main treatment aimed at removing the tumor, though it is difficult due to the tumor's invasive nature; it is particularly effective for grade 1 tumors, often followed by additional therapy for higher grades. Surgery is also a primary treatment for ovarian cancer, performed by gynecologic oncologists to remove tumors, determine cancer stage, and may involve staging and cytoreduction, with the response to surgery and chemotherapy determining maintenance therapy options. For breast cancer, surgery may involve mastectomy (removal of the entire breast) or lumpectomy (removal of a portion), and clips may remain until surgery. Surgery is a common treatment for head and neck cancer, anal cancer (including APR and complete removal of SISCCA lesions), and chondrosarcoma and other bone cancers. It is a treatment option for early or locally advanced NSCLC, pancreatic cancer (for stages 1, 2, or 3, depending on staging viability), and prostate cancer (particularly early-stage, involving removal of the prostate gland or metastatic tumors, and may be avoided or delayed for lower-risk patients). For thyroid cancer, surgery is the most common and effective treatment, involving lobectomy or total thyroidectomy, though targeted therapy is used for cancers that cannot be treated with surgery. Surgery is also a primary treatment for CSCC (cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma), involving excision of cancerous lesions and nearby lymph nodes for regional cases, and is the most common treatment for basal cell skin cancer, highly effective when caught early. Surgery may involve biopsy procedures, such as excisional biopsy for lymph nodes, and allows for pathologic staging by examining removed tissue, which is essential for determining treatment options. However, surgery is not normally used for primary CNS lymphoma due to the risks of removing deep brain tumors. Fertility is the ability to conceive and have children, and it is a significant health consideration for individuals of all genders affected by cancer. Cancer treatments—including chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and treatments for specific cancers such as acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), bone cancer, head and neck cancer, cervical cancer, and anal cancer—can damage the organs and bodily functions necessary for conception and pregnancy. As a result, fertility may be impacted either temporarily or permanently, and this risk is addressed as part of comprehensive cancer care.

Fertility concerns are discussed before and during treatment planning, and patients are strongly encouraged to speak with their care team about potential risks. Fertility preservation options—such as egg, sperm, or embryo freezing—are often considered and may involve referrals to specialists for counseling. These discussions are relevant across all genders and are integrated into treatment protocols for various cancer types, including those affecting the head and neck, bones, blood, cervix, and anus. Long-term effects on fertility are particularly noted in treatments like radiation therapy for cervical and anal cancers.

Overall, fertility is a key aspect of cancer treatment planning, and patients are advised to proactively address their reproductive goals with their healthcare providers to explore available preservation options before beginning treatment.

This book is organized into chapters on: Testing Treatment CML phases 2 Tests Test results General health tests Blood tests Fertility (all genders) Performance status Bone marrow tests Testing for CML biomarker and genetic changes Heart tests Key points Questions to ask Treatment planning starts with testing. Accurate testing is needed to diagnose and treat CML. This chapter presents an overview of possible tests you might receive and what to expect. Organize your medical documents, including insurance forms, medical records, and test results. Keep a list of contact information for your care team and update your primary care physician (PCP) regarding any changes. Include details about the specific type of cancer, treatment, and dates on your contact list. Ask your care team how best to communicate with them, especially in an emergency. Test results Results from blood tests and possible biopsy will be used to determine your treatment plan. Treatment will be based on these findings. It is important you understand what these tests mean. Ask questions about your test results. Online patient portals are one way to access your test results. Keep these things in mind: It's beneficial to have a support system in place during diagnosis and treatment. Enlist the help of friends, family members, or peers who can provide transportation, meals, and emotional support. These can be different people for different tasks or change over time. Consider bringing someone with you to doctor visits if possible, or have someone on the phone or join you for telehealth visits. Don’t hesitate to ask questions and take notes during appointments. Write down questions and ask a friend or family member to take notes. Caregivers should ask questions, too. Tests used to diagnose CML can be found in Guide

Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is a fastgrowing blood cancer that starts in diseasefighting white blood cells of your immune system called lymphocytes. In ALL, bone marrow makes too many immature lymphocytes called lymphoblasts (or blasts). Lymphoblasts can crowd out normal bone marrow. This leads to less blood being made. There are 2 main types of ALL: B cell or B-ALL T cell or T-ALL B-ALL B-cell ALL or B-ALL starts in B-cell lymphocytes. B-ALL is more common than T-ALL. Mature B-cell ALL (also called Burkitt leukemia), a rare subtype, is essentially the same as Burkitt lymphoma (a type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma), but is treated differently from B-ALL. Prostate cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ. This condition can manifest in two primary forms: early-stage (localized), where the cancer remains confined within the prostate, and advanced-stage (metastatic), where it spreads to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

Recurrence, also known as relapse, refers to the return of cancer after a period of treatment or remission. This phenomenon is common across various cancer types, including bladder, breast, cervical, ovarian, prostate, basal cell skin, primary CNS lymphoma, and head and neck cancers. Recurrence can manifest locally (at the original site), regionally (in nearby lymph nodes), or at distant sites in the body, depending on the cancer type.

For bladder cancer, recurrence is a frequent occurrence that necessitates ongoing monitoring and regular follow-up testing. In breast cancer, recurrence may be local or distant. Cervical cancer recurrence can occur locally, regionally, or at distant sites, and often requires imaging, exploratory surgery, and biomarker testing to guide further treatment. Ovarian cancer recurrence also demands further management and monitoring. Prostate cancer recurrence can be detected through imaging tests such as MRI or PSMA-PET scans, and is a key factor in risk assessment. Basal cell skin cancer recurrence involves the cancer returning to the original area or spreading to lymph nodes or distant parts of the body, indicating a need for continued surveillance.

Monitoring for recurrence typically involves imaging tests like MRI, PSMA-PET, and other surveillance methods, including regular physical exams and blood tests. In some cases, such as higher-risk thyroid cancer, TSH suppression is used as a monitoring strategy. Symptoms of recurrence can vary but may include pelvic pain, bloating, and fatigue, particularly in gynecologic cancers.

Treatment for recurrence depends on the location and extent of the disease and may involve additional therapies such as surgery, radiation therapy, radioactive iodine (RAI), or adjustments to chemotherapy regimens. Biomarker testing is often employed to guide treatment decisions. Certain cancer subtypes and features can increase the risk of recurrence, and radiation therapy may be used in high-risk patients to prevent it. Overall, recurrence requires vigilant follow-up and individualized management to address the return of disease effectively.
Prostate cancer monitoring involves regular tests and check-ups to track the cancer's status, especially during active surveillance or after treatment.

Imaging tests are medical procedures that create pictures of the inside of the body, used to detect, locate, and evaluate tumors, assess cancer extent, and check for cancer spread. These tests are essential for staging cancer, planning treatment, monitoring tumor response during chemotherapy, and detecting recurrence during surveillance. They are also used to visualize internal structures, guide biopsies, and identify abnormalities such as enlarged lymph nodes, organ involvement, or areas of infection or bleeding.

Imaging tests include a wide range of techniques such as CT scans, MRI, PET scans, FDG-PET/CT, ultrasound, X-rays, mammograms, and bone scans. These modalities are applied across various cancer types, including breast, prostate, colon, rectal, esophageal, liver, kidney, ovarian, thyroid, adrenal, bone, and throat cancers, as well as leukemias like ALL and AML, and lymphomas such as CBCL and NPC. For example, mammograms, ultrasounds, and MRIs are used to visualize breast tissue; CT and MRI are primary methods for colon cancer staging; and ultrasound is used to detect thyroid nodules and cancer.

Imaging tests are interpreted by a radiologist and are used to reveal a tumor’s location, size, and other features, as well as to detect cancer spread to distant sites. In certain cancers, such as early-stage prostate cancer, imaging may not be necessary, but in others, like leukemia, they help detect spread outside the bone marrow to areas such as the brain, lymph nodes, liver, spleen, and skin. Overall, imaging tests are indispensable diagnostic and monitoring tools in oncology, providing detailed visual information that guides clinical decisions across the cancer care continuum.

Imaging refers to a broad range of medical techniques used to create pictures of the inside of the body, including computed tomography (CT) scans, PET/CT scans, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), ultrasound, x-rays, and transvaginal ultrasound. These tests are essential for determining the extent and spread of cancer, which is critical for staging the disease and guiding treatment decisions. Imaging is used across various cancer types: for pancreatic cancer, it helps decide if surgery is an option; for cervical cancer, techniques such as FDG-PET/CT, CT with contrast, and MRI detect recurrence or spread, typically ordered based on symptoms or stage; for prostate cancer, imaging is used alongside PSA tests to evaluate presence and spread, visualizing the prostate and surrounding areas; for lymphoma, it identifies the location, size, and features of the disease; for adrenal tumors, it often detects them incidentally; for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), it assesses spread to lymph nodes and beyond; for bladder cancer, it visualizes the bladder and surrounding areas to stage and plan treatment; for brain tumors and gliomas, MRI and CT scans aid in diagnosis; and for anal cancers (stage II and III), imaging is used for surveillance after treatment, with yearly imaging recommended for three years to monitor for recurrence or further spread. Imaging is performed by specialists such as thoracic radiologists and is a key component of treatment planning and post-treatment monitoring across oncology.

A patient is an individual receiving medical care, diagnosis, testing, or treatment for a wide range of conditions, including various types of cancer (such as basal cell skin cancer, prostate cancer, primary CNS lymphoma, chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), rectal cancer, acute myeloid leukemia (AML), actinic keratoses, colon cancer, cervical cancer, follicular lymphoma (FL), anal cancer, bone cancer, bladder cancer, chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), ovarian cancer, mouth cancer, inflammatory breast cancer, and throat cancer) as well as other medical conditions. The patient may be diagnosed with, at risk for, or being evaluated for these conditions, and may undergo various diagnostic procedures, imaging tests, biopsies, and treatments as part of their care.

Patients are encouraged to be active participants in their own healthcare, including advocating for themselves, asking questions, making shared decisions with their care team, and managing their own health records, treatment side effects, and emotional well-being. They may also be advised to follow recommended exam schedules and to seek support and information about survivorship. The care team, which may include doctors, radiologists, and other specialists, coordinates the patient’s diagnosis, treatment planning, and follow-up care. The patient’s physical, mental, and emotional well-being are considered important throughout the process, and they may experience side effects, recovery processes, or challenges related to their condition and treatment. In some cases, factors such as claustrophobia, allergies, or kidney issues may influence the choice of imaging tests or procedures. Ultimately, the patient is the individual undergoing diagnostic and treatment procedures, with the goal of managing their health and receiving appropriate medical support.

Blood tests are a broad category of diagnostic procedures and laboratory analyses performed on blood samples to assess overall health, evaluate organ function, and detect, diagnose, and monitor various diseases—particularly cancer. These tests are used across a wide range of cancers, including liver, bladder, AML (acute myeloid leukemia), CML (chronic myeloid leukemia), ALL (acute lymphoblastic leukemia), cervical, bone, pancreatic, esophageal, FL (follicular lymphoma), ovarian, stomach, kidney, prostate, colon, adrenal tumors, primary CNS lymphoma, and NPC (nasopharyngeal carcinoma). They are also used in general health checks and to guide treatment planning, with results often included in medical records and binders for patient reference.

Blood tests measure various blood components, such as blood cell counts, blood chemistry, and organ function markers (e.g., liver and kidney function). Common tests include the complete blood count (CBC), comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP), blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine, liver function tests (LFTs), and chemistry profiles. Specific tests may also detect tumor markers or other indicators, such as carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) for colon cancer, CA-125 for ovarian cancer, PSA for prostate cancer, and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), thyroglobulin (Tg), and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies (Tg ab) for monitoring cancer recurrence. Blood tests can also measure hormone levels to detect abnormalities related to adrenal tumors or assess endocrine function.

These tests are essential for establishing the extent of cancer, guiding treatment decisions, and monitoring for recurrence or response to therapy. They are performed by drawing a blood sample through a needle from a vein in the arm. Blood tests are used to detect markers or abnormalities related to cancer, evaluate blood cell counts, and rule out other conditions. They are often ordered as part of initial testing, during chemotherapy, or if recurrence is suspected, and are critical for patients to understand and keep copies of their results.

There’s no single treatment that’s best for everyone. The best treatment for bladder cancer is the treatment that’s best for you. You’ll work with your treatment team to choose which option makes the most sense for you. This choice is based on your cancer stage as well as your overall health and personal preferences. Very often, the best option includes more than one type of therapy. Common treatments for bladder cancer include: Surgery Chemotherapy Immunotherapy Radiation therapy Targeted therapy Surgery, by itself or with other treatments, can be used in many stages of bladder cancer. For less advanced cancer, a minor surgical procedure can be used to remove just the tumor. For more advanced cancer, the entire bladder can be surgically removed. In addition, you may receive chemotherapy or immunotherapy directly into the bladder. For people with metastatic bladder cancer, chemotherapy or immunotherapy is used to treat cancer anywhere in the body. Another treatment option is to join a clinical trial. You’ll also receive treatment for any side effects caused by cancer therapy. Can bladder cancer be cured? Bladder cancer in an early (non-invasive) stage can usually be cured. Treatment for more advanced stage (muscle-invasive) bladder cancer can be complicated but it may still get rid of the cancer. Metastatic bladder cancer is not typically curable, but it is still treatable. And treatments are improving all the time. For most people with bladder cancer, treatment provides a longer and more comfortable life with fewer symptoms. It’s important to know that bladder cancer commonly comes back even after treatment. In fact, bladder cancer is more likely to come back than almost any other kind of cancer. From now on, you and your health care providers will have to keep watching for any sign that the cancer returns. Even so, there’s hope. If the cancer does come back, it can be treated. Many people live with bladder cancer and still have a good quality of life. Plus, new and improved ways to detect and treat bladder cancer are helping people live longer and with fewer side effects than ever before. Experts predict that treatment will improve rapidly over the next few years, with better results for all stages of bladder cancer. As a result of clinical trials, many new treatments for bladder cancer have been approved or are on the horizon. As always, you can try to join a clinical trial at almost any point during cancer care. Key points Bladder cancer happens when abnormal cells in the inner layer of the bladder grow out of control. Cancer of the urothelium can start in these areas instead of the bladder, although it’s less common. Other (non-urothelial) types of bladder cancer are much less common. These include squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, and small cell carcinoma. How is bladder cancer found? Bladder cancer is usually found when a person has symptoms. A symptom is a problem or feeling that may signal a disease or condition. The most common symptom of bladder cancer, and the one that usually appears first, is having blood in your urine (hematuria). How does blood get into urine? Bladder tumors are likely to release a little blood, which mixes with the urine in your bladder. The blood may turn your urine pink or bright red. Or, if there isn’t enough blood to be visible, your urine may look normal. But your clinical team can still detect blood by looking at a sample of the urine under a microscope. Blood in the urine can be caused by many other things besides bladder cancer. The most common cause is an infection in the urinary tract. So anyone with blood in their urine should see a health care provider to get their urine tested. Other symptoms of bladder cancer include: Frequent urination Urgency to urinate Painful urination Back pain Not every person with bladder cancer will have all these symptoms. Some people will have no symptoms. A person with one or more of these symptoms should visit a doctor or other health care provider who can recommend different tests. These tests are used to make a diagnosis. (A diagnosis means identifying an illness by using tests.) What does aggressive mean? Bladder cancer When health care professionals describe cancer as aggressive, they mean the cancer is likely to grow or spread more quickly than average. Bladder cancer is often described by how far it has spread into the muscle layer of the bladder. Here, the cancer tumor has grown through the inner lining (urothelial layer) and invaded the muscle layer in the bladder wall. This type of cancer is known as muscleinvasive bladder cancer. Aggressive can also be used to describe a treatment that’s stronger or more intense than other treatment options. Some people reading this book may have already been tested and given a diagnosis of bladder cancer. Many people wonder why they got cancer. Cancer experts don’t know exactly what causes bladder cells to grow out of control. What they do know is that bladder cancer and other cancers start with abnormal changes (mutations) in the genes of cells. Genes are tiny parts of a cell that carry the instructions for how cells behave. These instructions also control how new cells are made. Sometimes, mutations can mix up these instructions. This can turn normal cells into cancer cells. In most people with bladder cancer, these mutations aren’t passed down in families (hereditary mutation). They happen on their own and only in cancer cells. Still, you may have a higher risk for bladder cancer if another family member also had bladder cancer. In rare cases, mutations in these genes can be passed down in families. This results in an increased risk of getting bladder cancer. A risk factor is something that increases your chance of developing a disease. Risk factors don’t necessarily cause bladder cancer. Also, people with an inherited condition called Lynch syndrome have a greater risk of cancer in the urinary tract, including bladder cancer. Chemical exposure – Some chemicals used in dyes, rubber, leather, printing materials, textiles, and paint products have been linked to an increased risk for bladder cancer. Common areas of metastatic bladder cancer include the lymph nodes, bones, lungs, liver, and the inner wall of the abdomen. (Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped glands that transport a fluid called lymph and help fight infection. Lymph nodes are found around the urinary tract and all over the body.) A biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically under a microscope, to diagnose cancer and determine its characteristics. It is a key diagnostic tool used to confirm the presence of cancer cells, identify the specific type and histology of a tumor, and guide treatment decisions. Biopsies are performed on various organs and tissues, including the prostate, breast, lung, liver, brain (e.g., primary CNS lymphoma), ovary, thyroid, lymph nodes, bone, skin, bladder, kidney, esophagus, pancreas, adrenal gland, anal canal, and bone marrow, among others.

The procedure is often guided by imaging techniques such as ultrasound, CT, MRI, or EUS, or performed during scoping procedures like cystoscopy. Biopsies may be conducted after abnormal screening results, when a tumor is detected, or when follow-up examinations indicate growth or spread of cancer. In some cases, a biopsy is performed before starting chemotherapy or steroid therapy to avoid altering the appearance of cells, and it is sometimes combined with HPV testing or biomarker analysis to guide targeted therapy.

There are several types of biopsies, including fine-needle aspiration (FNA), fine-needle biopsy (FNB), core needle biopsy (CNB), incisional biopsy, excisional biopsy, stereotactic biopsy, and skin biopsy. The choice of biopsy type depends on the location and nature of the suspected cancer. For example, excisional biopsy is preferred for Hodgkin lymphoma, while stereotactic biopsy is standard for primary CNS lymphoma. Biopsy is an invasive procedure and may carry risks such as infection, bleeding, and pain, particularly in procedures like prostate biopsy, which is typically performed by a urologist.

Once the tissue or fluid sample is removed, it is sent to a pathologist, who examines it for cancer cells and writes a pathology report. The results of a biopsy are crucial for confirming a cancer diagnosis, determining tumor characteristics such as Gleason patterns and scores (in prostate cancer), hormone and HER2 receptor status (in breast cancer), and molecular features, and for staging the cancer. Biopsy results also influence treatment plans, and patients are encouraged to understand and keep copies of their pathology reports. In some cases, a biopsy may be the only way to confirm a cancer diagnosis, and it is essential for guiding appropriate and timely treatment.

DOCTOR is a healthcare professional and provider who plays a central role in diagnosing, treating, and managing a wide range of medical conditions, particularly cancers and other serious diseases. They perform physical exams, ask about personal and family health history, and order or interpret diagnostic tests such as imaging (MRIs, CT scans), blood tests, biopsies, and scoping procedures (e.g., laryngoscopy, panendoscopy, polypectomy). Doctors discuss test results with patients, guide treatment decisions, and plan next steps in care, including recommending therapies such as systemic regimens, surgery, or procedures like excision, cone biopsy, or hysterectomy. They also provide guidance on lifestyle factors (exercise, diet, aspirin use, bone density monitoring, smoking cessation), fertility and pregnancy planning, birth control options, and managing side effects. In specific contexts, doctors specialize in conditions such as basal cell skin cancer, bladder cancer, bone cancer, cervical cancer, prostate cancer, anal cancer, ovarian cancer, and ALL, and may conduct full skin exams, pelvic exams, digital rectal exams, or monitor for recurrence or spread. They may also discuss germline testing or refer patients to genetic counselors for inherited cancer risk assessment, and they coordinate with radiologists and other specialists to ensure comprehensive care.

Recurrence, also known as relapse, refers to the return of cancer after a period of treatment or remission. This phenomenon is common across various cancer types, including bladder, breast, cervical, ovarian, prostate, basal cell skin, primary CNS lymphoma, and head and neck cancers. Recurrence can manifest locally (at the original site), regionally (in nearby lymph nodes), or at distant sites in the body, depending on the cancer type.

For bladder cancer, recurrence is a frequent occurrence that necessitates ongoing monitoring and regular follow-up testing. In breast cancer, recurrence may be local or distant. Cervical cancer recurrence can occur locally, regionally, or at distant sites, and often requires imaging, exploratory surgery, and biomarker testing to guide further treatment. Ovarian cancer recurrence also demands further management and monitoring. Prostate cancer recurrence can be detected through imaging tests such as MRI or PSMA-PET scans, and is a key factor in risk assessment. Basal cell skin cancer recurrence involves the cancer returning to the original area or spreading to lymph nodes or distant parts of the body, indicating a need for continued surveillance.

Monitoring for recurrence typically involves imaging tests like MRI, PSMA-PET, and other surveillance methods, including regular physical exams and blood tests. In some cases, such as higher-risk thyroid cancer, TSH suppression is used as a monitoring strategy. Symptoms of recurrence can vary but may include pelvic pain, bloating, and fatigue, particularly in gynecologic cancers.

Treatment for recurrence depends on the location and extent of the disease and may involve additional therapies such as surgery, radiation therapy, radioactive iodine (RAI), or adjustments to chemotherapy regimens. Biomarker testing is often employed to guide treatment decisions. Certain cancer subtypes and features can increase the risk of recurrence, and radiation therapy may be used in high-risk patients to prevent it. Overall, recurrence requires vigilant follow-up and individualized management to address the return of disease effectively.

Family history is a comprehensive record of the health conditions and diseases—such as cancer, heart disease, and diabetes—that have occurred in a patient's blood relatives. It is a critical tool used by healthcare providers to assess an individual's inherited or genetic risk for a wide range of illnesses, including various types of cancer and other chronic conditions. The information gathered typically includes the specific diseases present in relatives, the nature of the biological relationship, and the age at which these conditions were diagnosed.

This assessment is particularly important in oncology, where a family history of certain cancers can significantly elevate an individual's risk. For example, having a close relative with prostate cancer increases the chance of developing the disease, and a family history of related cancers (such as breast, ovarian, colon, or pancreatic) also raises this risk. Similarly, a family history of thyroid cancer or related syndromes increases the likelihood of developing thyroid cancer. In the context of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), relatives of affected individuals are 7 to 8 times more likely to develop the disease, and a family history of leukemia can influence treatment decisions and prompt testing for leukemia predisposition syndromes. Family history is also a recognized risk factor for bladder cancer, and it is used to assess hereditary risk for ovarian and stomach cancers. In cases of acute myeloid leukemia (AML), understanding family history is vital for identifying potential hereditary factors.

Beyond risk assessment, family history plays a crucial role in guiding clinical care. It informs genetic testing recommendations, such as germline testing when cancer occurrences in relatives indicate an inherited risk, and helps in diagnosing conditions like basal cell skin cancer. While some cancers, such as head and neck cancers, are not typically inherited, family history is still collected to rule out any rare genetic predispositions. Ultimately, this information is used to create personalized screening plans, guide treatment decisions, and determine whether further genetic evaluation is necessary for the patient and their family members.

The bladder is a hollow, muscular organ located in the pelvis that stores urine before it is released from the body. In adults, it has a capacity of up to 2 cups. It is part of the urinary tract and is lined with urothelial cells. The bladder is situated near the prostate in males (which surrounds the urethra just beneath the bladder) and near the cervix in females. It is also adjacent to the seminal vesicles.

The bladder is the primary site where bladder cancer originates. It is examined for signs of cancer or cancer spread using procedures such as cystoscopy and various imaging tests. In the context of cancer treatment, the bladder may be targeted by intravesical chemotherapy (delivered directly into its interior) or radiation therapy aimed at the tumor area. An MRI can be used to get a more detailed view of the cancer within the prostate. It’s also used to see if cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes or to the bones in your pelvis. MRI scans can also help to plan treatment, and may be used after treatment to check whether the cancer has come back (recurrence). An appointment for an MRI scan can take 1 to 2 hours, including 30 to 60 minutes of actual scanning time. You’ll need to remain as motionless as possible during each scan. You may be positioned with pillows or bolsters to help you keep still. Because an MRI uses magnets, you can’t bring any metal objects (such as jewelry, phones, wristwatches, or belts with metal buckles) into the imaging room. CT scan A computed tomography (CT or CAT) scan uses x-rays and computer technology to take pictures of the inside of the body. CT takes many x-rays of the same body part from different angles. The computer combines all the x-ray pictures to make a single detailed image. A CT scan is usually completed in less than 30 minutes. PET scan A positron emission tomography (PET) scan highlights cells in your body that may be cancerous. You may have a PET scan after you’ve been diagnosed to determine the extent of your cancer or to see if it has metastasized. PET imaging can also show how well treatment is working. A PET scan requires injecting a radioactive substance called a tracer into your bloodstream. It takes about an hour for the tracer to circulate throughout your body. The tracer targets your cancer cells, which show up as bright spots on the scan. Afterward, the radiotracer is passed out of your body in your urine. A PET scan appointment can take 1 to 2 hours, including about 30 minutes of actual scanning time. Because PET uses a different imaging method, it’s often combined with other types of imaging, such as CT or MRI, to provide an even more PET imaging A positron emission tomography (PET) scan highlights cells in your body that may be cancerous. A PET scan can determine the extent of your cancer or see if it has metastasized. PET imaging can also show how well treatment is working. detailed image. This combined method is called a PET/CT or PET/MRI scan. PSMA-PET PET scans use different types of tracers. The most common tracer in prostate cancer locates a protein called prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) on the surface of prostate cancer cells. Prostate cancer cells can make a lot of PSMA, so doctors developed tracers that target this specific protein. Not everyone with prostate cancer will need a PSMA-PET scan. It’s mostly used to monitor prostate cancer for recurrence. It’s also used to determine whether targeted therapy can treat certain cases of metastatic prostate cancer. Prognostic stage also includes the assumption that you are treated with the standard-of-care approaches. Prognostic stages are divided into clinical and pathologic. Often, not all information is available at the initial evaluation. More information can be gathered as treatment begins. Doctors may explain your cancer stage in different ways than described next. Information gathered during staging: The extent (size) of the tumor (T): How large is the cancer? Has it grown into nearby areas? The spread to nearby lymph nodes (N): Has the cancer spread to nearby lymph nodes? If so, how many? Where? In this system, the letters T, N, and M describe different areas of cancer growth. Based on cancer test results, your doctor will assign a score or number to each letter. Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped glands distributed throughout the body, including the neck, armpits, groin, pelvis, near the rectum, stomach, thyroid, bladder, and colon. They are part of the lymphatic and immune systems, containing immune cells such as lymphocytes, and function to filter lymph fluid, remove foreign particles, germs, and harmful substances, and help fight infection and disease. There are over 300 lymph nodes in the head and neck alone.

Lymph nodes play a critical role in the body’s immune response and are a primary site where many cancers—such as breast, prostate, lung, colorectal, bladder, cervical, ovarian, pancreatic, kidney, thyroid, anal, stomach, esophageal, skin (including basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma), and head and neck cancers—may spread. Their involvement is a key factor in cancer staging (e.g., the N score in the TNM system) and prognosis, and they are often examined during physical exams for enlargement, which may indicate infection or cancer spread.

Lymph nodes can be assessed through imaging tests such as MRI, CT, FDG-PET/CT, ultrasound, PSMA/PET, and EUS, and may be biopsied (including sentinel or axillary lymph node biopsy) or removed during surgery (e.g., colectomy, neck dissection, or transabdominal surgery) to determine whether cancer has spread. Enlarged lymph nodes may also result from the buildup of cancerous cells, as seen in conditions like chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), follicular lymphoma, B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma, and mediastinal gray zone lymphoma. In some cancers, such as hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), spread to nearby lymph nodes is uncommon.

Lymph nodes are also involved in defining specific cancer stages, such as stage 3C cervical cancer (involvement of pelvic or para-aortic nodes) and stage 3 bladder cancer (nodes near the bladder). In lymphomas, cancer originating in lymph nodes can weaken the immune system, and involvement outside the nodes is termed extranodal disease. Overall, lymph nodes are essential immune organs whose status is crucial in diagnosing, staging, and treating many diseases, particularly cancers.

Prostate cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ. This condition can manifest in two primary forms: early-stage (localized), where the cancer remains confined within the prostate, and advanced-stage (metastatic), where it spreads to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

Metastasis is the process by which cancer cells spread from the primary tumor (the original site of cancer) to other parts of the body, forming secondary tumors. This spread can occur through the blood or lymphatic system, allowing cancer cells to travel to nearby lymph nodes (local metastasis) or to distant organs and tissues (distant metastasis), such as the bones, liver, lungs, or other internal organs. The specific sites of metastasis can vary depending on the type of primary cancer; for example, prostate cancer commonly spreads to lymph nodes and bones, while colon cancer may spread to the liver or lungs, and kidney cancer can lead to metastatic tumors outside the kidney. Metastasis is a key indicator of advanced-stage cancer, often defining stage 4 disease (e.g., stage 4B cervical cancer), and is a critical component of cancer staging systems, such as the TNM system, where the "M" category indicates whether metastasis has occurred. In some cancers, such as basal cell skin cancer, metastasis is rare but possible, especially in advanced cases, while in very high-risk cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), it is a recognized risk. To confirm the presence of metastatic cancer, a biopsy of the metastatic site may be required, with the type of biopsy depending on the location of the spread. Imaging techniques are also used to detect metastasis, particularly in cases like prostate cancer. Overall, metastasis signifies the spread of cancer from its original location to other body areas, such as lymph nodes or distant organs, and is a fundamental factor in determining prognosis and guiding treatment decisions.

entities.description:
Prostate cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ. This condition can manifest in two primary forms: early-stage (localized), where the cancer remains confined within the prostate, and advanced-stage (metastatic), where it spreads to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

Targeted therapy is a form of cancer treatment that uses drugs or other substances to precisely identify and attack specific molecules, genetic mutations, or abnormal proteins involved in the growth, progression, and spread of cancer cells. It is a type of systemic therapy, meaning it travels throughout the body, and is designed to focus on unique or specific features of cancer cells, thereby minimizing damage to normal, healthy cells compared to traditional chemotherapy.

This approach is used across a wide range of cancers, including acute myeloid leukemia (AML), cervical cancer, prostate cancer, bladder cancer, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, squamous cell skin cancer, and breast cancer (such as HER2-positive cases). It is often guided by biomarker testing or specific genetic profiling, such as identifying mutations like PIK3CA, the BCR::ABL protein, or markers like PSMA. Examples of targeted therapy drugs include PARP inhibitors, Gemtuzumab ozogamicin, Gilteritinib, quizartinib, midostaurin, sorafenib, ivosidenib, bevacizumab, mirvetuximab soravtansine-gynx, tisotumab vedotin, and EGFR inhibitors.

Targeted therapy may be used in various scenarios, including for cancers that have returned, metastasized, or are resistant to other treatments, such as radioactive iodine (RAI) therapy for thyroid cancer. It can be administered alone or in combination with other treatments like chemotherapy. While it can be highly effective, it may also have side effects, which can include allergic reactions, fatigue, low platelet counts, body aches, rash, high blood pressure, and abnormal bleeding. Context: "Tumor staging Tumors come in different shapes and sizes. So it’s not easy to compare one tumor to another. To solve this problem, cancer experts created the tumor, node, metastasis (TNM) system to describe any tumor. It’s based on the results of your imaging scans, biopsies, and blood tests. In this system, the letters T, N, and M stand for different areas of cancer growth: T (tumor) – Describes the size of the main (primary) tumor and if it has grown outside the prostate N (node) – Identifies whether cancer has spread to lymph nodes M (metastasis) – Indicates if cancer has spread (metastasized) to parts of the body outside of the pelvis Your provider will assign a number to each letter, based on your test results.
